issues.title: Why GTA 6 is the year's biggest campaign for a brand that refuses to sell ad space
issues.summary: Rockstar won't take a penny for product placement, yet half the world's brands are currently trying to look like Vice City. On the eve of launch, here's why I think GTA 6 matters to any creative profe...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Rockstar won't take a penny for product placement, yet half the world's brands are currently trying to look like Vice City. On the eve of launch, here's why I think GTA 6 matters to any creative professional.

I'm an enthusiastic gamer. But I skipped Grand Theft Auto V entirely. I just couldn't join the 230 million people who've snapped up a copy since it came out 13 years ago, because I couldn't play as a woman.

Tomorrow, that changes. GTA 6 unlocks at midnight. One of the lead characters, Lucia Caminos, will be waiting for me. And I've cleared my diary for the next week.

If you don't game, you might think that's a bit pathetic. Fair enough. But if you're an art director, illustrator or marketer who's seen those pink-and-orange sunsets flood your feeds lately and wondered what all the fuss is about – it's only a video game, surely? Well, no it isn't. Not really.

Not to be dramatic, GTA 6 marks one of the biggest cultural moments in a century. And that's hugely rewarding, especially for someone who grew up in an era when we still did things together.

A collective phenomenon

Alas, there isn't much left that everyone experiences together, all at once. We stream different shows on different nights and scroll different feeds. It's not like the good old days when we'd wait for our favourite programmes on one of four TV channels or get the bus to Hanley's Fezzy Park to see the latest blockbuster (and hope we bumped into Mark from the year above). GTA is one of the few exceptions. It's a single date that tens of millions of people have been anticipating for years.

The numbers are daft, too. The second trailer was watched 475 million times in a day. When Rockstar premiered a 27-minute preview on Netflix in August, it drew 31.1 million views in four days and topped the film chart in 87 of the 93 countries Netflix tracks. Strauss Zelnick, chief executive of Rockstar's parent company Take-Two, described that premiere as "one of the hors d'oeuvres". Now we're all hungry for the main course.

Analysts estimate 15.88 million digital pre-orders, worth around $1.54bn. So yeah, it's big. But the numbers aren't why I think creatives should be sitting up and paying attention.

Not for sale

As you can imagine, the most wanted media space on the planet right now is a billboard inside Vice City. Yet you can't buy it.

Zelnick has ruled out product placement and brand deals altogether, on the grounds that "all the brands are made up". So you'll not spot any real fizzy drinks or real trainers. Just the usual Patriot Beer, Sessanta Nove and hundreds of other parodies written and designed entirely in-house.

Naturally, the brands have done their thing anyway. Hyundai, BMW and Burger King are among those dressing their social posts in GTA's sunset palette. Perhaps they're hoping to enjoy some of that Vice City glow, too.

Paint, print and fashion

I've just spent a week in Miami Beach, and it was fun to walk around the city GTA 6 is based on. I spotted the ads for the game everywhere. I especially loved seeing street kiosks carrying ads for the game's fake brands, double entendres and all. A clever bit of marketing, and my friends at Creative Bloq agree.

In Williamsburg, Brooklyn, there's a vast mural of Jason and Lucia, hand-painted by Colossal Media – the New York sign painters who've worked with Rockstar since San Andreas in 2004.

Then there's the press. The first on-record interviews about the game didn't go to a gaming site – they went to Dazed, which put Jason and Lucia on the cover of its autumn 'New Idols' issue and dressed them in Vice City's fictional fashion labels. Just brilliant.

And in Wynwood, Miami's street art district, 10 new murals have gone up from artists including FAILE, Lady AIKO, Queen Andrea and DENIAL, alongside a deal that gives Miami-Dade residents free entry to the Wynwood Walls Museum through 2028. Rockstar says more than 50 real street artists painted the walls inside the game, too. And no generative AI was used.

What's in it for the rest of us?

OK, so most of us creatives will never have the luxury of a billion-dollar budget or 13 years for a project. But take away that scale and you're left with something pretty old-fashioned.

Rockstar just concentrated on building its virtual Vice City and everything you might find in it, from parody brands and radio stations to murals made especially for the game. When you think about it, the advertising came naturally. The campaign existed before anything appeared in the real world.

It also said very little. There was a year of silence between trailers, and the studio has barely given an interview. There's a lot of mystery around it all, and that's done Rockstar no harm.

And it even said no to the brand deals and easy money. It's quite impressive to see this kind of restraint at play. But Rockstar can afford to hold back. Analysts at Newzoo estimate the game could make between $3.3bn and $5.2bn in its first week alone. Does it really need anything more than that? Particularly with Take-Two forecasting record sales of more than $8bn (around £6bn) for its financial year?

And yes, I'm here for the violence

I've got to admit: this is still Grand Theft Auto. It's violent and crude, and the conversation around it remains overwhelmingly male. None of which is putting me off.

I'm a girl who loves the scene in 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood' when Brad Pitt throws a can of dog food into the face of an intruder. I roared "yessss" at the screen. I enjoy a bit of violent vengeance, yet I know the difference between reality and fun.

So does my nephew, who's now old enough to play it too. (I'd better get practising my shooting skills.) That might be the part I'm looking forward to the most: being part of something with family and friends. Comparing notes and being social rather than passively watching telly (which I find boring).

Can GTA 6 live up to all the hype? Will it be worth the 13-year wait for a female protagonist? Given Rockstar's track record, I know it will.

Most importantly, I love how a game got the whole world's attention at the same time, and it did it with a bit of paint, parody and a refusal to sell out. That alone is worth a week off work, sitting in my pyjamas and enjoying the ride. Lucia and I have plans. See you on the other side.

issues.title: 'It's going to be scary': a week on from Adobe MAX 2026, creatives get honest about the future
issues.summary: I left this year's Adobe MAX Sneaks feeling a bit wary. So I asked creatives what scares them most about their work, listened to what two of Adobe's most senior people had to say, and ended up facing...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
I left this year's Adobe MAX Sneaks feeling a bit wary. So I asked creatives what scares them most about their work, listened to what two of Adobe's most senior people had to say, and ended up facing a few of my own fears.

If you're familiar with Adobe's Sneaks, you'll know they've earned legendary status at Adobe MAX over the years. It's an hour or two when the people who build the experimental tools get up and show them off to a live audience, livestreamed to millions of creatives worldwide. A nerve-racking experience, I'm sure... Not just because the whole world is watching, but because anything could go wrong.

Usually, there are loud whoops and almost cult-like, frenzied excitement as Adobe proudly reveals its latest innovations. Not so much this year, from where I was sitting, or indeed the last. Certainly not as much since Adobe started to introduce AI into its suite; maybe the audience was just too stunned to applaud.

For more than a decade, I watched from my desk in Manchester in the middle of the night, scribbling down notes for readers who wanted to know what was coming next. How their working lives were about to get easier thanks to the software they'd spent ages learning. This year, I was right there in the room in Miami Beach, as an editor, sitting with the other British journalists. Terry Crews was hosting, dressed head to toe in a bright pink suit with shiny blue shoes and pink socks. And much like anyone who watched, I'm still processing it.

So what did Sneaks show us?

The tools come straight out of Adobe Labs, and none of them is guaranteed to ship, although some do. And yeah, AI played a leading role. Of course it did. The future is here.

As always, I'm pretty nuanced about these things. It's not so black-and-white. If Adobe can empower creatives to skip the mundane stuff and focus on their creativity, then brilliant. If it can open the playing field to those who previously didn't have the means to create, then I'm all for it. The computer, after all, opened the gates to so many more people back in the 1990s, and the internet welcomed even more.

But there are multiple fine lines. Where AI might be useful in one corner, it feels unwelcome in another.

Ten projects took to the stage. Some were very much welcome, and those were the ones that got the whoops. Project Rinse Repeat copies edits you've made in one area of an image to another, while keeping everything editable in Photoshop.

Project Link Up lets you drag design elements into a scene and sit back and watch their perspective, scale and style adapt to fit, landing as editable vector artwork. Project Deep Brush, my personal favourite, understands an image's shape, colour and lighting, so you can quite literally paint light into a scene. All clever, time-saving stuff.

Others were not so welcome. Project Screen Test lets you build a fictional character's look, voice and personality, and then chat to them. I mean, it was incredible, sure. But is it really necessary? Project Live Set changes a subject, a set or a camera move while the video is still playing.

Project Sight Span turns a single image into a 3D-style space that feels like you can step into it and walk around, framing shots that were never taken in real life. And then Project Sound Bender lets you describe a sound and pick it clean out of a finished mix. Mind-blowing, but I'm not sure the audience was happy.

As I sat there, looking around at my startled fellow attendees, I finally realised how fast things are moving. Casting, set design, location scouting, sound editing... whole corners of the industry flashed past in a few minutes each. I've been using AI tools for three or four years now. I'm an adopter, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But sitting there in that big conference hall, I felt a bit sick rather than excited.

So, still in Miami, I did what I always do in these situations. I asked you.

What keeps you up at night

I posted a simple question on LinkedIn: what are you most scared of in your work right now? More than a dozen replied, and their thoughts offered some brilliant insight.

For some, yes, the fear is real. "I used to have three to five projects monthly, and this year I had three to five in the year," says illustrator and lettering artist Ana Moreno Chávez. Tom Grattan, managing director and co-owner of consultancy EXP, has been meeting graduates who see a bleak future while watching "an Instagram feed of Adobe MAX attendees celebrating what feels like an accelerating decline of an industry".

Then there's what clients now expect. "I'm not afraid of the tools," says motion designer Oleksandr Merkulov. "I'm worried about clients getting used to 'fast and fine' and losing patience for that one extra round that makes the work 'good'." Designers Kieron Lewis and Bijesh Amatya see it too: people reaching for AI, as Kieron puts it, like "a takeaway because it's quicker and more convenient".

Elsewhere, others raised concerns about what we might lose if things get easy. "When the first attempt already looks finished, we lose the friction that turns a good idea into a great one," says Isabella Wordsworth, a designer at D&P in London. "Experimentation is becoming a luxury... It sits at the core of our industry." Francesca Oddenino, co-founder of Vicine, says her best work "is always born out of discomfort". Web developer Tom Harrison feels "very little pride making things this way".

Of course, juniors kept coming up. They're "being replaced by AI, but who do they train to become seniors?" asks brand designer Sophie O'Connor. A senior creative at a fast-growing start-up, who asked to remain anonymous, told me everyone at her company uses AI, and she misses the grunt work. "That's where I cut my teeth," she says, and she's scared for newcomers who won't get it. And she can't say any of this publicly. "I feel ashamed in a way, using it so much."

And then there's the even bigger elephant. "I'm scared of jumping on the 'bandwagon' and playing my role in the demise of my own role. And at the same time shunning AI and playing my role in the demise of my own role," says UX and UI designer Andrew Areoff.

Designer Bart Fish was the most forthright: "I am very concerned about how creatives are embracing this technology, even as it steals from them and threatens to replace them. I'm concerned that creatives think adoption will provide job security, even as they train the models and are asked to create systems intended to displace them."

Putting all this to Adobe

As it happens, I got the chance to sit down with two of Adobe's most senior people at MAX the day before Sneaks, and many of these same fears were swimming around my head. In fairness, much of what you told me you're scared of isn't Adobe's doing alone. And naturally, it's their job to be optimistic. But neither brushed my worries aside, which I really appreciated.

Karen Robinson is Adobe's vice president and associate general counsel, and she spends much of her time talking to lawmakers in the UK, EU, US and Australia. I asked whether the backlash from creatives in 2024, when the government floated its opt-out proposal for AI training, was justified. "I mean, yes, of course it was," she says. "You have people who are worried about what their livelihood is going to be like."

But two years on, she believes there's a reason for "some level of confidence". Artists are still earning a living, she argues, and "the sky did not fall". (Ana, with her three to five projects a year, might disagree.)

What was really interesting was her view that the fear itself has changed. Because what Adobe is hearing from creatives, she explains, is "candidly now less about the training and more about the output, because ultimately... AI-generated output is the thing that will compete directly with artists and creatives". She goes on: "And so what we're hearing is: we don't want to be pushed out of a market that our own art has created. So we want to talk about style protection. If I am an artist and I have a demonstrable style, I should be able to protect that." Right now, she says, you can't.

It's why she reckons licensing alone won't save any of us. She tells me about asking an illustrator Adobe works with how much licensing money would make it acceptable to be pushed out of the market by AI copies of her style. The answer? There isn't enough. "They want to control their art... If you're an artist and you make a very particular type of art, and now somebody comes, knocks off your style and starts putting it on aprons and oven mitts, that's not what you want," she says. "And so that requires protection on the output side that does not currently exist."

Essentially, we're in the Wild West again. The geeky lawyer in her (her words) also offers some perspective. When cameras arrived, photographs weren't eligible for copyright, because the machine supposedly did all the work. It took a series of court cases to recognise that the photographer (the human) was making creative decisions about subject, lighting and angle. And plenty of painters never picked up a camera at all. There will always be room, she says, for artists who don't want AI anywhere near their work.

She was candid about trust, too. The row over Adobe's terms of use in 2024 taught the company it had to communicate better. "In a time of uncertainty, companies aren't going to get the benefit of the doubt," she says. "And I don't mean that as a negative... It is our responsibility to clearly articulate what we're doing."

Eric Snowden, senior vice president of Adobe Design, is another optimist. He's also been a retoucher for 20 years, and he doesn't believe Photoshop is going anywhere. How do I know? I asked him outright with a cheeky chuckle: if AI can do pretty much anything, will anyone still need Adobe's tools? Will we even be using Photoshop in three years? "When I generate an image, I'm still editing every single one in Photoshop," he says. "I'm doing high-end retouching, I'm doing frequency separation, I'm doing all these things, like traditional Photoshop, and you'd be surprised at how much they still need that."

Without that human precision? "They come out looking good, and I think especially to an untrained eye they look good. But at the level our customers care about the details of these images, they do not look good enough."

He's not pretending these next few years will be painless, though. "Things are going to change. It's going to be scary... But there are some really bright spots, where we're also incredibly empowered to do things we've never been able to do before," he says. "Lean into that."

Scared? Yes. And still here

So, should we be scared? I think we're in a period of adjustment. A lull phase. A temporary era of people struggling, perhaps, before more work comes out of this revolution, not less.

But perhaps I'm deluded. Maybe I'm hoping optimism will overcome my fear. Fear for the juniors coming up behind us. Fear for my own career. And fear for the industry I've spent nearly two decades championing.

It's like being on a train with a party on board. Everyone's enjoying the champagne and the party food, knowing the track might run off into a deep chasm at any point. But we can't get off.

Much like you study the faces of the cabin crew on a bumpy, final descent, I realise I'd been studying Adobe's own people, looking for reassurance. Are we going to be OK? I kept thinking. What I got was honesty. Karen didn't tell me the fear was unjustified. And Eric didn't tell me it would be fine. "It's going to be scary," he said, with a smile. And then he told me to lean into it.

issues.title: Meet the strange and wonderful creatures of María Valeria Pazos' Anima Mundi
issues.summary: From crowned horses to fish covered in eyes, the Mexican artist brings together philosophy, poetry and generative technology to create a fantastical world. Gold leaf glows across María Valeria Pazos's...
issues.author: Ayla Angelos
issues.content_html:
From crowned horses to fish covered in eyes, the Mexican artist brings together philosophy, poetry and generative technology to create a fantastical world.

Gold leaf glows across María Valeria Pazos's images like candlelight on a chapel wall; fish drift through moonlight skies speckled with tiny eyes; a horse carries a procession of sun-faced saints on its back; and spiky-haired figures in dotted dresses stand among hens and herons. Her pieces nod to folk art, illuminated manuscripts and the hushed black-and-white photography of handmade sculpture – creating a world where every object seems to be watching you.

María lives in Mexico City and works between philosophy, poetry, visual art, sensory theatre, generative technology and imagination. "From a very young age, the imagination was a territory where I could find possibilities different from those my body was experiencing," she says. "Imagination allowed me to believe that reality could be otherwise, that there were other ways of inhabiting the world. And that possibility gave me hope."

For more than 10 years she devoted herself to sensory theatre, building rooms where "scents, textures, sounds and imagination could reorganise our perception of reality." She studied philosophy at UNAM and is now completing a PhD in Philosophy of Science on embodied imagination.

The theatre years still shape how her pictures feel, so much so that she wants an image to suggest a "temperature, a scent, a texture or a bodily sensation" – and you can certainly sense it in the warm honey of the gold, the cool blue of patterned fish and the frosty paper wings of a fox balanced on stilt-thin legs.

When it's not the theatre and sensory experiences driving her work, María will turn to language – in which a poem becomes a scene, a scene then becomes a character. A character grows into a small audiovisual story. She uses image and video generation models as one instrument among several others, alongside drawings, collages, and material references, and these tools have allowed her to realise universes she has carried in notebooks and poems for more than 25 years. "Artificial intelligence expands my possibilities for experimentation, while aesthetic decisions emerge from a continuous relationship between my imagination, my sensibility and the materials I work with."

Anima Mundi, her ever-growing project, runs on a method borrowed from the Surrealists. "Sometimes I take the head of one creature, the body of another, the limbs of an animal, the texture of a flower or the atmosphere of a dream," she says. "I mix and transform them, then observe what happens." She calls it a visual cut-up, and each new creature seems to belong to a family tree – a bird-legged fish, a lion-faced figure and a crowned horse all share the same eyes and the same dotted skin, for instance.

Gold has also become a recurring character for María, arriving after she found a text she wrote 15 years ago, full of golden beings, golden threads, and a woman immersed in a golden sea. "I had no conscious memory of writing these images, yet somehow, my unconscious had led me back to them," she says. "It fascinates me how certain images continue to live within us, quietly finding their way back into our creative worlds."

Of how she hopes her audience responds to her work, María has a wish – that they, too, can meet their own dreams. "I often imagine an image as a kind of Big Bang, an origami. Or a strand of DNA," she says. "I like to think that each image contains a sleeping universe, waiting for someone to encounter it and allow it to unfold within them."

issues.title: Elenor Kopka on turning her strange, squiggly animations into ceramic sculptures
issues.summary: The German artist's films are full of peculiar moments, humour and unexpected transformations. How do you turn something that's constantly moving into something that doesn't move at all? This is a que...
issues.author: Ayla Angelos
issues.content_html:
The German artist's films are full of peculiar moments, humour and unexpected transformations.

How do you turn something that's constantly moving into something that doesn't move at all? This is a question German artist Elenor Kopka has been exploring lately, as she takes the strange, shifting forms from her hand-drawn animations and turns them into ceramic sculptures.

The process involves making an object in 3D, animating it, then picking out individual frames to recreate in clay, leaving a series of frozen moments from something that was once wriggling about on screen. It's a curious process, and one that feels perfectly suited to Elenor's work, which is filled with eccentric shapes, unexpected transformations, and a nice dose of humour that makes you wonder what on earth will happen next.

Based in Lyon, France, Elenor originally studied illustration and printmaking, although she had always wanted to work with music and installations. Eventually, she taught herself how to animate her drawings and, as she puts it, "just ran with it". In 2025, she completed an apprenticeship in ceramics, opening up a whole new way of experimenting with the relationship between movement and form. "I find the juxtaposition between animation and sculpture fascinating: animation captures movement with the confines of a screen or projection, while sculpture exists in the physical world but remains frozen in a particular position," she explains. "I love exploring the relation between the two."

Taking a single frame from an animation and giving it a life of its own is a perfectly apt process for Elenor, whose films are so concerned with the strange things that can happen to a shape over time. And while turning those frames into physical objects requires plenty of planning, her approach to animation itself is surprisingly loose. "When working with animation, I love starting without a storyboard whenever I can," she says. "I prefer moving from one shot to the next and seeing where it takes me. My films are drawn frame by frame, so working without a plan can be a little dangerous – sometimes I end up animating things that I later have to cut entirely. But I do it anyway."

One great example is MOLD, a short film she made in 2025, for which she also composed the music. Created as a stream-of-consciousness animation, it began shortly before she became pregnant, something she now suspects found its way into the work without her realising it at the time. "Looking back, I think I subconsciously challenged a lot of what I was feeling at the time into it: the craziness of life beginning, a wondrous chain reaction that is both incredibly beautiful and completely silly."

That combo of wonder and silliness is a lovely way of describing Elenor's artistic outlook. She's especially fond of work that can provoke a laugh or leave someone feeling a little unsettled, and takes both responses equally seriously. "I like when my work makes people laugh, but I also find it cool if they're a little weirded out," she says. "I'm really serious about my work and don't want to make things that feel 'ironic'; I'd love for people to see humour in it but also beauty."

Another favourite of hers is a music video for Late June by Jazz musician Adam O'Farrill, a slow, extended animation. "It explores the awe and volatility of the passage of time," she says. The film's unhurried pace gives viewers time to sit with its movements, and for Elenor, the collaboration was also a chance to work with music she adores.

Recently, however, she's been finding her way back into making things after becoming a parent. Her baby was born around a year ago, and she describes her parental leave as a rather uncreative period, with little time to immerse herself in the art, films and music that previously fed her practice. Now, as she gradually returns to the studio, she's finding that working with her hands can be enough to get things going again.

"I often find myself looking inward and letting my hands lead the way, without overthinking too much. It's almost like waiting for muscle memory to kick in and seeing what comes out. With ceramics in particular, I find it inspiring simply to put my hands on the clay and see what happens."

issues.title: Lindye Galloway Brings Intimacy to a 10,000-Square-Foot Home
issues.summary: In Dana Point, California, the interior designer uses natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings to create a warm, inviting family residence
issues.author: Leo Lei
issues.content_html:
At 10,000 square feet, a home can easily feel more expansive than inviting. For a new residence in Dana Point, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway approached that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life.

Photography by Grace Combs

Galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair.

Photography by Grace Combs

Tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality.

Photography by Grace Combs

The attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House, while lighting comes from Ravenhill, Atelier de Troupe, and Roll & Hill.

Photography by Grace Combs

The kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area. Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property.

Photography by Grace Combs

Rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale.

Photography by Grace Combs

issues.title: ESR x Craig & Karl Bring a Pocket Full of Joy to Everyday Technology
issues.summary: The Pocket Full of Joy collection brings the creative duo’s colorful graphics to iPhone cases and magnetic wallets, combining bold design with everyday functionality
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
The objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a new collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

Behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

The collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

With Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

The ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

issues.title: Check In for the Holidays: Inside 16 Imaginative Christmas Suites
issues.summary: Hotels are going all out for the holidays, transforming guest rooms into festive retreats with imaginative décor and nostalgic details
issues.author: Colleen Sullivan
issues.content_html:
Hotel lobbies may feature towering holiday trees and elaborate gingerbread displays, but some of the season’s most imaginative designs are happening behind closed doors. Creative teams are giving guest rooms full seasonal makeovers—blending thoughtful décor with interactive touches. From nostalgic throwbacks to festive retreats, these design-forward suites make the stay itself the destination. Ahead, explore some of the most imaginative holiday suites to check into this season.

16 Festive Hotel Suites to Book for the 2026 Holiday Season

The Mills House in Charleston, SC

The Watercolor Wonderland Suite creates a whimsical, storybook setting with pastel ornaments, pink-wrapped gifts, and a miniature holiday village. Photography courtesy of The Mills House.

Inspired by the Lowcountry’s pastel façades and historic architecture, the Watercolor Wonderland Suite at The Mills House in Charleston, South Carolina, was created in collaboration with local artist Rebecca Meixner. Original watercolor illustrations of Charleston landmarks, including Rainbow Row and the city’s steepled churches, appear throughout the suite, while pastel ornaments bring a soft seasonal touch to the Christmas tree.

In the Watercolor Wonderland Suite, pink holiday wreaths adorn the bathroom’s geometric tile walls, adding a playful contrast to the black-and-white palette. Photography courtesy of The Mills House.

In the bedroom, a garland-draped headboard, a lit wreath, and festive stockings complement custom pillows featuring Meixner’s artwork. Guests also receive pink-iced holiday cookies, a hot cocoa kit with custom Mills House mugs, and a watercolor painting kit.

The Watercolor Wonderland Suite is available to book from Dec.1, 2026, through Jan. 3, 2027, at millshouse.com.

The Whitney Hotel in Boston, MA

The Evergreen Suite brings a woodland-inspired holiday look to the bedroom, with pinecone garlands, greenery, and deep navy accents. Photography courtesy of The Whitney Hotel.

The Evergreen Suite at The Whitney Hotel takes a quieter, nature-forward approach to holiday styling in Boston’s historic Beacon Hill neighborhood. Fresh seasonal greenery, tailored wreaths, garlands, and twinkling lights bring the outdoors inside. A palette of muted blue and forest green, accented by plush throw blankets, gives the space a serene, residential feel. Guests can opt for gingerbread cookies from local favorite Gingerbread Construction Company paired with hot cocoa, or a bottle of red wine served with warm spiced cashews. They also receive a printed copy of Beacon Hill Christmas, a 1951 poem by former neighborhood resident William Orville Thomson.

The Evergreen Suite is available to book from Nov. 14, 2026, through Jan. 16, 2027, at whitneyhotelboston.com.

Hamilton Princess & Beach Club in Bermuda

The Festive Suite pairs deep green pillows, a playful “fa la la” cushion, and a plush throw with warm wood and gold finishes. Photography courtesy of Hamilton Princess & Beach Club.

The Festive Suite at Hamilton Princess & Beach Club in Bermuda pairs Scandinavian-inspired Christmas décor with waterfront views of Pitt’s Bay and Hamilton Harbour. The suite features festive green-and-gold furnishings alongside commissioned artwork by Bermudian artists Ewan David Eason and Guy Gee.

The Festive Suite features an oversized evergreen wreath, white reindeer figurines, candles, and green-and-white knit stockings. Photography courtesy of Hamilton Princess & Beach Club.

Seasonal touches include a decorated Christmas tree, a welcome basket filled with holiday treats, an Advent calendar, and an Elf on the Shelf. Guests receive gingerbread cookies, a spiked hot chocolate kit, and a custom s’mores station on the private balcony. A personalized voicemail from Santa adds another playful touch.

The Festive Suite is available to book from Dec. 1, 2026, through Jan. 3, 2027, at thehamiltonprincess.com.

Beaches Turks & Caicos and Beaches Negril

The Elf on the Shelf Caribbean Vacation Suite carries its Scout Elf theme into the bathroom, with custom character wallpaper, red-and-white towels, and festive holiday accents. Photography courtesy of Beaches.

The Elf on the Shelf Caribbean Vacation Suite at Beaches Turks & Caicos and Beaches Negril features Scout Elves trading the North Pole for a Caribbean getaway. Custom wallpaper depicts Scout Elves on vacation among palm trees, seashells, and coconuts, while themed bedding, festive collectibles, and a Christmas tree carry the holiday concept throughout.

A miniature Christmas tree, Scout Elf dolls, and festive pillows bring a tropical twist to the holidays in the Elf on the Shelf Caribbean Vacation Suite. Photography courtesy of Beaches.

At Beaches Turks & Caicos, the suite features a dedicated kids’ bunk room stocked with holiday storybooks, games, and plush toys, while a Jingle Shell Butler delivers playful perks like miniature milk and cookies and marshmallow bubble baths.

The Elf on the Shelf Caribbean Vacation Suite is available to book from Nov. 25, 2026, through Jan. 3, 2027, at beaches.com.

Amway Grand Plaza in Grand Rapids, MI

The adjoining children’s room at Amway Grand Plaza embraces the Grinch theme with character-printed bedding, bright green pillows, and playful holiday touches. Photography courtesy of Amway Grand Plaza.

The historic Amway Grand Plaza in downtown Grand Rapids, Michigan, offers families two connecting rooms with their own holiday themes: the Tower Luxury Suite takes a traditional approach, with decorated Christmas trees, seasonal artwork, and Santa-inspired details, while the adjoining Two Queen River View room features a colorful, Grinch-themed escape tailored for younger guests.

A red Santa mailbox, complete with a holiday wish list and letters addressed to the North Pole, gives young guests a festive way to share their Christmas wishes. Photography courtesy of Amway Grand Plaza.

In-room treats include hot cocoa bombs, chocolate chip cookies from The Kitchen by Wolfgang Puck, and postcards to Santa that receive replies.

The Santa Suite is available to book from Nov. 20 through Dec. 31, 2026, at amwaygrand.com.

Club Wyndham Midtown 45 in New York City

The Holiday Rewind Suite recreates a nostalgic Christmas kitchen with retro floral wallpaper, red bows, vintage-inspired table settings, and festive nutcrackers. Photography courtesy of Club Wyndham.

At Club Wyndham Midtown 45 in New York City, the Holiday Rewind Suite turns back the clock to Christmas 1999. The living room features a Christmas tree, retro-patterned wallpaper, and vintage holiday décor, plus a library of classic VHS tapes. A rotary-style landline, vintage holiday cards, and era-defining toys reinforce the late-’90s nostalgia. The separate bedroom leans into a full-on Y2K teen dream, complete with glow-in-the-dark ceiling stars and a CD player loaded with late-’90s hits.

A decorated Christmas tree, red sofa, nostalgic games, and holiday memorabilia bring a throwback feel to the Holiday Rewind Suite’s living and dining areas. Photography courtesy of Club Wyndham.

The suite includes a kitchen stocked with hot chocolate and Rice Krispies Treats kits, as well as take-home keepsakes like a disposable camera and virtual pet keychain.

The Holiday Rewind Suite is available to book from Nov. 6, 2026, through Jan. 6, 2027, at clubwyndham.wyndhamdestinations.com.

The Untitled Nashville Hotel in Nashville, TN

Evergreen garland draped across the mirrored headboard and teal holiday pillows bring seasonal touches to the Christmas Chapter suite, complementing its deep blue walls and eclectic artwork. Photography courtesy of The Untitled Nashville Hotel.

The Untitled Nashville Hotel takes a personal, music-inspired approach to the season with The Christmas Chapter, a seasonal suite decked out in teal, white, and gold, with natural greenery and festive accents. A decorated Holiday Tradition Tree serves as the room’s focal point, inviting guests to write a favorite family tradition on an ornament-shaped card and hang it on the tree. An in-suite record player stocked with holiday vinyl sets a nostalgic soundtrack, while seasonal books and personalized postcards, which the front desk will mail to loved ones, add thoughtful touches.

The Christmas Chapter is available to book from Nov. 20, 2026, through Jan. 3, 2027, at theuntitlednashvillehotel.com.

Westgate Las Vegas in Las Vegas, NV

Deep green sofas, a decorated Christmas tree, and garlands draped along the ceiling create a festive setting in the Christmas Suite, along with nutcrackers and Santa figures. Photography courtesy of Westgate Las Vegas.

Christmas lasts all year long at Westgate Las Vegas, where the 1,500-square-foot Christmas Suite is styled like a holiday lodge in the desert. Three decorated trees, seasonal greenery, and an electric fireplace set the tone, while a festive in-suite bar and Elf on the Shelf details in the bathrooms add a playful note.

A decorated Christmas tree, plaid throw, and glowing “Ho ho ho!” neon sign bring holiday cheer to the Christmas Suite’s bedroom. Photography courtesy of Westgate Las Vegas.

Unlike seasonal holiday suites, this one stays up all year, so guests can plan a winter getaway or celebrate Christmas in July.

The Christmas Suite is available to book year-round at westgateresorts.com.

Manchester Grand Hyatt in San Diego, CA

Vintage Christmas books, brass reindeer, and colorful ornaments create a nostalgic holiday display in the Santa Suite. Photography courtesy of Manchester Grand Hyatt San Diego.

The Santa Suite at Manchester Grand Hyatt San Diego brings a traditional North Pole aesthetic to the California coast, with rich crimson and gold setting the tone. A towering Christmas tree dressed in classic ornaments and velvet ribbon anchors the room, complemented by pine garland draped across the headboard and traditional tartan accent pillows. Under the tree, vintage sleds and toy trains add a nostalgic touch, while shelves display brass candlesticks and Santa figurines. Younger guests can post letters in an in-suite North Pole mailbox or browse a collection of holiday picture books.

The Santa Suite is available to book from Nov. 23, 2026, through Jan. 5, 2027, at hyattexperiences.com.

Lotte New York Palace in New York City

A towering Christmas tree, wrapped gifts, red stockings, and woodland-inspired accents give the Après Ski suite a festive retreat. Photography courtesy of Lotte New York Palace.

Holiday decorating takes center stage at the Lotte New York Palace, where four suites have been transformed in partnership with Balsam Hill, each showcasing a distinct seasonal personality.

Wrapped presents, a plush bunny, holiday cookies, and milk set a welcoming scene beneath the Christmas tree in the Après Ski suite. Photography courtesy of Lotte New York Palace.

The Après Ski suite leans classic with red-and-white tartan ribbons, wool plaids, and statement nutcrackers, while Parisian Palace takes a romantic turn with blush hues and jeweled accents. The Golden Glow suite layers shimmering gold with sparkling crystal for a glamorous look, while the Arctic Room creates a whimsical wonderland of nostalgic, vintage-inspired ornaments. Balsam Hill Christmas trees serve as the focal point in each suite, complemented by matching garlands and festive accents. Guests receive homemade chocolate chip cookies and a commemorative ornament to take home.

All four suites are available to book from Nov. 23, 2026, through Jan. 10, 2027, at lottenypalace.com.

Barnsley Resort in Adairsville, GA

A decorated Christmas tree, glowing fireplace, and evergreen garland set a cozy holiday scene in a Christmas Cottage Suite, with red stockings and classic seasonal accents completing the look. Photography courtesy of Patrick O’Brien for Barnsley Resort.

Barnsley Resort draws inspiration from its North Georgia woodland setting for its Christmas Cottage Suites, where understated seasonal décor complements the natural surroundings. Long-needle pine garlands, cedar boughs, and native pinecones create a freshly gathered feel, while stockings hang from the mantel over a wood-burning fireplace, and velvet-wrapped ornaments add rich texture to the Christmas tree. Garland-lined porches and exterior lighting extend the warmth outside.

The Christmas Cottage Suites are available to book from Nov. 18, 2026, through Jan. 4, 2027, at barnsleyresort.com.

Waldorf Astoria in Washington, D.C.

A rendering of the upcoming Holiday Suite shows an elaborate canopy of greenery, oversized ornaments, and cascading ribbons transforming the bed into a holiday focal point, while a life-size nutcracker adds a traditional Christmas accent. Rendering courtesy of The Belle Noel.

The Holiday Suite at Waldorf Astoria Washington, D.C. balances luxury with playful, family-friendly seasonal charm. The 1,500-square-foot retreat features a soft palette of periwinkle, mint green, and blush pink, with elegant holiday accents throughout. In the bedroom, an elaborate canopy of greenery, oversized ornaments, and cascading ribbons makes the bed a dramatic focal point. The suite’s fitness room has been transformed into a children’s play nook, complete with a tent, plush rugs, and soft pillows. Other seasonal touches include a life-size nutcracker, two decorated Christmas trees, bespoke wreaths, and a record player stocked with holiday classics. Guests receive hot chocolate and cookies.

The Holiday Suite is available to book from Nov. 16, 2026, through Jan. 3, 2027, at hilton.com.

Hilton Anatole in Dallas, TX

A festive hot chocolate station welcomes guests to the Santa Suite, with whipped-cream-topped mugs, seasonal cookies, evergreen garland, and a display of sweet treats. Photography courtesy of Kayla Enright.

The Santa Suite at Hilton Anatole in Dallas brings the magic of Christmas to a spacious family retreat. Designed to give parents privacy while keeping everyone under one festive roof, the suite pairs a king-size primary bedroom with a dedicated bunk-bed area for children. Traditional crimson and evergreen accents blend with warm neutrals and cozy textiles, while an illuminated Christmas tree serves as the focal point. The stay also includes four complimentary tickets to the hotel’s outdoor ice-skating rink.

The Santa Suite is available to book from Nov. 27, 2026, through Jan. 3, 2027, at hilton.com.

Canopy by Hilton Sioux Falls Downtown in Sioux Falls, SD

A snowman-embroidered pillow and oversized paper snowflakes add playful seasonal details to the Holiday Suite bedroom. Photography courtesy of Canopy by Hilton Sioux Falls Downtown.

The Holiday Suite at Canopy by Hilton Sioux Falls Downtown offers a modern, seasonal retreat that blends natural evergreens, gold accents, and rich reds with the hotel’s contemporary architecture. Highlights include a 7.5-foot decorated Christmas tree beside floor-to-ceiling windows, snowflake-inspired pendant lighting, and a garland-trimmed private balcony with seasonal mugs. Guests receive a welcome delivery of local treats, including peanut brittle, gingersnaps, and snickerdoodles.

The Holiday Suite is available to book from Nov. 20, 2026, through Jan. 3, 2027, at hilton.com.

Fairmont Grand Del Mar in San Diego, CA

A festive train filled with candy canes and ornaments, a whimsical reindeer, and a decorated Christmas tree bring classic Christmas charm to the Santa Suite’s living room. Photography courtesy of Fairmont Grand Del Mar.

The Santa Suite at Fairmont Grand Del Mar in San Diego pairs traditional Christmas details with playful touches, starting with an 8-foot live tree decorated in colorful ornaments and candy canes. Green garland and plaid stockings dress the fireplace mantel (personalized stockings are available upon request), while shelves display Santa figurines and frosted mini trees. Knit pillows shaped like gingerbread men, snowflakes, and trees add a whimsical touch, while live white poinsettias appear throughout the suite. Guests receive holiday cookies, a fireside patio s’mores kit, a Santa’s Hot Chocolate Bar, and a Grand Del Mar keepsake ornament.

The Santa Suite is available to book Dec. 1 through Dec. 31, 2026, at fairmont.com.

The Fifty Sonesta Hotel in New York City

A decorated Christmas tree, vintage-style ornaments, plaid stockings, and a classic Radio Flyer wagon filled with presents bring a nostalgic holiday feel to the Rockin’ Retro Christmas Suite. Photography courtesy of The Fifty Sonesta.

Christmas gets a midcentury makeover at The Fifty Sonesta Hotel New York, where the Rockin’ Retro Christmas Suite takes inspiration from holiday traditions of the 1950s and ’60s. The space is a nostalgic time capsule, with vintage-inspired wallpaper, a chenille bedspread, and a living room Christmas tree decorated with Shiny Brite ornaments, glass bead garland, and silver tinsel. A retro turntable, faux fireplace, bedroom toys, and original Sears Wish Books evoke the Christmases of decades past. In the bedroom, a silver aluminum Christmas tree glows beneath a rotating color wheel that washes its branches in red, blue, green, and amber. Guests receive a welcome bag of nostalgic treats, including a miniature New York City snow globe, hot cocoa, holiday candy, a mini tinsel tree with its own rotating color wheel, and a custom ornament.

The Rockin’ Retro Christmas Suite is available to book from Nov. 22, 2026, through Jan. 6, 2027, at nyc.sonesta.com.

issues.title: Arcadia’s New Almeya Collection Marks A New Era of Flexible Design
issues.summary: The Almeya Collection offers a fluid seating experience that adapts to modern shifts in productivity and collaboration
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Hybrid and remote work have changed what people expect from a modern workspace. No longer do people want fixed seating or single-purpose design. Instead, they are looking for modular, multi-use furniture that boosts productivity while maintaining comfort and style. When Chris and Jon Panichella set out to design their latest seating collection for Arcadia, they turned to everyday life for inspiration.

“The idea for Almeya began with a woman working from an inflatable raft at the beach,” the Panichellas explain. “She could recline and read in one position, then sit up and work in another—a simple moment that captured how much people now expect from their spaces: comfort, flexibility, and function. That observation became the very first concept sketch that eventually evolved into the Almeya offering we know today.”

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

With a full family of products—including modular, lounge, work-lounge, benches, and occasional tables—the Almeya Collection offers a fluid experience that adapts to these modern shifts in productivity and collaboration. Across the series, soft, organic forms invite comfort and ease, while integrated tables, flexible configurations, and strategic power stations allow for both focus and sociability.

Almeya began with a single lounge chair and an integrated two-tiered side table. The idea was simple: the combination could function as a self-contained work island, with two separate surfaces, power access, and an optional rotating tablet. With this concept in mind, the Panichellas developed a standalone lounge chair, love seat, and sofa with the same flexible spirit. (Case in point: The swivel-base lounge chair allows for adaptability and easy collaboration). Finally, the complete collection came together, designed to support the various—and often unpredictable—ways people work and gather.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

To inspire interaction, designers are encouraged to group lounge seating intermittently to foster spontaneous connections. To create pathways or natural flow within a space, they can explore Almeya’s modular capabilities. The organic curves of the lounge models also create an inviting warmth, blurring the line between contract and residential. And for healthcare and education settings, optional clean-outs are offered between the seat and back.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

Completing the collection, occasional tables carry the same gentle, organic language for a cohesive experience. Available in multiple sizes and shapes, tables feature upholstered sides and are offered with ash or walnut veneer, laminate, Corian, and Fenix top surfaces.

See the full Almeya Series at arcadiacontract.com.

issues.title: CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall
issues.summary: US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple. The post CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Jenna McKnight
issues.content_html:
US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson. The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project's inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

Drawings and photography

    Drawings and photography

    "The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living," said Jackson-based CLB Architects.

    The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

    "In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place," said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

    A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

    The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.

    "Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing new landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings," the architect said.

    The team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

    Both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.

    The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

    “Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

    Read:

    CLB Architects wraps Caju House in Wyoming in weathering steel

    The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

    The clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.

    "A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends," the team said, noting the project was completed in about nine months.

    The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

    “With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.

    "As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward."

    Other ADUs in America include a small, cedar-clad dwelling in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a compact, metal-clad building in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

    Project credits:

    Architecture and interior design: CLB Architects
    Architecture and interior design team: Eric Logan (partner), Darcey Prichard (partner), Sarah Kennedy (principal), Paige Hobson (project manager), Stephanie Wright (project coordinator)
    Contractor: Dembergh Construction, Mike Prichard (partner)
    Structural engineer: Tectonic Design
    MEP Engineer: Jim Bob Schell
    Landscape: Agrostis and The Tree and Landscape Company
    Lighting: Helius Architectural Lighting
    Owners: Darcey and Mike Prichard

issues.title: Cotswolds barn renovation by ConForm creates a "dialogue between old and new"
issues.summary: London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a new space for a working farm in the Cotswolds. The post Cotswolds barn renovation by ConForm creates a "dialogue between old and new" appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Jon Astbury
issues.content_html:
London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.

Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

Drawings and photography

    Drawings and photography

    ConForm Architects' design responds to the dual nature of the barn's surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

    "The design centres on a dialogue between old and new. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other," studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.

    "The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond," he added.

    "The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings."

    A defining feature of the barn's new rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

    In the ground floor's flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.

    Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn's roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

    "The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond," said Edgley.

    "Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame," he added.

    "The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project."

    Read:

    Prest Vale Architects extends historic stone rectory in the Cotswolds

    ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.

issues.title: Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
issues.summary: Nendo founder Oki Sato has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen's 20/20 project. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn't find design inspiring. The post Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Nat Barker
issues.content_html:
Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen's 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn't find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

"How I think is not typical design," she told Dezeen. "So I'm never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it's just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece."

"I've never been so inspired by design in general," she added. "It's a skill that fits very well to me, but I'd rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline."

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn't have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

"I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them," she explained. "For me, it's sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be."

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year's Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

Explaining the studio's decision to select her as a 20x20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder's approach for being "both remarkably gentle and quietly bold".

"Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked," the studio told Dezeen.

Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).

These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder's studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.

"I'm inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings," she said. "I think it's just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design."

"In the history of architecture there's so much to tell," she continued. "For me it's more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that's what interests me so much."

"And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration."

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.

In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder's atelier space.

She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing. Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there's so much investment in each project

"I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well," said Tangelder. "The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn't really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more new for me."

"I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years," she considered. "There's a lot happening right now."

It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.

Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.

"That has been super important for me," she said. "Each material that I really love, I have a partner now."

But moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.

"I really like it, so for me it's the best way to spend my time," she said, before pausing.

"I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it's also a struggle. You're always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made."

So that means you take risks all the time. It's maybe more intense, but also more fun

Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

"In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing," she remembered. "Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there's so much investment in each project."

Over time, she says she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.

"I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental," she explained.

"So that means you take risks all the time," she added. "It's maybe more intense, but also more fun."

Most of Tangelder's work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.

A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.

This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.

I just think the material is very me. That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It's really in between a sculpture and a functional object

It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.

Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.

"So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process," she said.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Tangelder's current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.

"I just think the material is very me," she remarked. "That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It's really in between a sculpture and a functional object."

Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.

And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.

In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.

She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.

For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.

"I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it's also a reaction to what he's done," she said.

"He's so clear in the decisions that he makes, he's a master in it, and I'm really grateful that he sees what I've been doing."

The main photo is byAlexander Popelier.

issues.title: The joy of reading The Power Broker with strangers at 3 AM.
issues.summary: No one is well served by listening to pedants, but I think I’ve found an exception. This past weekend, I was a reader at The Power Broker Marathon, where 400+ volunteers took turns reading the entirety of Robert Caro’s magisterial
issues.author: James Folta
issues.content_html:
Screenshot

" />

No one is well served by listening to pedants, but I think I’ve found an exception.

This past weekend, I was a reader at The Power Broker Marathon, where 400+ volunteers took turns reading the entirety of Robert Caro’s magisterial book, in ten minute chunks, over the course of 66 hours. The event’s organizers found their readers through an open call. A startling number of my friends and family forwarded the sign up form to me. It asked, among other things, when you would be available to read. I selected “Afternoon,” “Evening,” and after a pause, “Morning” too. I’m an early riser with a young son, after all, so I didn’t foresee any issues.

A few week’s later I got my assigned time: 3:10 AM on Sunday. Technically, a morning slot. But I’m more of a fan of Robert Caro than I am of sleeping in. I confirmed.

I’m a devoted reader of Caro, and I’ve taken up the Bob beat on Lit Hub too, where I’ve covered fellow Caro-heads, his posts on Instagram, and the 50th anniversary of The Power Broker, Caro’s 1162 page book about Robert Moses and his transformative tenure as New York City Parks Commissioner, during which he built miles and acres of highways, roads, bridges, and parks, at the expense of low-income families, farmers, and other less powerful New Yorkers. It’s a great book.

So much to say, I had no trouble popping up with my 1:15 AM alarm and heading out into the cold to read. I traveled northwest across Brooklyn towards the harbor, where the marathon was 50-hours or more old, having stretched from Thursday, through Friday, Saturday, and now into Sunday. I guessed that the story was probably well into the mayoralty of Robert Wagner at that point. I walked by a few giggly couples, walking in the other direction and on a different timeline, enjoying the end of their late Saturday, and soon found myself at Judgy Baby.

Judgy Baby is an industrial warehouse space in the shadow of Moses’s Gowanus Parkway; the event was organized by Brad Vogel, their director of special projects. Vogel told The New York Groove that the idea for the marathon came out of a Power Broker reading group he ran last year.

“Instead of people saying ‘no that’s ridiculous,’” he said, “people were actually excited.”

I’d seen the set-up inside Judgy Baby on social media, later covered glossily in places like The Times: a banner, a microphone, and a podium with a copy of the book. In pictures of the marathon’s opening, the stage was filled with luminaries like Caro’s editor, the voice of the NY subway system, and a number of current government officials. Power Broker fans are everywhere, like some kind of nerd Illuminati.

None of those big names were in attendance when I arrived at 2:00 AM, but I was happy to see a small and dedicated crew of volunteers, readers, and fans. The big warehouse was much livelier than I’d anticipated; a few people were curled up napping, but the majority were awake: hanging out, chatting, grabbing a quick meal. At least one person was engrossed in a novel. There was coffee, and wine, and a pile of commemorative t-shirts. I took a cup of coffee and a small.

A volunteer checked me in and oriented me. When it was my time, a volunteer would point out where the last reader had left off, and then step back on stage when my ten minutes were up, when I would need to find a natural place to stop. He stressed that this might not be the end of a full sentence, so I might need to find a comma to pause on. Caro is long winded, I was warned, but little did this volunteer know that I was hoping for one of Caro’s famous lists to be in my section (though the most famous one, inspired by Homer, had already long passed.)

I was also asked to read slowly, if I could. The readers before me had been over-eager, and the marathon was ahead of schedule. Caro really does get people excited.

I still had about an hour until my slot, so I found a seat in a back pew (appropriately devotional seating) and listened. In the book, the Tavern on the Green controversy was just coming to a head, one of the rare moments when Moses was personally exposed to public scrutiny. One by one, each reader was replaced by a guiding volunteer, with hearty applause at each transition. Unlike a typical reading, there was no introduction of each new reader (though all our names were in a program, in a tiny font). We were each anonymous, a succession of Vestal priestesses keeping the flame of this project warm.

One reader took the slowdown command very literally, and read his section with long and deliberate pauses between each word. There was some delirious laughter at the careful pacing, and he ended with a round of appreciative cheers and applause.

At 2:50 AM, I was shown to a chair next to the stage. To my right was the on-deck reader, with her own copy of the book to follow along. When she was brought on stage, I took her seat and her warm-up Power Broker. I forgot how small the typeface was in this book, and immediately started feeling like a panicked sixth grader again, skimming ahead and trying to count paragraphs. We were in chapter 43, “Late Arrival”, with the press finally starting to get wise to Moses and his vast, unelected power. Over 1,000 pages in, Moses was nearing the end of his public life.

And then I was up and on stage, following the volunteer’s finger. “Robert Moses still ran the show,” my section began. I stumbled once or twice—“daises” briefly looked like “daisies,” and I read “Rockefeller 3d” as “three d” until I corrected to “the third.” But I was delighted to find a list in my three pages, a comma-laced sentence detailing all the elements that were a part of Moses’s plan for Lincoln Center.

When my time was up, I rejoined the crowd for a few more pages, and then tiptoed into the green room to gather my things. I talked with a few of the volunteer organizers, and compared notes on how the reading went, when we had first finished the book, and which of Moses’s highways confounded us the most in our daily lives. The bleary but bright-eyed energy reminded me of other big efforts I’d been a part of, like the City Marathon or the WGA Writers Strike. Everyone was stretched, but proud. We were doing something, together, and no one would risk letting the rest down. No wonder we were speeding through the book ahead of schedule.

I took a longer walk home, since my train was skipping stops, and passed under the Gowanus Expressway, feeling the crumbling yet still powerful hand of Moses’s ghost on my shoulder.

The feeling of history’s living nearness is why this book is catnip for New Yorkers. It’s a way for us to navel gaze, to talk about how much we love our big, beautiful, messy town, and to gush about how exceptional it is, that even its flaws are so grand to be worth a thousand pages of beautiful prose. But it’s also a way into our other favorite topic of conversation: which trains are delayed, why, and how it’s ruining our day. As one volunteer put it, reading The Power Broker in New York feels like running into an ex—every corner you turn, there Moses is again, standing in your way.

It was nice to be home at 4:30 AM, and nice to know that the Marathon was still marching along. The next day—or rather, later the same morning—I pulled up the livestream on my phone to catch the last sections of the book.

Clocking in to read the last page was Robert A. Caro himself, there on pre-recorded video, the final volunteer reader. Watching the livestream on my phone, I misheard the penultimate line, swapping “he” for “we”: “Couldn’t people see what we had done?”

I teared up a little—from sleep deprivation as much as anything else—to hear it in Caro’s thick, New York accent.
