issues.title: Gillian Welch on Her Favorite Record, The Legendary Stanley Brothers
issues.summary: If I could have only one Stanley Brothers album, The Legendary Stanley Brothers (Recorded Live), Volume One—the record with the yellow band at the top, which means it’s volume one—is what I would choose. In fact, if I could have
issues.author: Gillian Welch
issues.content_html:
If I could have only one Stanley Brothers album, The Legendary Stanley Brothers (Recorded Live), Volume One—the record with the yellow band at the top, which means it’s volume one—is what I would choose. In fact, if I could have only one bluegrass album, I would probably choose this one. Because it’s perfect. You know how when you see a snapshot and, years after the fact, you can’t believe how much information is in it, how much detail, and how the profound essence of a thing is conveyed in that snapshot? This record is like that perfect snapshot. It captures what could never have been captured in a studio album, the pinnacle of what the Stanley Brothers did. I don’t know what I would do if this record didn’t exist.

In some ways, this record is kind of a mysterious thing. It was out of print for many, many years—but sometimes it seems like maybe it’s back in print. There are virtually no credits on it. James Shelton, who played guitar for Ralph Stanley for many years, told me that it may have been recorded by Peter Kuykendall, who started the magazine Bluegrass Unlimited, and it might have been a show in Culpeper, Virginia. He must have had a Nagra and a microphone out in the audience, because the applause is unbelievably loud and distorted. David Rawlings, my musical partner, and I used to joke that it sounded like the audience was breaking plates between the songs, but it’s all part of the charm and the record’s undeniable perfection.

This record is like that perfect snapshot. It captures what could never have been captured in a studio album.

I first heard this record when I was twenty, in Santa Cruz, in a group house on Highland Avenue, at the base of the campus. I was living with a bluegrass mandolin player named Mike McKinley, who had a great record collection. And one day, I was in the bathroom scrubbing the bathtub—as you occasionally do if you wanna take a bath in a six person housemate situation. I’m down on the floor, and Mike puts on side A of The Legendary Stanley Brothers, “Dream of a Miner’s Child.” It was like I was in a tractor beam: I had to walk over to the turntable and see what this was. Not only was it the first time I’d ever heard this record, but it was the first time I’d ever heard the Stanley Brothers. And it just went through me like a bolt of lightning. I’d grown up playing acoustic music, playing acoustic guitar since I was nine, but I’d never heard anything this visceral. It was like a missing piece of the puzzle for what I thought music should be. Suddenly everything kind of made sense. I’d wanted to play music, but I didn’t really have signposts for which direction to go. When I heard this album, it would not be an overstatement to say it changed the course of my life.

The recording was really unfussy, so the sound was really unfussy, and kind of hard, even a little bit gnarly. The harmonies were beautiful, but there was something edgy about it that really appealed to me. And then, the songs are Stone. Cold. Classics. “Rovin’ Gambler,” “Banks of the Ohio,” “He Will Set Your Fields on Fire,” “Roll in My Sweet Baby’s Arms.” And “Knoxville Girl,” which is probably my favorite: It’s such great storytelling—like a movie in my head, except it’s even better than that: It’s like a book. Except it’s even better than that: It’s a song!

And beyond the songcraft, the subject matter had this timeless quality to it that is in no way dated. Maybe a vocabulary word here and there has fallen out of use, but the subjects are heartbreak, gambling, addiction, murder, judgment, sin, the supernatural, love, loss, the hereafter, redemption. There’s absolutely nothing unmodern about any of this. Looking backward, I find it more relevant now than when I heard it at twenty. I’m pretty sure I’ve performed every song on this album; every song became a part of my repertoire at some point.

This album showed me what I was shooting for—or at least the direction I knew I had to go in. ’Cause, quite honestly, I wasn’t hearing acoustic music that hard-hitting, that true, or that adept at dealing with the depth of human experience and human emotion as I perceived it. I’m one of those people who mostly reacts to hard times, not good times. The good times just happen. I have nothing to say about them. But the more trying moments that life throws your way, that’s what I find myself trying to respond to, and I felt that up and down in this music.

It’s like a magic window on a world. You feel the audience, you hear Carter talking, and then you hear them playing.

This cover photograph is what I mean when I say this whole thing is perfect. I have stared and stared at this incredible photograph so much, especially the look on Carter Stanley’s face. He didn’t live much longer after this was taken. And the fact that it’s a live album, as opposed to a studio album, allows for the little pieces of spoken-word commentary between some of the songs, all of which have gone all the way into my cortex. I pretty much have what Carter says onstage in this performance memorized, even the cadence of his speech. (I know that it has influenced the color of David’s and my banter onstage.) It’s like a magic window on a world. You feel the audience, you hear Carter talking, and then you hear them playing.

The last time I returned to it, I put it on because I wanted to sing along with them again. I hadn’t been listening to as much old-time and bluegrass music in the last six months to a year. It was harder to find on the radio. I’d just got home from a tour, and I wanted to check in, to recalibrate, because that was so important to my learning how to do what I do. When I was younger, I basically just wanted to sing like Ralph Stanley—or like a cross between Ralph Stanley and James Taylor, if that’s possible. So, I put on the record and just sang along, three-part, adding a tenor, or a second tenor above Ralph. It’s a very important kind of touchstone for me. And when I put it on, I realized that this has to be the record I talked about.

I remember the first time I played The Legendary Stanley Brothers for David, and it blew his mind. He was screaming and pounding on the tabletop, because he’d never heard the Stanley Brothers. So, I got to turn him on to it, and he completely flipped. We dubbed a cassette tape of it, and all the first couple years of our touring, driving up and down and back and forth across the country, we would just sing three-part or four-part along with this record. That’s how we learned to sing together. So, it has deeply influenced what we do. Like I said, I just can’t imagine that I could be doing what I do without this album.

______________________________

issues.title: Mysteries and Thrillers You Might Have Forgotten About
issues.summary: A list of mysteries and thrillers you might have forgotten about, gems published 10 or more years ago that are well worth the (re)read.
issues.author: Vanessa Diaz
issues.content_html:
I regularly co-host a couple of different book podcasts, and it’s a fairly regular occurrence for me to say on air, “Oh you know, this one book that came out last year, I think?…” only to find out it’s at least three to five years old, if not older. This week’s “what is time” incident happened while recording the latest episode of All the Books, where I shouted out Nick Harkaway’s new release (The Taper Man). I shared how much I loved Harkaway’s Angelmaker, a title I was sure was just a few years old.

Reader, it came out in 2012. It now has a Vintage Contemporaries edition. Am I a vintage contemporary edition? Perhaps, but you know what else is true? That’s a damn good book.

This got me wondering about what other crime reads I hadn’t thought about in a minute, so I dusted off my old Goodreads account in search of titles from my reading past. Maybe you haven’t thought about them in a minute either, or maybe they’ll be new to you entirely. Either way, they’re worth the (re)read.

Here are five fantastic mysteries and thrillers you might have forgotten about, all published 10-15 years ago.

Angelmaker by Nick Harkaway (2012)

Older lady sleuths may be all the rage now (Vera Wong, Detective Aunty, Miss Hortense, and these killers of a certain age, to name a few), but there’s another senior citizen kicking ass and taking names who predates all of those, and I’m not talking about Miss Marple. Edie Banister was once a British secret agent, but she’s been long out the game when she’s approached by a man named Joe Spork who’s in quite the pickle. The son of an infamous London mob boss, Joe has chosen not to follow in dear ol’ dad’s footsteps and instead fixes clocks for a living. But when his latest repair job inadvertently triggers a 1950s doomsday machine, he enlists Edie’s help to escape a suddenly long list of enemies and save the world. Just like that, Edie is back on a mission she thought she’d seen the last of long ago.

P.S. For the uninitiated, Nick Harkaway is the son of John le Carré!

The Cutting Season by Attica Locke (2013)

You might know Attica Locke for her excellent Highway 59 series that began with Bluebird, Bluebird, but her sophomore novel is another absolute stunner. In 2009, Caren Gray is the general manager at the Belle Vie plantation, a historic landmark in Louisiana’s Sugar Cane country. When she discovers a body on the grounds of the estate, she is drawn into not one mystery, but two: the one of the dead woman she found, and one who was killed at Belle Vie long ago.

Reconstructing Ameliaby Kimberly McCreight (2013)

I recently told someone I’d never read Kimberly McCreight when asked if I’d read A Good Marriage. Survey says that was a lie! I completely forgot that I’d read McCreight’s debut back in 2013, a gripping read about a lawyer and single mother, Kate, reconstructing her teenage daughter Amelia’s tragic death. It’s initially ruled a suicide, but then Kate receives a chilling anonymous message: “She didn’t jump.” She sets out to prove what really happened to Amelia, going through all of her emails, texts, and social media to piece together the last days of her life. It’s sobering to think about the state of cyberbullying today and remember how much this book affected me in 2013, in the earlier days of the internet when this sort of thing felt new and maybe still preventable.

The Unquiet Dead by Ausma Zehanat Khan (2015)

Esa Khattak is a second-generation Canadian Muslim and newly appointed lead of a community policing unit formed by the Canadian government to handle cases involving minorities. When a local man falls off a cliff, Esa and his partner, Detective Rachel Getty, are called in to work the case. As they look into the victim’s life, they realize he may have been living under a false identity—and that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Zehanat Khan combines gorgeous writing with layered characters and complex mystery plots in every book in this series. And if you like these, move on to her extensive backlist.

Turn of Mind by Alice LaPlante (2011)

Retired orthopedic surgeon Dr. Jennifer White is battling dementia and all of the adjustments that come with this life-changing diagnosis. When her best friend is killed and found with four of her fingers removed with surgical precision, Dr. White is named the prime suspect in her murder. This thriller is well-paced and handles the subject of dementia thoughtfully. It will keep you guessing and get you thinking about the frailty of memory.

Read more about The Taper Man and more new releases in this roundup of November’s new mysteries and thrillers, and get even more recommendations in our mystery and thriller archives.

issues.title: Graphic Novels to Read Based on Your Favorite Thanksgiving Dish
issues.summary: Let your favorite Thanksgiving dish help you pick a new graphic novel to enjoy after the big dinner.
issues.author: Susie Dumond
issues.content_html:
Thanksgiving is all about sharing a delicious meal with loved ones and reflecting on gratitude. But, like all good holidays, I’d argue it’s also about books. After all that cooking, eating, cleaning, and family time, you’re going to want a nice quiet moment to curl up with a book as you digest. Graphic novels and comics make for great Thanksgiving reading, as they wake up every part of your creative brain with vivid illustrations and unique storytelling, which can help cut through that post-turkey fog.

Which 2026 graphic novel should be your date to the family Thanksgiving celebration this year? The answer lies in what dish you’re most excited to eat. After all, the way to a reader’s heart is through their stomach-brain connection or something like that. I’ve paired some of this year’s best new graphic novels and comics with the most iconic Thanksgiving dishes. Load up your plate — and your bookshelf!

If You Love Turkey:

Homer’s The Odyssey: A Graphic Novel adapted by Steve Barlow and Steve Skidmore, illustrated by Martin Bustamante

You appreciate a good centerpiece, a prolific classic, the dish you’ve got to have on the holiday table and the book you’ve got to have on the well-rounded bookshelf. Some people accuse turkey of being dry and overhyped. Some might say the same of Homer’s The Odyssey (or of Christopher Nolan’s 2026 blockbuster film adaptation). But like a perfectly brined and baked turkey, this new graphic novel adaptation of The Odyssey can prove the haters wrong. It’s an action-packed, accessible introduction to one of the world’s oldest and most well-known stories.

If You Love Stuffing/Dressing:

To Dance the Moon and Stars by Tasia M.S. & Barbara Perez Marquez

Turkey could be considered the “serious literary fiction” of the Thanksgiving table. And if that’s true, then dressing (or stuffing, depending on who you ask) is the genre fiction that brings the fluffiness and well-seasoned flavor to the table. Romantasy may be considered “fluff” by some readers, but this graphic novel showcases the rich, layered, complex storytelling those snobs are missing out on by refusing to give the genre a shot. To Dance the Moon and Stars is a lush romantic fantasy about a teenager destined to become High Priestess who must save her kingdom from an ancient evil. It’s a treat for the brain, like stuffing is a treat for the palate.

If You Love Mashed Potatoes & Gravy:

Major Taylor: The World’s Fastest Man by Frederick Nolan

You like a side dish with some substance, topped with a spoonful of savory excitement. That means you should read this hearty graphic biography of Marshall Walter “Major” Taylor, a record-breaking Black American cyclist who grew up during Jim Crow and became an iconic early 20th-century champion athlete. Written by cartoonist and cyclist Frederick Nolan, it tells Taylor’s fascinating life story alongside an exploration of how the bicycle shaped the world we know today.

If You Love Green Bean Casserole:

As I Dream of You by Jennifer Lee and LeUyen Pham

Green bean casserole is a nostalgic comfort food beloved by many. The green beans give it a solid veggie base, the cream-of-mushroom soup brings a rich warmth, and the crunchy onions on top keep it texturally interesting. You’ll also find a classic story with an engaging twist in Jennifer Lee and LeUyen Pham’s As I Dream of You. It’s a gorgeously illustrated Orpheus and Eurydice retelling about two teens whose love story is ruptured when reality and fantasy become tangled, forcing them to fight for a future together.

If You Love Sweet Potato Casserole:

To All the Boys I Loved Before: The Graphic Novel by Jenny Han, illustrated by Akimaro and Li Lu, adapted by Barbara Perez Marquez

If you’re a fan of cinnamon-y, heartwarming sweet potato casserole, you should spend this Thanksgiving reading the graphic novel adaptation of Jenny Han’s bestselling YA rom-com To All the Boys I Loved Before. Lara Jean Covey never intended for the five love letters she wrote to her past crushes to reach their addressees. But when the letters get mistakenly dropped in the mail, things get complicated. Fluffy and a bit nutty, it’s a book that can unite the marshmallow topping and pecan topping camps of the sweet potato casserole fandom.

If You Love Dinner Rolls:

Encore! by Miles Toriko Burks

Dinner rolls are the unsung hero of Thanksgiving. They’re warm, cozy, comforting, and help sop up all the extra tasty bits left on your plate. And, like the best of theatrical performances, they leave you wishing you could enjoy a little more. In Encore!, Clay wants to spend his senior year giving his best performance to his high school theater program. But when his ex-best friend Aron ends up assigned as his improv partner in theater class, Clay has to manage some complicated feelings threatening to derail his senior year plans. It’s a warm, joyful YA rom-com for fans of Heartstopper (and lovers of a warm, yeasty dinner roll fresh out of the oven).

If You Love Cranberry Sauce:

Anxietyland by Gemma Correll

Some find cranberry sauce to be too tangy, sour, and sharp. But not you, my friend. You can carry the sweet and the sour at once in your heart. That’s why you’ll appreciate Gemma Correll’s darkly humorous memoir about life with severe anxiety. Playful, tender, healing, and deeply relatable, Correll’s signature art style makes this story about the ups and downs of mental health a truly enjoyable ride.

If You Love Pumpkin Pie:

Punk’n Heads by Dave Baker and Nicole Goux

Was my choice for pumpkin pie lovers influenced by the fact that this book involves pumpkins? Honestly, yeah. But isn’t pumpkin pie, a dessert made out of a weird giant gourd, also a little punk rock? Hannah is figuring out what to do with her life now that she’s dropped out of art school and gone through a breakup. She begrudgingly becomes the singer for a struggling horror-punk band known for performing with papier-mâché pumpkins over their heads. The music gives her a pathway to figuring some things out about herself — although hooking up with her bandmate and roommate also makes things even more complicated.

If You Hate All Thanksgiving Food:

Opting Out by Maia Kobabe & Swati “Lucky” Srikumar

If you think all Thanksgiving food is nasty and you’d rather opt out altogether, I get it. That’s valid. (Even if I think you maybe just haven’t been invited to the right chef’s Thanksgiving table.) You’ll feel seen by Opting Out, a new middle grade graphic novel about a junior high student named Saachi who, as the other kids start hitting puberty, realizes they don’t really feel like a girl or a boy. Coauthored by Gender Queer author/illustrator Maia Kobabe and debut author Lucky Srikumar, it’s a great story for readers of all ages who don’t like being told who they should be or what they should like.

We hope this helped you find the perfect graphic novel to read this Thanksgiving! Find more great comics on these lists:

6 Delicious Graphic Novels and Memoirs Spotlighting Food

Turning Inward: 4 Thought-Provoking Graphic Novels and Nonfiction Books

Falling Leaves (of Books): Graphic Novels That Are Giving Autumn

issues.title: Mom Is in Her Shapeshifting Era
issues.summary: The Original Mother The original mother brought out the toenail clippers and sat cross-legged in front of the La-Z-Boy, steadying her husband’s narrow foot with her left hand, his calloused heel wedged in her palm. His eyes were pointed at the TV. Jeopardy. “Who was it?” he asked. There had been a knock at the […] The post Mom Is in Her Shapeshifting Era appeared first on Electric Literature .
issues.author: Young Rader
issues.content_html:
The Original Mother

The original mother brought out the toenail clippers and sat cross-legged in front of the La-Z-Boy, steadying her husband’s narrow foot with her left hand, his calloused heel wedged in her palm. His eyes were pointed at the TV. Jeopardy. “Who was it?” he asked. There had been a knock at the door a short while ago.

“A man.”

“Huh.”

“Selling fish from a pole,” the original mother said.

Her husband dug at his jaw. “Who is Vasco . . .” he said. “Vasco da Gama!”

“Is that his name?”

Her husband’s face fell. “Huh?”

“The man,” the original mother said, suddenly finding herself curious for anything that might shed light on the stranger that had come to their door. “Does he sell fish here often? Vasco?”

“Oh, right,” her husband said, concentrating on the next clue. “Sure.” He wriggled his toes. His ankle let out a frivolous little crack.

They lapsed into silence.

The original mother pursed her lips and tried to clip his gray toenails, but the hot ache in her old, arthritic fingers was too much to bear.

“Ah . . . oh! What is the Law of Reflection?” her husband said.

The original mother let her eyes go soft. Her husband’s toes grew indistinct. As she reckoned with the crude geometry of this latest defeat, another woman, her mirror image, brought out a second pair of toenail clippers, sat cross-legged before the La-Z-Boy, and steadied the husband’s other foot with her right hand.

The original mother’s husband jerked the legrest down and grasped both women by their wrists, shaking the toenail clippers from their hands. The mothers appraised each other and said, “Who are you?” Then they looked at their husband, gawking at them like a carp.

He tightened his grip and held on well past the evening news.

The second woman coughed harshly and then, quite astonishingly, crumpled in on herself, until a fox emerged from the folds of a uniform of a mother. “Get out of here,” her husband growled. The fox regarded the original mother before bolting out the door through the pet flap, unused since the beagle’s death, but the original mother hadn’t seen a thing. She’d made herself absent, her eyes shut tight to brace against the pain of her husband’s grip, but also to better heed her heart.

Remarkable, the way it beat!

The original mother’s older brother came to visit, the first time in nearly forty years, spurred by their younger sister’s coming-out message in their otherwise uneventful group chat on KakaoTalk. When he arrived, his shirttail got caught in the taxi’s door, the tiny wheels of his mean aluminum suitcase burst asunder over a crack, and he immediately stubbed his toe on the doorjamb. “Sister,” he said, between dramatic breaths and staring incredulously at the pet flap, “what is this? This American existence?”

The original mother knew why he had really come: to lay bare his love and resentment to the woman for whom he had long nursed a quiet crush, foolishly believing her to be nothing more than their younger sister’s best friend. It didn’t matter that he was old, that they were all old, the geometry of their ways long set fast. He had come to make a point. He would have the original mother drive him a short distance to the sister’s apartment, where he’d condemn her for the wickedness of homosexuality, disown her in the same breath, and then turn his frustrations on the original mother, enumerating all the ways American life had tarnished her character.

As the original mother cooked him a lavish meal, she flung open the windows to air the house so her husband wouldn’t carp about the smell of their “exotic” food encroaching on his enjoyment of Jeopardy. “My hands are dry, sister.” She gave her brother almond-scented hand lotion, envying the straightness of his fingers. “I’m thirsty,” he whined. She handed him a glass of cold water. “America has made you fatter than you should be.” The bean curd stew boiled furiously. The stuffed perilla leaves steamed into her face. Her brother proceeded to explain how she was to blame for, well, everything. He had an enlarged prostate and had developed an irrational fear of death, and even that was her fault. “I’m hungry. I’m hungry.” Just as she set down the bowl of rice, another hand, not her own, placed a bowl of rice beside it. It belonged to a woman who looked exactly like her. They stood at the table and appraised each other and said, “Who are you?” Then they looked at their brother, glaring incandescently at them like a lacquered scorpion.

“Ahn-nyah! Now, sister, what is this?” Her brother’s eyes narrowed as he ripped into her for such brazen chicanery. Only in America, he fumed, would a brother be served a dinner conjured by some kind of black magic, almost certainly purchased on Amazon. He shouted so loudly that the original mother’s husband had to crank up the TV.

Her brother shouted well past the evening news.

The second mother plugged her ears with her fingers, then puffed out her cheeks and emitted an uncanny whine. The sound was enough to stop the original mother’s brother mid-rant. As the air escaped the woman’s body, she crumpled in on herself, quite miraculously, until a fox emerged from the folds of a uniform of a mother. “Get out of here,” her brother growled. The original mother hadn’t seen a thing. She’d made herself absent, her eyes shut tight to brace against her brother’s words, but also to better heed her heart.

Remarkable, the way it beat!

The original mother once had a mother, and her mother a mother as well, the uniform of the original mother passing from one generation to the next.

Earlier, her son had called, but she wasn’t in the right mindset to answer, crushed, as she was, by the geometry of her exhaustion.

She should have answered, or at least called back. Now, an intrusive guilt keeps her awake long after the late-night news.

The original mother blinks into the dark, thinking. If her son had answered the door, he would have bought a fish from—what was his name again? She opens her mouth very slightly and focuses on the puckered shadow cast by the curtain, situating herself in the moment the name was spoken. Finally, it comes to her, bright as happiness: Vasco.

Her son, keen to avoid confrontation in any form and unwilling to risk seeming an inconvenience to anyone but his mother, would have taken one look at Vasco, spun a private story about his troubles, and bought a fish, because who went around selling fish like that? He would have carried it inside and left it in its taut plastic bag on the kitchen counter beside the instant coffee and her husband’s glazed donuts, where she would have had to contend with the fish’s pouting mouth and its eyes, gaping up at her in troubled amazement.

Her son’s birth had been a very difficult one.

The original mother eases out from under the sheets, pads past the extraordinary sounds of her husband’s snoring, past her brother’s faltering puffs and snorts, and pauses before the cheval mirror, an heirloom from her husband’s mother, and the only thing her brother allowed any measure of approval as he wended unbidden through every room, drumming his index finger against his lips. Even in the dark, she sees the woman standing on the other side who looks exactly like her. She is wholly present now, heeds her heart—remarkable, the way it beats!

She slips into the utility room and opens the drawer that only a mother would ever think to open, a drawer that only a mother would even know exists. From beneath a bright orange box of dryer sheets, she pulls out a uniform of a fox. She contorts into it, her joints and muscles screaming, thinking all the while, “When will it be done?”

It is done.

She will return before sunrise, before the morning news, to resume her duties as the original mother, of course. But until then, the night is hers. She darts through the pet flap—but not before appraising the woman in the mirror—and vanishes tenderly into the dark.

issues.title: Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel Satirizes the Idea That Black Men Are Invincible
issues.summary: Rumor has it that now—in our world of alternative facts, of journalists replaced by influencers, experts replaced by AI, and of news constantly deemed fake—we’ve finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “truth.” Hard data is tough to come by, since sensationalism’s better for algorithms. It’s difficult to tell if any given video […] The post Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel
issues.author: Jalen Giovanni Jones
issues.content_html:
Rumor has it that now—in our world of alternative facts, of journalists replaced by influencers, experts replaced by AI, and of news constantly deemed fake—we’ve finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “truth.” Hard data is tough to come by, since sensationalism’s better for algorithms. It’s difficult to tell if any given video is secretly an ad. Not even our Google searches can be trusted. They’re calling it a “post-truth society,” and here we are, left in constant skepticism over the fabric of our reality. Did we really have a White House Press Secretary between October 12th and October 16th, 2026? Is Manon of KATSEYE really on “hiatus”? Could we really “see everything”? Ugh. We can’t even trust our documentaries anymore.

Multi-award-winning, National Book Award longlisted author Nafissa Thompson-Spires knows none of this is new. Her second book and debut novel, The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford (a current First Novel Prize finalist) is set in the all-Black town of 1920s Newville, where the town has finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “Richard Milford.” An infamous moonshiner, an unloyal womanizer, and just plain mean, the town will tell you—collectively—that this is good riddance. That is, except for his four wives and his beloved housekeeper Alberta. They’d surely remember him differently, right? Unless they somehow had reason to kill him . . . Wait, how many times did Rich die?

With slick wit, a wry sense of dark humor, and a hefty dose of whimsy, Thompson-Spires deconstructs the idea of truth before our very eyes in this tightly wrapped satire/whodunnit. Over Zoom, the author and I discussed how our imaginations can deceive us, the careful game of Black satire, John Edgar Wideman’s concept of “Great Time,” and how she brought herself back to play after years of fearing the sophomore slump.

Jalen Giovanni Jones: Your previous book, the short story collectionHeads of the Colored People, grappled with being Black in a world that constantly gaslights you. Given thatThe Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milfordinterrogates our notion of a concrete truth, I’m curious to know if you were expanding on those ideas that you set up in your first book.

Nafissa Thompson-Spires: You know, I was. All these women in the book have been gaslit in many different ways. The town of Newville is gaslighting, too, when it comes to how they approach Rich—how they think about his trauma, and how they see him as this cursed, evil figure that they’re happy to be rid of. And gaslighting plays a huge part in how the book’s climax manifests. My writing is still interested in that overall project.

JGJ: What was your experience like, transitioning from short story writing to novel writing? Do you find your approach to be vastly different between each form?

NTS: They were very different at first. I found novel writing really difficult. God bless all the people who can write novels, who can just pop them out so quickly. This book took me five years. It’s a slim book, but ultimately my editors gave me some good advice—to lean into my talents as a short story writer, and to lean into what made Heads work, in order to write this book. That’s why the book consists of short chapters that are almost standalone, yet are all linked in their own way.

The process for me involved a lot of prayer, a lot of worrying, a lot of fretting. Things really crystallized, though, when I told RO Kwon that I really wanted to make Richard Milford die in five different ways. I was really stuck on the structure, but she was like “well why don’t you make him die five different ways?” After those deaths dictated the structure, everything else came together. That’s true for my stories in general—once I have the structure, then I know what I’m doing.

JGJ: Speaking of structure, you take on many different POVs throughout the novel—six perspectives, which is impressive in under 200 pages. How’d you know which perspectives to include, and when?

NTS: I knew I wanted all of the women to have a part, including the housekeeper Alberta. I organized it by each death—who held the first baton in the murder-relay race, and then who passed it off to the next person, and to the next. Alberta specifically is central to the book because she’s known Rich all his life. She can speak to how he was as a child in the same way that the town of Newville can, but with more intimacy and perhaps more honesty, because I think Newville gets a lot of things wrong.

Newville brought a tall tale quality to the novel’s structure, which built out as I thought more about who I wanted Rich to be. Initially he started as an attempt to satirize the traditional trauma plot. But I wanted to write his traumas without limiting his backstory to solely those experiences. He has so many different things that you can blame for his bad behavior, all of them outlandish: getting thrown from a horse, getting struck by lightning, the murder-suicide of his parents, being double dipped during his baptism, and so on. I wanted to play with origin stories, to question how we become who we are.

JGJ: I took note of the novel’s tall-tale quality. Even though I’d call it realist, it still has elements of the fantastical and surreal. There’s lightning strikes, visions that people are having, and Rich just refuses to actually die. Were you intentionally turning away from realism with this novel?

NTS: I’m not sure it was an intentional turn away from realism, but I knew that I wanted the realism to be spiced and peppered with that magic. I was really thinking of tall tales and fables, and how somebody can grow so big in your mind that they’re no longer a real person to you. I was hesitant to do that with Rich at first, because I didn’t want to feed into the idea of an “invincible Black man who can’t be killed, can’t be tamed.” I wanted to write a Black man who was a real person, as much as he was a figment of people’s imaginations. That’s part of what the book is satirizing—how we think about Black men as indestructible. Why do police have to shoot Black men at all? Why so many times? Why taze and shoot and kick? All of those mini-deaths that Rich dies are part of that commentary. The way that he won’t die is part of this questioning of why the Black man lives this way in the figments of our imagination.

JGJ: The idea of a person can end up becoming something entirely separate from who they are in reality. I see that manifesting a lot in today’s world especially. So what was it that made you want to set this novel in the 1920s?

NTS: I wanted an all-Black town. I knew that from the very beginning. This story is based on my real life great-grandfather, who grew up in the 30s and 40s, had 40 children and three wives, and beat them all with a horse whip. I wanted to see what it would be like for the women in his life to get revenge on him. My great grandfather was known as both a menace in his town, as well as this beloved figure. I wanted to hold space for both of those things, and setting the story in an all-Black town had the locale that could.

Oklahoma made the most sense because it historically had 50 all-Black towns, and only 13 of them remain. That’s where Newville’s goal for self-preservation came into play—the idea that people are competing for versions of the truth, because they’re competing to be historicized, to make sure that they’re remembered and have a legacy. I wanted to draw attention to the legacies of these real-life towns as well, because so many of them—while remembered by the people who live near them—are forgotten by history in so many ways.

JGJ: While the Newville sections of the novel capture more widely held beliefs of the townpeople, those sections also feel very biased and gossipy. What was your process in determining Newville as a collective narrator “character?”

NTS: Newville represents the messiest and worst people of the town, and also demonstrates all of the civic engagement of real life Black people during this time period. These small towns were involved in projects of civic engagement, grappling with real questions: What should Blackness look like? What should a Black Nationalist project look like? What kind of Black Nationalism should we practice? How do we have our own spaces without white interference, how should we run our own towns, our own governments, and our own finances as much as possible? It had to be a made-up town so that I could play with history a little bit, but there are real nods to historic moments at that time—like Booker T Washington passing through on his way to Boley. Obviously, Tulsa’s in the book, and then there is the anti-lynching committee, which would have been like so many other committees in other towns. All of those things were meant to draw both attention to the real towns, and to allow me space to play.

JGJ: One aspect that I really loved in this book was this meta quality of the narration. What do you find useful about the more meta qualities in your writing?

NTS: I love metafiction because most people get it. With satire, some things are hard for everyone to be in on the joke about. Metafiction is not like that most of the time. You can see when a book is commenting on the act of writing or the art of storytelling pretty easily. And I’m always really interested in literary allusion. Postmodernist writers really inform my work. Ishmael Reed and the way that he plays with time and history. John Edgar Wideman talks about Great Time in his work, which describes how for Black people, time is a circle. Everything is happening at the same time and at a different time, and it’s repetitive. I wanted to think about that with storytelling. All texts are related to each other in some way or another. Newville is both a Greek chorus, and it’s specific to these Black people in this 1920s space.

JGJ: You’ve stated that you write for expository reasons—to expose things going on in the world, sometimes to shame people for doing them, but also to work things out and disarm people. What were you trying to expose or disarm in this novel?

NTS: I wanted to expose how time is cyclical, and for Black people, the same things are going on now that have been going on ad nauseum. This story could very well apply to the now. We still have real-life lynchings happening often.

There’s a really horrible story in my family, where I walked up to people who lynched one of my relatives when I was two. We were in a Dairy Queen in Texas, and everybody knew about it. Everyone knew that these were the loved ones of this person who had lynched my relative. You could be a two-year-old innocent child just trying to get an ice cream cone, friendly enough to walk up to some people, and those very people could be the perpetrators of this horrific crime, unpunished. That story has always stuck with me as a reminder of Great Time—that nothing is new under the sun. I wanted to think about that, expose that.

JGJ: I want to ask how you imagined your audience as you were writing this. Especially sinceFour Wivesis your second book, I’m wondering if you had to reimagine who was going to be reading this new project.

NTS: I thought a lot more about audience with this book than I did with the previous one. With the first one, I was just playing. I was pissed that I had a revise and resubmit from some agent who hadn’t agreed to represent me, and I wrote Heads of the Colored People really, really fast (instead of the book that I was supposed to be revising and resubmitting). I call it naughty writing—when you get stuff done, because you’re not supposed to be getting it done. This new book was not naughty writing. There was a machine and pressure behind it.

7 Smart and Hilarious Books that Brilliantly Satirize Race

These writers will make you look at racial identity in a new way

Jan 28 – Z. Hanna Reading Lists

A lot of people talk about the sophomore slump—this idea that the second book is just so much harder. I had so much fear that I was going to fall into a sophomore slump, that I was going to have a really trepidatious time writing it. And so I had a trepidatious time writing it. It was really, really difficult to write this book.

I thought about audience in that I wanted my old audience to be pleased with it, to still want to read me. I was very afraid of how the book would be received because it’s very different from Heads. I had some people in my life who were saying that succeeding projects were “just not like Heads! Just not the same as Heads!” That put a lot of pressure on me. It made it difficult to go forward. I had to overcome a lot of fear in order to really engage with audience in this book.

JGJ: Knowing that, I want to know how you came back to your sense of play. Reading it, there’s plenty of playfulness: the humor, the metafiction, the satire, the sly voice. How did you make sure to keep those qualities that are true to your writing style still embedded in this novel?

NTS: I had to keep reminding myself of what I tell my students, which is that play always has to come back into the picture. If you’re stuck, play. If you don’t know where to go, play. If you’re not playing, you’re not doing it; you’ve forgotten part of your motivation for writing—and I had forgotten that, momentarily. At one point I had done something funny, and my editor left a note saying “Oh, can we see more whimsy?” I know everybody’s saying whimsy lately, but that was literally her note. As soon as I felt like I had permission to be playful, I ran with it. Like the line dances that structure the book—slide to the left, slide to the right. I created this Goddess Rosemary. All these things that were more interesting, and more in line with my own aesthetic. It felt good to get back to play.

The post Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel Satirizes the Idea That Black Men Are Invincible appeared first on Electric Literature.
