issues.title: A world of wealth: 12 of the richest people who ever lived
issues.summary: How do you weigh Genghis Khan’s empire against Elon Musk’s shares? Meet 12 people from world history whose fortunes reveal just how many ways there are to be rich
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
When it comes to sifting through history’s uber-wealthy and deciding exactly who was rolling in the biggest pile of cash, a myriad of issues arise. One that stymies historians and economists is how to go about adjusting values across different epochs and different, even defunct, currencies.

Then there’s how to distinguish between personal wealth (essentially, how much money a person has stuffed under their mattress) and the worth of holdings, whether that is in assets, land or glittering treasures. This is especially tricky with sovereign leaders: their domain might bring in spectacular wealth, but that does not necessarily make it their money.

Is it possible to compare Elon Musk – who, in June 2026, made history when a rise in his shares temporarily made him the world’s first trillionaire – with Genghis Khan, who built a colossal empire filled with lucrative resources and industries?

Identifying the richest people in history, therefore, is fraught with difficulty and open to infinite interpretation. Regardless, there's no doubting that these rulers, businessmen and bankers all had the deepest of deep pockets.

Amenhotep III (Unknown–c1353 BC)

Egyptian pharaoh whose wealth is estimated in the trillions of US dollars, though his personal fortune is unknown.

The pharaohs of ancient Egypt were, to put it mildly, not embarrassed about flaunting their wealth. Standing tall above them all as the wealthiest was Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty, during the 14th century BC.

His reign witnessed a golden age both for Egyptian culture and political power. Diplomats and leaders from other nations would write to Amenhotep simply to ask him for gifts of gold, such was his reputation. There is no knowing the value of his domain, or personal fortune, but suffice to say that it ran into the trillions, and since he was deified as a god, all of Egypt’s glory was indeed his.

Marcus Licinius Crassus (c115 BC–53 BC)

Roman statesman and general worth approximately 200 million sesterces, according to Pliny the Elder.

While Marcus Licinius Crassus reached the top of Roman politics as one-third of the First Triumvirate, he is better known as “the richest man in Rome”.

As a general, he prospered thanks to proscriptions (the confiscation of property belonging to enemies of the state) and as a businessman, he was a ruthless estate agent and bought up many of the houses in Rome. One of his tricks was to set up his own fire brigade and offer to put out any houses that caught ablaze when the owners promised to sell it to him for slashed prices.

Crassus’s wealth is hard to gauge in modern terms, although Pliny the Elder claimed he had 200 million sesterces, which equated to the entire annual budget of the Roman Republic. Such was his reputation for lucre that a rumour spread after his death in 53 BC that his enemies had poured molten gold down his throat.

Augustus (63 BC–AD 14)

Roman emperor worth approximately US$4.6 trillion, based on his estimated share of the imperial economy.

Calculating the personal wealth of a historical ruler is enough to give historians and economists alike a headache, but the sums attached to Augustus are truly head-spinning.

Not only did he oversee the finances of a mighty empire, but, after defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra, he took ownership over Egypt. To be clear, the land of the pharaohs did not just become part of the Roman world – it was a personal province of Augustus. Estimates about what this did to his wealth suggest that he owned one-fifth of the imperial economy, which has been translated into a modern-day value of $4.6 trillion (almost £3.5 trillion).

Wu Zetian (AD 624–705)

Empress of China who ruled an economy valued at approximately US$16 trillion.

On top of being the only female emperor in China’s history, Wu Zetian may well hold the title as the richest woman of all time.

Having ruled the Tang Dynasty alongside her husband and in the name of her sons for decades, in AD 690 she proclaimed her own Zhou Dynasty and acted as sole sovereign for 15 years. Under her efficient and brutal leadership, the empire expanded and the economy flourished with the tea and silk trades to western nations. In fact, while she was empress, China accounted for around 23 per cent of the global GDP, which has been estimated to be at the $16 trillion (almost £12 trillion) mark. For context, the richest woman today – Alice Walton, the heiress of Walmart – has a fortune 120 times smaller.

William the Conqueror (c1028–1087)

King of England worth approximately US$230 billion.

After seizing the English throne in 1066, the conquering Duke of Normandy set about confiscating vast swathes of land and bringing the resources of the country under his personal control. For the next 20 years, revenue poured in through rents, taxation and plundered treasures, and William the Conqueror protected his position and his purse with new castles, most famously the White Tower, the central fortification of the Tower of London.

Not content with accumulating wealth for himself alone, he also handed out huge sums to his allies. One relative, Alan Rufus, received such extravagant rewards for his military service in the Norman Conquest that his fortune ballooned to around $194 billion (almost £145 billion), just off the pace of William’s $230 billion (£170 billion).

Mansa Musa (c1280–c1337)

Ruler of the Mali Empire worth approximately US$400 billion, by a speculative estimate.

A name that crops up on every list of the historical rich is Mansa Musa.

In the first half of the 14th century, he presided over the pinnacle of the Mali Empire, a vast realm in West Africa rich in gold and salt, and strategically placed for trade routes. Mansa Musa is often credited as the richest person in history due to his dragon-sitting-on-a-treasure-sized piles of gold, with his mines supplying the Islamic world. Most famously, when he embarked on a hajj to Mecca in 1324, he travelled with 60,000 people and long caravans of slaves, dressed in Persian silk, each carrying gold bars.

According to accounts of his fabulous parades in Cairo, Mansa Musa handed out so much gold that it caused a major devaluation of the precious metal and a currency crisis that lasted years. A conservative estimate of his adjusted wealth is $400 billion (almost £300 billion), although many historians refuse to give a figure at all, instead claiming his wealth was beyond calculation.

Jakob Fugger (1459–1525)

German merchant and banker worth up to US$400 billion.

As the man behind the scenes and pulling the purse strings of medieval politics, Jakob Fugger was far wealthier than emperors, kings and popes.

Born in 1459 into a successful merchant family, he possessed a canny head for business and bookkeeping, shifting from Italian textiles to a more diverse portfolio. Most lucratively, he engaged in silver and copper mining, and tried his hand as a banker. Offering loans to the rich and powerful made him even richer and more powerful, with every deal negotiated bringing in assets and compounding wealth. He funded military campaigns, loaned to the Vatican and acted as chief financier of the Habsburgs, securing the position of Holy Roman Emperors.

On his death in 1525, he left a fortune of 2 million guilders; in today’s money Fugger the Rich may have been worth as much as $400 billion (£300 billion).

Heshen (1750–1799)

Chinese imperial official worth up to US$270 billion.

Heshen has been described as the most corrupt official in Chinese history.

As a favourite of the Qianlong Emperor in the 18th century, he gained control over ministerial posts and imperial revenue, which allowed him to steal funds and take bribes on an almost-industrial scale. At the same time, he built his own commercial empire of banks and pawnshops. During a revolt in 1796, he made sure the military campaign to put it down was prolonged so that he could pocket money being allocated to the army. It all came crashing down with the death of the emperor in 1799, with Heshen arrested and forced to put himself to death. His property was seized, valued at 1.1 billion taels of silver, or possibly as much as $270 billion (£200 billion) in today’s money.

Andrew Carnegie (1835–1919)

Scottish-American steel industrialist worth over US$300 billion before his major charitable gifts.

Andrew Carnegie made his fortune with steel.

Born to a poor family in Scotland and immigrating to the United States as a child, he built a career at the Pennsylvania Railroad Company before setting up the first steel plants in the country in the 1870s. By the time he sold Carnegie Steel in 1901, it was worth around two per cent of the entire US gross domestic product (GDP). While that fortune – adjusted to over $300 billion (£225 billion) – earns his place on this list, Carnegie did not die in 1919 as one of history’s wealthiest people. After retiring, he dedicated his life to philanthropic pursuits and gave way most of his money, espousing the mantra: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”

John D Rockefeller (1839–1937)

American oil industrialist worth well over US$300 billion.

The Rockefeller name is a bulwark of American business: throughout the 20th century, it became synonymous with wealth and success, thanks to its patriarchal figurehead. John D Rockefeller founded Standard Oil Company in 1870, correctly predicting the potential impact of oil on the modern world, and under his leadership, the company grew so powerful that it refined more than 90 per cent of all the oil in the United States. He held the monopoly on what was quickly becoming one of the most precious resources, accruing a fortune worth well over $300 billion (almost £225 billion) today.

In 1916, he was recognised as the first American to hit the magic ten figures to become a billionaire.

Henry Ford (1863–1947)

American automobile industrialist worth up to US$200 billion.

Henry Ford forever changed the world of the 20th century by making the automobile available to the mass market and revolutionising industrial practices through the introduction of assembly line production.

His Ford Motor Company, founded in 1903, unveiled the Model T and sold 15 million of them around the world over the next two decades (no car sold more until the Volkswagen Beetle). Needless to say, this made Ford a fabulous fortune. He joined the billionaire club in the 1920s, only a few years after John D Rockefeller, and by the time of this death in 1947 he had the equivalent of up to $200 billion (£150 billion) today. And, of course, Ford's company is still going strong.

Osman Ali Khan (1886–1967)

Nizam of Hyderabad worth upwards of US$200 billion.

Here’s how rich Osman Ali Khan was: he used the Jacob Diamond – a 184-carat masterpiece and one of the largest diamonds in the world – as a paperweight. During his 37-year reign as nizam (ruler) of the Indian state of Hyderabad (1911-48), he built his monumental wealth by issuing his own currency and controlling the world’s primary diamond mines, including where the Jacob and Koh-i-Noor were unearthed.

His private treasury was reportedly bursting with gold, silver and precious jewels, which would be worth upwards of $200 billion (almost £150 billion) today. No wonder the cover of a 1937 issue of Time magazine described him as “the richest man in the world”.

issues.title: The Odyssey has a "bizarre" sequel, but it's been forgotten for a good reason
issues.summary: The hero of Homer’s epic poem didn’t just relax when he finally got back to Ithaca. Instead, Odysseus soon set out to sea again
issues.author: Serafina Kenny
issues.content_html:
The Odyssey is a long book, but it doesn’t cover the whole story of its hero. As well the Iliad, which shows us Odysseus as one of Agamemnon’s most trusted commanders at Troy, there was a sequel called the Telegony. This covered what Odysseus did once he returned from his travels, although sadly its full text has been lost.

You might think that, after being away from home for decades, Odysseus would have wanted to stay put for a while. Not at all, says says Dr Daisy Dunn, classicist and author, speaking on the HistoryExtra podcast. “[In the Telegony], he decides that he can’t just sit still. After all that travelling, he can’t just be done with it, so he continues on his travels,”

  • Read more | Is The Odyssey based on a true story? The movie's historical accuracy explained

The Telegony involves yet more years spent away from home and yet another two families for Odysseus, before concluding with his untimely end.

The Epic Cycle in the literature of ancient Greece

To understand how the Telegony came to be written, it helps to understand that it was part of the Epic Cycle, a collection of narrative poems that told the story of the Trojan war.

“The whole idea with this Epic Cycle is that [its poem] are prequels and sequels to the Iliad and the Odyssey,” Dunn says. Furthermore, there is debate among scholars about whether the Odyssey and the Iliad themselves should be included in the Cycle.

It’s also not clear if the various poems were originally intended to be one cohesive collection of stories. Instead, they may have originated separately, and then been edited and tidied up so that there were no overlaps.

  • Read more | Did the Trojan War really happen? Here's why even Odyssey experts can't agree

They all probably come from the oral tradition, meaning they weren’t written by one person and were instead told verbally with variation each time. Despite this, the poems have been attributed to various people – most notably a group conveniently called the Cyclic Poets – over the years.

The Telegony was often attributed to Cinaethon of Sparta in antiquity, whereas another source says it was stolen from the polymath Musaeus by Eugammon of Cyrene. This makes it hard to date, since Cinaethon was writing in the eighth century BC and Eugammon was around in the sixth century BC.

Words that didn’t endure

This much we do know about the Epic Cycle: unlike the Odyssey and the Iliad, any records of the content of the Epic Cycle poems have been mostly lost. However, we know about their existence through summaries of their plots from other ancient sources, although these have vague provenances.

The most notable is Venetus A, a manuscript from the 10th century AD that is one of the most famous sources of the full text of the Iliad. Although it was produced up to 1,800 years after Eugammon was around, it is also one of the best records we have of the Epic Cycle, because its preface contains summaries of their stories. These summaries are taken from a longer work called Chrestomathy by Proclus, a figure scholars struggle to identify definitively because his name is shared by a fifth-century philosopher and earlier grammarians.

Whoever wrote down the plot, the Telegony picks up on after the Odyssey ends. It tells of a further voyage Odysseus makes to a place called Thesprotia. It moves on to tell the story of his son, Telegonus. Some scholars think these may in fact have been two different epics, but others think the story starring Odysseus may have just been a chapter called the Thesprotis within a wider poem.

Odysseus leaves home. Again

The Telegony opens with Odysseus finally at home in Ithaca with his wife, Penelope, and their son, Telemachus. He is burying all of the men who had been competing to marry Penelope while he was believed dead, those he killed at the end of the Odyssey.

Unhappy to just sit put at home, Odysseus sets off for further travels on the mainland of Greece, ostensibly to make sacrifices at the behest of a prophet we encounter in the Odyssey.

But true to form, he soon gets distracted in Thesprotia, where he meets another queen, called Callidice. They get married and have a son, Polypoetes, before Odysseus fights with the Thesprotians in a war with a neighbouring kingdom.

We don’t know how long Odysseus stays in Thesprotia, but it’s long enough for Callidice to die and for Polypoetes to become old enough to inherit the kingdom. Odysseus leaves Polypoetes to rule Thesprotia and returns to Ithaca.

An epic soap opera

The Telegony says that Odysseus fathered a son called Telegonus by the sorceress Circe when, as recounted in the Odyssey, he lived with her in Aeaea for a year.

In the second part of the Telegony, Telegonus sets off to try to find his father. For protection, Circe gives him a spear that has been tipped with the poison barb of a stingray.

He doesn’t know his father is in Ithaca, but meets him by accident when a storm forces him to land on the island. Telegonus is really hungry, so he starts stealing cattle that belong to Odysseus, who comes to fight off the stranger trying to take his property.

  • Read more | Was Telemachus a real person? The history behind The Odyssey character explained

“There’s a proper tussle between Odysseus and the Ithacans, and this new stranger,” Dunn says. Telegonus stabs Odysseus with his stingray barb, fulfilling a prophecy in the Odyssey that says death will come for Odysseus “out of the sea”. It’s only as Odysseus lies dying that the two recognise each other.

“Quite bizarre, but it doesn't end there,” Dunn says. Accompanied by Penelope and Telemachus, Telegonus brings the corpse of Odysseus back home to Aeaea to bury him. At which point, Circe makes them all immortal.

“And then, even more bizarre, Penelope decides to marry Telegonus and Telemachus, her son, marries Circe,” Dunn says.

Certainly, a strange epilogue to one of history's greatest stories.

issues.title: Hungary's freedom fight: how one nation's resistance to Soviet tyranny changed history forever
issues.summary: Seventy years ago, Hungarians incensed by repression rose up against the country’s communist regime – and were brutally crushed. Martyn Rady reveals how the memory of 1956 rehabilitated the nation’s reputation, and is still used today as a political weapon
issues.content_html:
The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was not a media event. The surviving photographs of its course and suppression by Soviet tanks are mostly grainy, and the few snatches of film are frustratingly short. But one photograph stands out: a portrait of a girl in a padded jacket and fur cap holding a sub-machine gun. Taken in Budapest by the Danish photographer Vagn Hansen on 1 November 1956, a week after the outbreak of the uprising, it was first published in the Danish magazine Billed Bladet and reproduced across the world. It became the face of resistance to Soviet tyranny.

Hansen was not the only journalist to take an image of the girl, but it was not until the late 2000s that her identity was confirmed as Erika Széles, a catering apprentice just 15 years old at the time. Erika did not live long enough to see her face in the international press. By the time the photo appeared in Billed Bladet on 13 November, she had been dead for a week – killed in a shoot-out with Soviet troops after she’d gone to rescue a wounded companion. A square in Budapest is now named in her honour.

The portrait of Erika does not just commemorate courage. It stands, too, for Hungary’s rehabilitation and for the way in which the 1956 revolution altered perceptions of the country.

Rewriting history

Hungary’s story in the first half of the 20th century makes for a bad one. It fought on the ‘wrong’ side in both world wars and, in 1920, was the first modern European power to pass antisemitic legislation. Its native fascist movement, the Arrow Cross, had in 1944–45 been no less genocidal than its Nazi counterpart, slaughtering tens of thousands of Jews, many of whom they shot on Budapest’s Danube embankment.

With the Soviet takeover after 1945, Hungary’s new communist rulers became the most slavish of Stalin’s acolytes, brutally imposing a rigid ideology with the help of a sadistic secret police force. Possibly as many as one-tenth of its people were hauled before the courts on political grounds or on charges of economic ‘sabotage’. Purges, show trials, torture and internment without trial were parts of everyday life. When, in his 1949 novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, George Orwell described the future as a “boot stamping on a human face”, he could have been writing about postwar Hungary.

The 1956 revolution redeemed the country. Not only did its people prove that they were not Stalinist stooges, they also demonstrated and fought in the streets. Up to 3,000 were killed in battles in Budapest and other Hungarian cities. The revolutionaries took on a Soviet army of 200,000 men and 5,000 tanks equipped with only light arms and petrol bombs. Their bravery inspired another portrait, this time an artist’s generic impression: the ‘Hungarian Freedom Fighter’, chosen by Time magazine as its 1956 ‘Man of the Year’.

In the wake of the revolution’s violent suppression, refugees flooded out. Over several months, 200,000 Hungarians fled to the west, some 20,000 of whom came to the UK. Most of the refugees were less than 40 years old, and many belonged to the professions. Altogether, about 20 per cent of Hungarians who had received a post-secondary-school education migrated to the west, including about half of the faculty and students of the Sopron School of Forestry, which relocated en masse to the University of British Columbia in Canada.

Young and versatile, some of the refugees went on to become world-leading scientists, academics and literary figures. Others would use the skills that they had already mastered in the service of their new homelands. Chef Lajos Permayer set up the Louis patisserie on Heath Street in Hampstead, north London. And after several years in the sporting wilderness, legendary footballer Ferenc Puskás moved to Spain in 1958 and signed for Real Madrid. Almost universally, the refugees proved themselves ‘good citizens’ whose example did much to eclipse the more disagreeable features of Hungary’s recent past.

Reputational damage

Hungary’s rehabilitation came at the cost of Soviet communism’s reputation. Throughout western Europe, communist parties suffered a haemorrhaging of membership. The aggressive defence of the Soviet military intervention by the Italian, French and British Communist Party leaders disillusioned the rank and file; roughly a third of their members now drifted off to join the mainstream socialist movement or fringe Trotskyite groups. Many eventually embraced the democratic alternative of Euro-Communism and the ideal of a communism freed from Soviet oversight.

Among those leaving the Communist Party of Great Britain was the journalist Peter Fryer, who wrote for the Daily Worker (later renamed the Morning Star) and went to Budapest in 1956 to report on the revolution. Fryer was outraged by the Daily Worker’s editorial decision to call the Hungarian uprising a “counter-revolution”, and by the continued spiking of his articles. One of his pieces, which the Daily Worker did not print, gave this account of the revolution’s origins: “After 11 years the incessant mistakes of the communist leaders, the brutality of the State Security Police, the widespread bureaucracy and mismanagement, the bungling, the arbitrary methods and the lies have led to total collapse. This was… the upsurge of a whole people… against a police dictatorship dressed up as a Socialist society.”

Fryer’s assessment was shrewd, but the bungling also went right to the top of the Soviet bloc. Ultimately, it was the Soviet leadership that misjudged events and made Hungary ripe for revolution.

  • Read more | Why did the Soviet Union adopt the hammer and sickle, and how did it become a symbol of communist revolution?

With Stalin’s death in March 1953, the collective Soviet leadership – headed first by Georgy Malenkov then, after 1955, by Nikita Khrushchev – began the dismantling of the old dictator’s legacy. The gulags started to open, consumer goods became available, and economic priorities shifted from heavy industry to light manufacturing and housebuilding. Soviet cities such as Moscow and Kyiv suddenly brightened up, with restaurants opening to cater to a smart clientele, food stores offering more than just bottled vegetables, even a scattering of teddy boys dressed in what they took to be western fashions.

The Soviet leadership intended that the ‘New Course’, as it was known, would be adopted by the satellites – and that meant that the old guard who had dominated the Hungarian Communist Party would have to give way. Power there had been concentrated in the hands of Mátyás Rákosi, who was simultaneously prime minister and head of the Communist Party, known after 1948 as the Hungarian Workers’ Party. An engaging personality with fluent English and a distinctive Yul Brynner profile, Rákosi was also vicious and manipulative.

Summoned to Moscow in June 1953 to meet Soviet party bosses, Rákosi bore the full brunt of their criticism. Everything he had done had been wrong, Khrushchev explained, from backing heavy industry to orchestrating purges and show trials. The other Soviet leaders chimed in, accusing Rákosi of bossiness, abuse of power, and disregarding legal process.

Rákosi did what was expected of a good communist. He admitted his mistakes and agreed to give up the office of prime minister, while retaining leadership of the party. His successor as prime minister was the veteran communist Imre Nagy. The Soviet leadership trusted Nagy, who had long reported on his colleagues to the Soviet secret police, but they had underestimated Rákosi. When Nagy did as he thought the Soviet leadership wanted by relaxing controls over society and easing up on industrialisation, Rákosi mobilised the party against him, accusing Nagy of “splintering revisionism”. In the contest between the two communist leaders, Hungarian writers and intellectuals lined up behind Nagy but the Soviet leadership reluctantly backed Rákosi as a flawed but more reliable communist. The Kremlin was worried in particular that Nagy’s talk of political pluralism and of broadening decision-making could only weaken communist control in Hungary.

Nagy’s fall was swift. At Moscow’s direction, the 70-strong Central Committee of the Hungarian Workers’ Party denounced him in March 1955 for “party-damaging, anti-Marxist, opportunistic and right-leaning tendencies”. Nagy was progressively stripped of his offices and, at the end of the year, expelled from the party altogether.

Winter of discontent

In November 1955, a new theatre production opened in Budapest: Shakespeare’s Richard III. It was a sell-out, attracting theatregoers who easily read the politics of the day into “the winter of our discontent” and the villainy of the king. That show was typical of the way that arts and culture began to define Hungarian politics. Theatres, poetry readings and discussion groups increasingly provided forums for the coded criticism of communist policies and of Rákosi’s leadership.

But Moscow was giving mixed messages. In February 1956, at the Twentieth Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, Khrushchev denounced Stalin and the brutality and incompetence of his rule. Supposedly secret, the speech was soon leaked and gave hope to reformers throughout the Soviet bloc. Amid conditions verging on civil war, the communist party in Poland broke free of Moscow’s control, appointing Władysław Gomułka as leader despite Khrushchev’s disapproval of him. (Significant, enduring democratic reforms would, however, have to wait until 1989).

  • Read more | Churchill vs Stalin: did this one speech cause the Cold War?

In Hungary, meanwhile, pressure grew for a political amnesty and pardon. These rumblings culminated in the ceremonial reburial of one of Rákosi’s victims, László Rajk – a communist mass-murderer as odious as Rákosi himself, but hanged on bogus charges in 1949 – which attracted as many as 200,000 onlookers. Student halls of residence and university classrooms became centres of political discussion; one academic debate on freedom of the press drew an audience of no fewer than 7,000.

Visiting Hungary in July 1956, the senior Soviet politician Anastas Mikoyan found only chaos. He reported back to Moscow in alarm:

“Day after day the comrades are further losing their grip on power. A parallel centre is forming from enemy elements operating actively, decisively and self-confidently. The press and radio are not under Central Committee control any more… In this dangerous situation, the party leadership practically exists in a state of prostration.”

There was only one thing for it: jettison Rákosi. But the Soviet decision in July 1956 to appoint another communist dinosaur, Ernő Gerő, as Rákosi’s successor and party boss showed the limits of the Kremlin’s thinking. Communists tend to believe that they have the masses on their side. When they find that they do not, they panic – history is not turning out as it should. On 23 October, a student demonstration to show solidarity with the reformers in Poland turned violent when the security police shot at the crowd. The demonstrators responded by seizing weapons and pulling down the massive statue of Stalin that loomed over the city centre. As the fighting intensified, with revolutionaries taking on Soviet tanks, Gerő rang up Moscow to ask for military help.

Moscow was uncertain what to do. The leadership was divided between hardliners who favoured armed intervention and pragmatists – led by Khrushchev – who hoped for a political solution. In the event, Gerő was dismissed, Nagy was brought back as prime minister and the party leadership was given to the moderate János Kádár. On 28 October, the Soviet commander Marshal Georgy Zhukov ordered all Soviet troops in Hungary to return to barracks.

It looked as if the revolution had won, but Nagy was not in control of events. The Hungarian leadership earnestly debated how to repair broken windows and rewrite history textbooks in schools, while simultaneously giving way to increasingly radical demands from the streets – for the removal of all Soviet troops from Hungary, for a multiparty democracy with free elections, even for breaking Hungary’s military alliance with the Soviet Union. Meanwhile, revolutionaries slaughtered several hundred Workers’ Party officials and shot captured secret policemen.

It was the murder of communists, “our people”, that forced Khrushchev’s hand. On top of this, as Khrushchev explained to his colleagues in Moscow, the progress of the revolution in Hungary made it likely that a ‘capitalist’ restoration was imminent, which could only diminish Soviet prestige. So, on 31 October, Khrushchev gave the order for a full-scale military invasion. What followed was a textbook operation. Over several days, Soviet troops and tanks began covert manoeuvres which effectively sealed off Budapest and other cities. Then, on 4 November, with Budapest encircled, the assault commenced with armoured columns punching their way into the capital along the main highways. The countdown to Erika Széles’s murder had begun.

János Kádár became Moscow’s man in post-revolutionary Hungary. He saw to the prosecution and judicial murder of the leading revolutionaries – including Imre Nagy, latterly the figurehead of the revolution, who was hanged in 1958.

Signs of progress

Kádár ruled Hungary for the next 32 years. His regime was mostly benign: there was censorship, but an underground press flourished. Dissidents were harassed but seldom jailed. The shops were full. Coming to Budapest as a postgrad student in the late seventies, I was surprised and relieved to find that my local ABC had as great a variety of food on offer as the West Hampstead International supermarket (now a Sainsbury’s) where I had shopped in London.

Political debate was allowed, but discussion of 1956 was off limits; the revolution was euphemistically referred to as ‘the events’. My landlord in Budapest, an old conservative, blamed the west for not coming to Hungary’s aid. “We won’t go onto the streets again,” he would say with a shrug of his shoulders.

In fact, Hungarians did not need to return to the streets. Once Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev had let the communist bosses of the satellites know that they could not expect Moscow to intervene on their behalf, the game was up.

In June 1989, Hungary’s communist leaders ceded to popular demands for the ceremonial reburial of Imre Nagy, giving him a state funeral in front of 300,000 mourners. Over the following few months, they peacefully surrendered power in return for immunity from criminal prosecution and their pension entitlements.

Contested memory

After 1989, memory of 1956 became one of the symbols around which Hungarians built a new democratic nation. As one of its first acts, the new Hungarian parliament made 23 October an official holiday, while Plot 301 – where the communist leaders had ordered the burial in unmarked graves of Nagy and other murdered revolutionaries – was made into a site of national mourning.

Even so, memory of 1956 is still contested by left and right. For the left, the revolution was a fight for democracy, civil liberties and the rights of the individual. For the right, it was, above all, a struggle against tyranny of all types. Viktor Orbán, the long-serving rightwing prime minister of Hungary (in power 1998–2002 and 2010–2026), likened his country’s fight against the Soviet Union to his own battle against the ‘tyrannical’ rule of Brussels and the European Union.

  • Read more | This secret speech gave people heart attacks: when Khrushchev denounced Stalin

Orbán and his political party, Fidesz, have a bad reputation – and deservedly so. Accused of harassing migrants with razor-wire fences and tear gas, closing down opposition media, gerrymandering elections and undermining the judiciary, Orbán and his lackeys seemed little different from the tyrants they claimed to despise. Indeed, Orbán happily lined up with fellow authoritarians – not only Vladimir Putin (“a fair partner”) but also Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (“one of my personal friends”) and President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan (“a model state… stable, predictable and successful”).

On top of this, Orbán’s stooges plundered the state to make themselves Hungary’s richest men, unashamedly advertising their wealth with private jets and castles. Kickbacks, single-bidder contracts and smears, often loaded with a dose of antisemitism, made what had been a functioning democracy into a kleptocracy.

Since Fidesz was roundly defeated in the parliamentary election of April 2026, the photogenic Péter Magyar has been Hungary’s new prime minister. A former Fidesz stalwart who broke with Orbán as recently as 2024, Magyar heads up an umbrella party with little ideological glue. In Magyar’s rhetoric, 1956 is a key plank – one that he invokes in the name of national unity, of making a clean break with the recent past, and of reorient ing Hungarian policy away from Moscow. Even so, after Orbán’s tenure, Hungary’s reputation as one of Europe’s bad boys is close to where it was before 1956. Péter Magyar has work to do.

Martyn Rady was a student in Hungary in the late 1970s, and is now Masaryk professor emeritus of central European history at University College London. His next book, Eastern Europe: A New History, will be published by Allen Lane in 2027

This article was first published in the December 2026 issue of HistoryExtra Magazine

issues.title: Depraved art: a disturbing history
issues.summary: Can art ever be genuinely dangerous? Daisy Dixon reveals how views on obscenity and censorship have shifted through history
issues.author: Jon Bauckham
issues.content_html:
For millennia, humans have created art with the power to shock, disturb and offend. But what makes an artwork truly dangerous? And should it ever be censored?

From Hitler’s paintings to the racist caricatures of Jim Crow America, Daisy Dixon takes Jon Bauckham on a tour of history’s most depraved art, revealing both its capacity for cruelty and its use as a tool of oppression.

issues.title: A 30-minute walk helps sustain brain activity during mental task switching, study finds
issues.summary: Can a short walk change how your brain handles a mental challenge? In a small study, walking altered brain activity during a task-switching test, with some effects differing by age, though performance did not improve.
issues.author: Vladimir Hedrih

issues.title: Scientists finally pin down what a mysterious Alzheimer’s gene does
issues.summary: CASS4 has been tied to Alzheimer’s risk since 2013, but nobody knew what it did in the brain. New mouse research suggests it lets immune cells physically grip and compact amyloid plaques.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
Deleting an Alzheimer’s-linked gene called CASS4 in mice impairs the ability of brain immune cells to surround and compress toxic protein plaques, according to new research published in Journal of Experimental Medicine.

Without this gene, mice bred to develop Alzheimer’s-like pathology accumulated larger, looser plaques, suffered worse nerve-fiber damage, and struggled to adapt when a learned task changed. The findings indicate that CASS4 helps immune cells maintain the internal anchoring machinery needed to move toward brain damage and contain harmful deposits.

A cancer-linked gene inside the brain’s immune cells

Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurological condition that erodes memory and thinking, marked in the brain by clumps of amyloid-beta protein and tangled tau fibers. Genetic research increasingly points to microglia, the resident immune cells stationed inside the brain and spinal cord that sweep branching arms through tissue to watch for injury or disease. Human brain mapping, including an analysis of 3.4 million individual brain cells, suggests that after a gradual early loss of certain inhibitory neurons, Alzheimer’s shifts into a rapid phase of widespread inflammation, microglial changes, and accelerating plaque buildup.

Many inherited DNA variations tied to late-onset Alzheimer’s sit near genes active mainly in microglia. One prominent example is CASS4, first linked to Alzheimer’s risk in a 2013 genetic meta-analysis of more than 74,000 people. Microglia are virtually the only resident brain cells that switch this gene on, yet what CASS4 does in the brain has remained largely unknown.

CASS4 belongs to a family of scaffold proteins, which have no enzyme activity of their own and instead act as docking stations where signaling molecules assemble. Studies of tumor cells show that CASS4 and its relatives organize focal adhesions, microscopic anchor points made of structural actin fibers at a cell’s outer membrane that let the cell grip surfaces, extend projections, and crawl. Because earlier work focused on cancer migration, the authors of a 2014 review argued that although CASS4 was known to guide cell movement, its function in the brain and in Alzheimer’s remained unexplained.

In parallel, neuroscientists found that physical gripping forces are central to how microglia limit amyloid-beta damage. Rather than only swallowing debris, microglia swarm plaques to form a tight cellular barrier, and a 2015 brain-imaging study in mice showed that this shield compacts loose, toxic amyloid threads into dense, rounded bundles that cause less harm to nearby nerve fibers. Connecting these threads, lead author Adeline E. Walsh, senior author John R. Lukens, and their colleagues in the Lukens Lab at the University of Virginia tested whether losing CASS4 disrupts microglial focal adhesions and weakens plaque containment.

“Despite CASS4 being recently identified as a major risk gene for Alzheimer’s disease, little is known about how it functions to influence brain health and disease,” Lukens, the William R. Kenan Jr. professor of neuroscience and Harrison distinguished teaching professor in the university’s Center for Brain Immunology and Glia, told PsyPost. “Findings presented in our recently published paper sought to bridge this gap in knowledge.”

Larger plaques, nerve injury, and reduced mental flexibility

The researchers used gene editing to generate mice lacking CASS4 throughout the body and bred them with an Alzheimer’s mouse model carrying five human mutations that trigger rapid amyloid-beta buildup. The team posted their sequencing datasets, source data, and analysis code publicly online.

To keep plaque development consistent across animals, all cohorts consisted of female mice, which develop amyloid pathology faster and more uniformly than males in this strain. Every mouse also inherited the Alzheimer’s mutations from its father, controlling for recent evidence that plaque burden varies depending on which parent passes the genes down.

At five months of age, the scientists stained slices of the hippocampus, a memory hub, and the outer cerebral cortex with a fluorescent plaque dye, imaging 9 to 12 fields per region per mouse. Compared with Alzheimer’s-model littermates with intact CASS4, mice missing the gene had more numerous and larger plaques in both regions.

Microscopy also pointed to worse nerve-fiber injury near those deposits. Mice lacking CASS4 had greater hippocampal buildup of amyloid precursor protein, which is distinct from the amyloid-beta fragments in extracellular plaques and instead serves as a standard marker of neuronal damage when it pools inside swollen nerve fibers. They also showed elevated levels in both the hippocampus and cortex of ATG9, a cellular recycling protein that similarly collects inside unhealthy axons.

To examine gene activity across cell types, the team pooled hippocampi from six five-month-old mice per group and sequenced RNA from 33,985 cell nuclei across 10 cell populations. Deleting CASS4 did not alter cell-type proportions and confirmed that microglia are the main resident brain cells expressing the gene.

Even so, nearly 3,000 genes shifted in excitatory neurons, which send activating signals, with increased expression of genes and pathways tied to spatial working memory and motor learning. Over 200 genes changed in inhibitory neurons, which quiet brain circuits, including lower expression of genes that maintain neural circuitry.

The team next assessed cognition at four months of age in the Morris water maze, training 10 Alzheimer’s-model mice per group over four days to find a submerged platform in opaque water using wall cues. Following a fifth-day memory probe with the platform removed, the researchers relocated the platform to the opposite quadrant for four more training days to test cognitive flexibility, the ability to abandon an old rule and adapt to a change.

During initial training and the first memory probe, differences between the groups were not statistically significant, indicating intact spatial learning and recall. Once the platform moved, however, CASS4-deficient Alzheimer’s mice swam farther from the new location and lingered in the old quadrant, whereas littermates with CASS4 adjusted to the new target.

Differences in swim speed, distance traveled, and anxiety-like behaviors in separate maze tests were not statistically significant, ruling out sluggishness or fear as likely explanations. In a control test of 14 CASS4-deficient and 12 normal mice without Alzheimer’s mutations, deleting CASS4 caused no detectable deficits, indicating that impaired cognitive flexibility arose specifically alongside amyloid pathology.

Microglia lose their grip around amyloid plaques

To learn why plaques caused worse damage without CASS4, the scientists examined microglia at five months using microscopy and flow cytometry, which sorts cells with lasers. Differences between groups were not statistically significant for microglial counts, cell division, activation markers, or the share of microglia engulfing fluorescently tagged amyloid-beta over three hours in six to seven mice per group. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing backed up those imaging results, showing equivalent proportions of resting homeostatic microglia and protective disease-associated microglia in both groups.

Instead, the defect involved physical contact at plaque borders. CASS4-deficient mice had markedly fewer microglial branches positioned right next to plaques, and their deposits were less dense, less spherical, and surrounded by a higher proportion of loose, diffuse amyloid-beta relative to compact cores in both the hippocampus and cortex.

Deleting a gene across the entire body from conception leaves open whether developmental changes or immune cells outside the brain contributed to the results. To isolate the role of brain-resident microglia, the researchers bred a conditional mouse line in which CASS4 could be switched off later in life using a drug-activated enzyme in microglia and related immune cells.

Young Alzheimer’s-model mice ate food laced with the drug tamoxifen for two weeks after weaning to trigger that deletion, then returned to regular chow. Over the following months, short-lived immune cells in the bloodstream were naturally replaced by new cells with intact CASS4, whereas long-lived microglia in the brain remained CASS4-deficient.

At five months, mice lacking CASS4 only in microglia matched the full-body knockouts, showing more and larger hippocampal plaques, poorly compacted deposits, and greater nerve-fiber damage alongside unchanged overall microglial volume. Because neurons do not produce CASS4, the authors suggest that poor microglial plaque containment exposes brain tissue to looser, more toxic amyloid-beta that harms nearby nerve cells.

Disrupted focal adhesions and a blunted injury response

Looking inside microglia, hippocampal RNA sequencing showed lower activity in gene pathways that build contractile actin filaments, the internal cables cells use to pull and move. Because focal adhesions are controlled largely by phosphorylation, the chemical tags that switch signaling proteins on or off, the team isolated brain microglia from five mice per group and screened 1,318 protein sites across two antibody arrays.

Averaging the two arrays without formal statistical testing, the researchers flagged 93 altered proteins using an asymmetric cutoff that required a steep jump to count an increase (an average log fold change above 1.4) but a much smaller dip to count a decrease (below -0.4). Roughly 17 percent of those 93 proteins belonged to focal adhesion pathways.

Under those criteria, CASS4-deficient microglia had fewer activation tags on downstream proteins that drive cell extensions and on an activating site of the receptor for macrophage colony-stimulating factor, a signal that prompts immune cells to migrate. Several upstream surface adhesion proteins showed increased tagging, which the authors propose may reflect a cellular effort to compensate for the downstream block.

Follow-up experiments tested focal adhesions and movement directly. Cultured microglia from newborn CASS4-deficient mice formed smaller patches of paxillin, a core focal adhesion protein, and bone marrow macrophages from five CASS4-deficient mice crawled more slowly across a scratched gap over 12 hours than cells from five normal mice when stimulated with migration-triggering proteins.

Finally, the scientists implanted tiny glass windows into the skulls of four to five live mice per group with fluorescent microglia and created a microscopic laser burn in the cortex while imaging for 40 minutes. Normal microglia rapidly extended branches onto the injury, whereas CASS4-deficient microglia mounted a blunted response.

The starkness of that live-imaging result stood out to the team. “Surprisingly, the microglia that were lacking CASS4 barely responded to the laser injury at all, suggesting that CASS4 plays a key role in this very important microglial function,” Lukens noted.

“This work suggests that therapeutics that promote CASS4 function in microglia could provide a novel strategy to limit Alzheimer’s disease progression,” Lukens said. “Moreover, our work suggests that the downregulation of CASS4 expression could also potentially serve as a much-needed biomarker to detect the early stages of Alzheimer’s disease.”

In medicine, a biomarker is a measurable biological indicator that can signal a condition before major symptoms take hold, in this case a drop in CASS4 gene activity. Together with the molecular data, the authors suggest that supporting CASS4 and related focal adhesion pathways might help keep microglial barriers intact.

Study caveats and future directions beyond Alzheimer’s

There are a few caveats to keep in mind. All experiments took place in mice and cultured cells, using an aggressive amyloid-producing mouse strain that lacks tau tangles and does not mirror the decades-long course of human late-onset Alzheimer’s disease. Completely deleting CASS4 is also a much starker change than the single-letter DNA variations linked to human risk, and as the authors note, future studies must test those human variants directly.

In addition, the Alzheimer’s pathology and behavioral experiments used only female mice to keep plaque timing consistent, leaving open whether CASS4 loss affects males identically. The dish-based wound-healing assays also used bone marrow macrophages as a stand-in for microglia, though the live laser-injury experiments confirmed that microglia inside intact brains similarly struggled to mobilize without CASS4.

“Our recent findings indicate that CASS4 is a pivotal regulator of microglial responses in the brain,” Lukens added. “Given that microglia have also been shown to be major players in multiple other neurological disease settings, we are particularly interested in investigating if CASS4 also plays important roles in other neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s, ALS, and multiple sclerosis. In addition, we are also eager to work with collaborators at the UVa Manning Institute to develop first-in-class CASS4-targeting drugs that can be pursued in future clinical trials to treat neurological disorders.”

Unlike existing Alzheimer’s drugs that primarily remove amyloid plaques directly, a first-in-class CASS4 therapy would aim to work through a new biological mechanism by strengthening the immune cells involved in conditions ranging from Alzheimer’s to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the motor-neuron disease commonly known as ALS.

The study, “Alzheimer’s genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis,” was authored by Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo, and John R. Lukens.

issues.title: Past experiences with classical music predict a taste for sophisticated genres
issues.summary: A newly developed scale finds that emotional experiences with classical music during childhood predict a preference for sophisticated genres like jazz and opera later in youth.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
Children and teenagers who have spent time listening to classical music are more likely to appreciate complex musical styles like jazz and opera. A recently developed survey tool indicates that past emotional engagement with classical music is linked to a stronger preference for these genres. The research was published in the journal Psychology of Music.

Psychologists classify genres like classical, opera, jazz, and world music under the umbrella term of sophisticated music. The MUSIC model is a standard framework researchers use to categorize auditory tastes. In this model, sophisticated music is characterized by its perceived complexity and by being predominantly instrumental. Listeners generally perceive these genres as intelligent and inspiring.

Most children and teenagers gravitate toward pop, rock, or contemporary music in their daily lives. They rarely select sophisticated music to regulate their moods or socialize with friends. Music education programs frequently attempt to increase appreciation for classical music among younger generations.

Past studies have shown that young children are generally open to many types of music. This openness to different styles narrows dramatically during adolescence. During the teenage years, preferences tend to align strictly with what is popular among peer groups. As young people transition into adulthood, their willingness to explore diverse musical styles typically rebounds.

Researchers wanted to know if a person’s specific history with classical music could predict their current musical tastes. Valnea Žauhar, a researcher at the University of Rijeka in Croatia, led the study alongside colleagues Igor Bajšanski and Sabina Vidulin. They developed a new questionnaire called the Past Experience with Listening to Classical Music Scale.

They designed this tool to measure how often children and adolescents listen to classical music. The survey also asks how much they enjoy it, and whether the music has evoked strong emotions for them in the past. The researchers created the survey by compiling items that assess voluntary listening during leisure time.

The survey questions also capture the vividness of listeners’ emotional responses. Statements asked the students if listening to classical music gives them goosebumps, makes them cry, or brings them joy.

In their first study, the researchers recruited 151 students from a general secondary school. The participants ranged in age from 15 to 18. The students listened to six 15-second audio clips of sophisticated music and rated how much they liked each one.

The researchers deliberately selected obscure, unreleased tracks of professional quality. This ensured that the students would be rating the music itself, rather than their familiarity with a famous song. After the listening task, the students completed the newly developed past experience questionnaire.

They also filled out surveys detailing their general music consumption and their tendency to use music for specific purposes. The researchers categorized these purposes as emotional listening, cognitive listening, or background listening. Emotional listening involves using music to change a mood, while cognitive listening involves analyzing the musical elements intellectually.

The secondary school students generally reported low levels of past experience with classical music. However, those who did report more past experience were more likely to use music for emotional and cognitive purposes. Past experience with classical music also strongly predicted how much the students liked the sophisticated music excerpts they had just heard.

Initially, the researchers noticed that formal music education seemed to predict a preference for sophisticated music. Students who had taken formal lessons preferred the excerpts more than those who had not. But when the researchers factored in past experiences with classical music, the statistical results shifted.

Formal training no longer predicted preference once past exposure was considered in the analysis. Having positive, emotional experiences with classical music in the past emerged as the sole positive predictor of liking the sophisticated clips. This suggests that emotional engagement is strongly linked to musical taste regardless of formal instruction.

The researchers then conducted a second study with 286 children attending a primary music school. These participants ranged in age from eight to 14. This experiment took place during a regular group music lesson.

The children listened to a two-minute excerpt from Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 9, commonly known as the “From the New World” symphony. The researchers selected an energetic, highly expressive section of the music featuring striking brass instrumentation and strong rhythms.

Immediately after listening, the children rated how much they liked the music and how immersed they felt. They also completed the past experience questionnaire. In addition, they took a survey measuring the specific emotions the music evoked, such as feelings of activation or calmness.

The children generally liked the Dvořák excerpt. They reported that it produced moderate to moderately high levels of emotional activation. Their past experience with classical music reliably predicted how much they liked the symphony piece.

Older children and those with more past exposure to classical music reported higher levels of enjoyment. The strongest predictor of liking the music was the level of emotional activation the children felt during the listening session.

Music-evoked activation refers to feelings of power, tension, wonder, or joyful energy sparked by the audio. Children who felt these active emotions intensely were the most likely to rate the excerpt highly. Calmness, on the other hand, did not predict how much the children liked the fast-paced excerpt.

The study relies on self-reported data from the children and teenagers. This means the results depend on the participants accurately remembering and reporting their past listening habits. A person might not fully recall how often they heard classical music during their early childhood.

The researchers note that experience with classical music is a multifaceted concept. Future research should track participants over a longer period to see exactly how these musical experiences accumulate and shape preferences over time. Studies might also use objective methods, like having parents or teachers record the children’s exposure to classical music.

Because the research only included children and adolescents, the results do not show how these preferences evolve into adulthood. A longitudinal study, which follows the same individuals as they age, would offer a more precise picture of how early exposure influences lifelong tastes.

The study, “The Role of Past Experience With Listening to Classical Music in Liking Sophisticated Music,” was authored by Valnea Žauhar, Igor Bajšanski, and Sabina Vidulin.

What do you think?

What are your perspectives on the debate? Has the i-frame vs. s-frame debate influenced your work? Where do you agree, and where do you disagree? What related questions are you grappling with? Where do you think the applied behavioral science goes next?

Share your perspective via our “letter to the editor” form.

Share your perspective

Five questions to consider

In advance of the event, I asked each of our five guests to prepare a question for the group. We didn't get to all of them during the discussion, so I thought it might be valuable to share them with everyone. The questions can serve as leaping off points to advance your own thinking and for your discussions with colleagues.

Here they are:

1. Systems-level change (from Nick): How can behavioral science most effectively help with system-level (s-frame) change?

2. Inadvertent harm of the i-frame vs. s-frame argument (from Michael): From where you sit, do you think the i-frame vs. s-frame argument could inadvertently diminish interest in applying behavioral science to public policy?

3. Equity (from Crystal): How does an equity focus complicate (or settle?) the i-frame/s-frame question?

4. The case of gambling (from George): Considerable research suggests that online gambling is causing extensive harm, particularly to poor and young people. How can behavioral insights inform interventions at both the individual level and the system level? And which level do you expect to be more effective?

5. The next generation of behavioral scientists (from Chiara): How does this debate translate into action, such as the training and mentoring of the next generation of behavioral scientists?

issues.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
issues.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinct
issues.author: Evan Nesterak
issues.content_html:
Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen?

Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work they’re asked to do, as well as the work they’d like to do?

These are all questions that applied behavioral scientists are grappling with as they try to realize the promise of the field—to leverage the scientific understanding of psychology, behavior, society, and culture to help one another live happier, healthier, and more peaceful lives.

On October 14, join Editor-in-Chief Evan Nesterak and five leading behavioral scientists—Nick Chater, George Loewestein, Crystal Hall, Michael Hallsworth, and Chiara Varazzani—for a roundtable discussion about these questions and more. The leaping off point will be the i-frame vs. s-frame debate initiated by Chater and Loewenstein, first in an academic article and now in their new book, It’s on You. (Further background on the debate below.)

The guests of the roundtable don’t all agree on how to answer the questions above. In fact, in many cases they sharply disagree. But they all have extensive experience working in both academic and applied settings, especially in public policy, so we have the opportunity for an interesting and constructive conversation. The goal isn’t to settle the debate but to explore areas of agreement and disagreement, open a dialogue about how applied behavioral scientists approach their work, and surface the questions that can move the debate forward.

The event will take place online and is free to attend. You can reserve your spot here.

  • Date: Wednesday, October 14
  • Start time: 9:00am San Francisco | 12:00pm New York | 5:00pm London | 6:00pm Berlin | 7:00pm Nairobi | 9:30pm Delhi
  • Duration: 90 minutes
  • Location: Online
  • Cost: Free to attend
  • Register:Reserve your spot
Reserve your spot

A recording will be made available to all registrants after the event, in case you're not able to attend live.

We hope to see you there,

Evan Nesterak, Editor-in-Chief

Background on the debate

In their 2022 article in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, psychologist Nick Chater and behavioral economist George Loewestein ignited the i-frame vs. s-frame debate within applied behavioral science. The two argued that, in the decade since the field burst on the scene, applied behavioral scientists, themselves included, had focused too much on trying to influence individual behavior (i-frame) and not enough on trying to influence the systems in which individuals behave (s-frame).

The result, they said, especially as it related to public policy, was that interventions were coming up short, attention was being directed away from system-level solutions that could have a tangible impact, and, perhaps most seriously, that applied behavioral scientists “may have unwittingly promoted the interests of the opponents of systemic change.”

Perhaps unsurprisingly, not everyone agreed. One focus of Chater and Loewenstein’s criticism was nudging, which for them epitomized the i-frame approach. The format of the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences is to feature a target article (in this case Chater and Loewestein’s) and then invite other scholars to respond to that article. Both Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, authors of Nudge, issued a response. “Nudging is being framed,” Thaler wrote. Sunstein argued, “Their complaint is baseless. In the real world of policymaking, behavioral science is mostly being used to reform systems, not to alter individual behavior.”

And Michael Hallsworth, a leader of the Behavioural Insights Team, wrote:

“I greatly respect the authors of the target article. However, in contrast to the target article's assertion, practitioners of behavioral public policy are indeed involved in developing and promoting systemic solutions. Its ‘i-frame’/‘s-frame’ distinction is incoherent, unhelpful, and obscures promising future directions for behavioral public policy. Its content and presentation undermine its stated goals and encourage sweeping dismissals of the field.”

Chater, Loewenstein, Thaler, Sunstein, and Hallsworth all believe that applied behavioral science can be a positive force in improving people’s lives. The question is: How does the field get there?

Earlier this year, Chater and Loewenstein expanded their argument about the i-frame and s-frame in their book, It’s on You. And the question of how applied behavioral scientists should approach their work continues to bubble up in commentaries and conversations.

We wanted to use this moment to bring together diverging viewpoints about the i-frame vs. s-frame debate and how the field fulfills its promise. At the roundtable discussion, in addition to Nick Chater and George Loewestein, we’ll be joined by Crystal Hall (Professor, University of Washington and President, Behavioral Science & Policy Association), Michael Hallsworth (Chief Behavioral Scientist, BIT), and Chiara Varazzani (Lead Behavioral Scientist, OECD).

Reserve your spot

About the roundtable guests

Nick Chater is a professor of behavioral science at the Warwick Business School. In 2023, he was awarded the Rumelhart Prize for lifetime achievement in cognitive science. He has advised the UK Government and co-founded Decision Technology, a research consultancy. He is the coauthor of It’s on You (with George Loewenstein).

George Loewenstein is the Herbert A. Simon University Professor of Economics and Psychology at Carnegie Mellon University. He is one of the founders of behavioral economics, neuroeconomics, and behavioral public policy and has advised many leading companies and government bodies. He is the coauthor of It’s on You (with Nick Chater).

Crystal Hall is the John and Marguerite Walker Corbally Endowed Professor in Public Service at the University of Washington, as well as the president of the Behavioral Science & Policy Association. She has served as a fellow with the White House Social and Behavioral Sciences Team and the Federal Office of Evaluation Sciences at the General Services Administration, and has advised government agencies, nonprofits, and community organizations. She is the coauthor of Antiracist by Design (with Mindy Hernandez).

Michael Hallsworth is the chief behavioral scientist at BIT. He has two decades of experience in developing policy and designing services for national governments and international organizations. He is also a distinguished lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania, and was previously visiting lecturer at Princeton University and assistant professor (adjunct) at Columbia University. He is the author of TheHypocrisy Trap and coauthor of Behavioral Insights (with Elspeth Kirkman).

Chiara Varazzani is lead behavioral scientist at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). She is also a senior visiting fellow at the London School of Economics and Political Science. Previously, she served as a member of the Technical Advisory Group on Behavioural Insights for the World Health Organization (WHO), advised the Australian government, and was an adjunct research fellow at Monash University.

issues.title: A 5 a.m. Alarm Didn’t Fix My Mornings
issues.summary: I tried waking up at 5 a.m. When that meant too little sleep, I could manage a few good hours, and then I crashed. The rest of the day was a struggle. Brooks naturally wakes early. I’m no sleep doctor, and I won’t turn his schedule or mine into a credential. Build a good start […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I tried waking up at 5 a.m. When that meant too little sleep, I could manage a few good hours, and then I crashed. The rest of the day was a struggle.

Brooks naturally wakes early. I’m no sleep doctor, and I won’t turn his schedule or mine into a credential. Build a good start to your day around your sleep needs.

What actually sat between me and meaningful work was the preparation. Sorting email. Checking the calendar. Reviewing meeting history. Deciding where to start. I was doing all of that before I had touched anything that mattered. Now an agent assembles the context, and I begin the day with a direction.

Inbox triage can be the only reason for an early start. Hand that sorting to an agent and the administrative reason for the early alarm can disappear. A later start tells me that reason was gone. It does not tell me how much additional sleep came with it.

Hand the night-before plan to an agent

I still plan the night before. I used to do the whole pass myself. At 9 p.m. the repetitive part now runs as an AI workflow.

The agent reviews unfinished tasks. It inspects tomorrow’s calendar. It compares both against my goals for the next 30 days. From that, it proposes one thing to do first the next morning, then secondary options.

I kept the benefit of planning ahead. The preparation is what I delegated. The agent recommends. I decide.

Already doing some version of this by hand? Turn that evening checklist into a repeatable instruction. Give it the same inputs: unfinished tasks, tomorrow’s calendar, and your goals for the next 30 days. Ask for a single first priority and a short list of backups. Read the proposal before you adopt it.

Replace the inbox scan with a brief

Do you open email to figure out what your day is?

I stopped using the morning inbox scan as my launcher. An agent reviews email, calendar commitments, and relevant meeting history before I start, then surfaces the day’s priorities and the messages that need attention. I want a clear starting point and a short reply list. That’s the brief.

This is a workflow you configure. Connect only information sources you have approved. While you are still establishing whether you can trust it, check the brief against the originals.

One question before you start

AI can prepare my priorities. I still choose them.

Brooks warns that agents can gravitate toward tasks with due dates and overlook important work that is not urgent. A clean brief can still be aimed at the nearest deadline.

I let the agent assemble the options. Then I check the proposed first task. What important, non-urgent work is missing? If the top item only clears a deadline, I start with the work that advances a meaningful goal.

Flip the script

I used to ask for a personalized workflow and hope a generic prompt captured how I work. Now I flip the script. The agent asks me four to six targeted questions before it proposes a solution. Those questions reveal the context it was missing.

Paste this in before you ask for the brief:

“Before designing my morning brief, ask me four to six questions about my goals, schedule, information sources, and notification preferences.”

Answer them. Then look at what it proposes.

Two delivery windows

My updates arrive in two windows, and the rest of the morning stays quiet. A short morning brief carries priorities and essential information. Around 11 a.m. I get the fuller pass: email replies, follow-ups, and relationship news. The agent gathers in the background. My morning stays available for focused work.

11 a.m. fits me. Put your fuller delivery after your first focused block. Collection can run whenever. Interruption should wait.

The later window is where relationship news shows up. My agent reviews public updates about people I know and includes the relevant bits. A personal note, if one is warranted, is one I write and send myself. Monitoring on one side. The human note on mine.

Want to try a smaller version? Use public sources. Keep the pilot small. Decide yourself whether you respond and how.

Write the permissions down

My line is simple. Preparation can be automated. Actions that affect money or reputation require a human sign-off.

The agent can read relevant information and draft communications. Messages that go out under my name are ones I have personally reviewed. Finances stay read-only. Reputation-sensitive work stays read-only. Writes wait for manual approval. I send outbound messages myself, on purpose. I want the calmer morning and I want the final say on what I commit to.

Read access. List the email, calendar, and meeting history it may see. Mark finances and reputation-sensitive sources as read-only.

Drafting. Let it prepare priorities and draft replies. A draft still belongs to you.

Your approval. Money, commitments, and anything sent under your name wait until you say so.

Here’s the only move I’d make tonight. Identify one recurring morning preparation task. Just one. The email triage, the calendar check, the meeting-history review, or the decision about where to start. Hand that task to an agent with a clear instruction, and in the morning ask what important, non-urgent work it left out.

issues.title: Four Meetings, No Lunch, and the Dinner That Brought My Energy Back
issues.summary: Right before a vacation, I squeezed roughly four meetings into 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Short breaks. No lunch. I finished depleted. Dinner that evening was with three friends I hadn’t seen in a while. On the walk home, I had energy I didn’t have at 3 p.m. I used to think recovery meant being […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
Right before a vacation, I squeezed roughly four meetings into 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Short breaks. No lunch. I finished depleted.

Dinner that evening was with three friends I hadn’t seen in a while. On the walk home, I had energy I didn’t have at 3 p.m.

I used to think recovery meant being alone or doing nothing. Time with the right people gave me energy back. I still needed the lunch I skipped. Food, sleep, and breaks belong in the day too. Name one relationship or social plan that leaves you more energized, and make room for it.

A full calendar can still exhaust you

I use a frame I call TEA: time, energy, and attention. You can manage time well and still end exhausted, because energy ran out.

Creative writing is where I notice it. I can sustain one strong writing session in a day. I can’t repeat that same session morning, afternoon, and evening.

An open slot tells me the time is free. My energy for a second writing session may already be gone.

The goal is meaningful work I can repeat. Before you fill tomorrow, find one demanding task sitting in a low-energy window and one recovery break that is missing.

Hero mode

Hero mode is simple. Demanding work goes in the window where I’m sharpest. Lately mine has been roughly 10 a.m. to noon.

List ten tasks you do most weeks. Label each H, M, or L for high, medium, or low energy. Are the H tasks landing while you’re sharp? An empty afternoon is a lousy home for deep work if that’s your dip. Move one high-energy task.

On a good window I can focus for about 90 minutes to two hours. That’s my experience. I’m no doctor.

Four energy layers

Sometimes the answer really is sleep. I still check four layers, so I fix the one that’s actually thin.

Physical energy. Sleep, movement, food, and recovery all sit here. Skipping lunch hit me on this layer.

Emotional energy. Stress, relationships, and emotional load. The four meetings took from this. Dinner with three friends gave some back.

Mental energy. Overload, ambiguity, and decisions.

Spiritual energy. Meaning, identity, and alignment with what you care about. Religion might be part of that for you. I use this layer as a coaching frame on my own weeks.

Choose the biggest bottleneck and write one small improvement for this week.

Two leaks I keep paying for

New AI tools excite me and overload me. The pace of change, the pile of tools, the stimulation of trying things. A tool can be useful and still cost attention. Is your AI exploration helping you finish meaningful work, or adding mental load? I deal with that overload myself.

Ambiguity is the quieter leak. No finish line, and I tweak and rearrange after the useful progress has slowed. I struggle with this. Defining done is an energy decision and a project decision.

Pick one lingering project and write what done looks like before you touch it again. If AI is part of that project, write the finish line before you experiment further.

Ask the last three days

Before I design a week, I audit the last three days with three questions.

When did I feel sharpest?

What drained me more than I expected?

What gave me energy back?

I look at physical energy, concentration, and emotional steadiness. You can finish a lot and still be flat. Treat the answers as a gut check, then plan for the person those three days described. Ignore the imaginary you who is equally focused all day.

Write the answers in a note before your next planning session.

Recovery menu

A break is easier when the choice is already made. I keep a recovery menu where I can see it.

Two minutes. I get up and fetch a glass of water. I’m away from the screen.

Ten minutes. I walk.

Twenty minutes. I take a longer walk, away from the workspace.

I want movement, a screen break, and a change of environment. Your menu should match what restores you. People kept asking what a break should be, so I made a menu. Some people keep theirs as a desktop background.

Make a two-minute option, a ten-minute option, and a twenty-minute option. Keep the menu visible. Test one default this week.

Mine is a ten-minute walk after lunch. Familiar route. No phone, no headphones, no audio. I call it my Daily Reset. I tried to hold an evening walk and my evenings were often booked, so the habit wouldn’t stick. I moved it to midday.

I grew up with the Dutch practice of uitwaaien, and the lunch walk is my version of that. I stop taking information in. I come back to the desk more able to focus. Try one device-free walk after lunch and notice how you feel when you sit down again.

Two lists

Write what occupied most of the last three days. Write the values that matter most to you. Look at both.

Does the second list show up anywhere in the first?

Work and bills can own a lot of hours. Let them. What you care about still needs a deliberate spot, including a value like quality time. That dinner was a small block of it, and it restored me. Schedule one small action for a value that has been living on leftovers.

Five days

Rate your energy from 1 to 10 at a few points each day, for five days. Find the strongest window. Put one important, demanding task in it. Add one recovery ritual and keep it.

Then write an Energy Blueprint: your biggest energy bottleneck, and one commitment you can remove, renegotiate, or buffer.

Tonight, answer those three questions in a note. Tomorrow, put the thing that gave you energy back on the calendar.
