issues.title: What makes the Amex Platinum stand out among premium rewards cards?
issues.summary: See how the Amex Platinum compares with other premium cards on lounge access, hotel perks, rewards and credits — and where it falls short.
issues.author: Matt Moffitt
issues.content_html:
An airport lounge membership, hotel perks and a handful of statement credits used to be enough to set a premium travel rewards card apart. These days, that sounds like the starting point.

The American Express Platinum Card® faces competition from the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees), Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (see rates and fees). All four offer transferable rewards and airport lounge access, along with benefits designed to offset their high annual fees.

Still, the Platinum makes a compelling case for a place in a frequent traveler's wallet. Its strengths include extensive lounge access, generous earnings on flights booked directly with airlines and hotel benefits that can make a stay considerably more comfortable.

At $895 a year (see rates and fees), it's also the most expensive of these four cards.

Here's where the Platinum stands out — and where another premium card might be a better fit.

Airport lounge access is its biggest advantage

Complimentary Priority Pass lounge access is a shared benefit across these cards (enrollment required). What makes the Platinum stand out is the additional lounges available through the American Express Global Lounge Collection.

The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes Centurion Lounges, eligible Delta Sky Clubs and other participating partner lounge networks.

The Centurion network has a larger footprint than either Capital One's or Chase's own branded lounge network. Citi doesn't operate its own network, although Strata Elite cardholders receive four Admirals Club passes per calendar year.

For me, the Centurion Lounges at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston are particularly useful when connecting to and from Austin. I enjoy the food at the lounges, but after an international flight, the opportunity to shower before my final flight of the day is what I appreciate most.

Delta Sky Club access is another reason to consider the Platinum. Cardmembers receive 10 visits per benefit year when flying on eligible itineraries. (Basic economy tickets don't qualify, and unlimited visits require $75,000 in eligible annual spending.)

There are other limits to consider. Centurion guest access costs extra unless you meet a spending requirement, and the biggest network won't necessarily be the most useful at your home airport.

Check the lounges along your regular routes before choosing a card based on access alone.

Related: My 5 top travel credit cards — and how they elevate my trips

Hotel benefits can deliver value well beyond the credit

The Platinum offers up to $600 in annual lodging statement credits, split into two allowances of up to $300: one from January through June and another from July through December.

Eligible purchases include prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®, plus qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe stays booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

THC and eligible Airbnb Luxe bookings require stays of at least two nights. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require a two-night stay to qualify for the lodging credit.

I tend to use my credit for THC stays because I often find lower prices than at FHR properties. For January, I've booked two nights at The Standard, Bangkok Mahanakhon for $362. After applying the $300 credit, the stay will cost me $62 out of pocket.

My stay includes daily breakfast for two and a $100 credit toward eligible on-property charges, which I plan to use at an on-site restaurant or for room service. I'll also be eligible for early check-in, late checkout and a room upgrade (subject to availability). Breakfast is an additional benefit at this particular property; it isn't standard across THC.

FHR offers a more consistent package, including daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout. That last benefit can be especially useful before an evening flight.

Competing premium cards have their own hotel programs. The Platinum's appeal is the combination of its credit and booking benefits. Just make sure to compare the total price with other available rates before deciding how much you're saving.

Related: A comparison of luxury hotel programs from credit card issuers

Strong flight earnings don't require booking through a portal

The Platinum earns 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through Amex Travel (on up to $500,000 of airfare purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The ability to book directly is a meaningful advantage. You can earn generously while dealing with the airline directly if you need to change your reservation or something goes wrong.

The Sapphire Reserve earns 4 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly. It earns a higher 8 points per dollar through Chase Travel℠, while the Strata Elite earns 6 points per dollar spent on flights through Citi Travel.

Here's an example of earnings on a $500 flight:

Booking methodTotal earningsValue of points* Amex Plat booking directly or through Amex Travel 2,500 Membership Rewards points $50 Sapphire Reserve booking directly 2,000 Ultimate Rewards points $41 Sapphire Reserve through Chase Travel 4,000 Ultimate Rewards points $82 Strata Elite through Citi Travel 3,000 ThankYou points $59

*Based on our November 2026 valuations

The Platinum also earns 5 points per dollar spent on eligible prepaid hotels through Amex Travel and prepaid Airbnb bookings through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel app. The Airbnb earning rate applies beyond the Luxe properties eligible for the lodging credit.

Those points offer plenty of redemption options.

Membership Rewards airline partners provide access to Oneworld, SkyTeam and Star Alliance flights through programs such as British Airways Club, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Air Canada Aeroplan. Hotel partners include Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy.

All four cards have useful transfer partners, so consider which programs you actually use. A strong earning rate matters more when it earns points you know how to redeem.

Related: The best premium credit cards: A side-by-side comparison

The welcome offer can provide a substantial head start

Eligible Platinum Card applicants can find out their offer and see if they are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on our valuations, the maximum 175,000-point offer is worth up to $3,500 — the highest value among the current publicly advertised offers on these four cards.

The high spending requirement deserves attention. Make sure you can meet it through purchases you already planned to make, and assess the card's ongoing value separately from its first-year bonus.

Lifestyle credits can help justify keeping the card

The Platinum's long list of credits makes more sense when you focus on the ones that fit your existing spending.

Its up to $300 annual digital entertainment credit is one I particularly like. It provides up to $25 monthly toward eligible purchases with participating providers.† I use it for YouTube Premium and Disney+/Hulu; the monthly allowance is shared across eligible subscriptions.

Uber users have two benefits to consider. The card provides up to $200 in annual Uber Cash for eligible U.S. rides and orders (up to $15 monthly, plus an extra $20 in December; you must add the Platinum to your Uber account and use an Amex card to pay). A separate credit provides up to $120 annually toward an eligible auto-renewing Uber One membership.

The up to $400 annual Resy statement credit (available in quarterly allowances of up to $100) can also be straightforward to use if you already dine at qualifying U.S. restaurants.†

There's also an up to $300 annual Equinox statement credit for eligible Equinox memberships or an Equinox+ digital subscription (subject to auto-renewal).† I use mine for the digital subscription.

These benefits can help cover the annual fee, but only assign them the value they have to you. Signing up for a service you won't use doesn't save money. Monthly expiration dates and U.S. restrictions also make some credits less useful for certain cardmembers.

†Enrollment required

Related: The gift card trick that helps me maximize my US restaurant credits while I'm abroad

Status and airport benefits round out the package

Platinum cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold, Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite and Leaders Club Sterling status.† The benefits vary by program, but having status without meeting the usual stay or spending requirements is a useful starting point.

Perks with Avis, Hertz and National† can also improve the experience of renting a car.

The card provides up to $219 in statement credits per calendar year toward a Clear+ membership (subject to auto-renewal),† plus either a $120 Global Entry application fee credit or an up to $85 TSA PreCheck application fee credit (every four years) when you pay with your Platinum.

Clear+ handles identity verification at participating airport checkpoints, while TSA PreCheck provides expedited security screening. Global Entry expedites eligible arrivals into the U.S. and includes TSA PreCheck.

You can also select one qualifying airline to receive up to $200 in statement credits for eligible incidental fees† charged to your Platinum card each calendar year. (Note that it isn't a general airfare credit.)

†Enrollment required

Where another premium card may be better

Outside its limited bonus categories, the Platinum earns just 1 point per dollar spent. Dining and everyday purchases are usually better placed on another card.

The Venture X offers a simpler alternative: a $395 annual fee, at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, a $300 annual Capital One Travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles. There are fewer credits to track to make the annual fee worthwhile.

The Sapphire Reserve has advantages in travel protections. Its included rental car coverage is primary, while Platinum's included coverage is secondary**.

The Sapphire Reserve also offers baggage delay insurance, reimbursing eligible essentials up to $100 daily for five days after a qualifying delay exceeding six hours. Platinum's baggage insurance*** covers eligible lost, damaged or stolen baggage, but it doesn't offer a comparable standalone baggage delay benefit.

Finally, the Strata Elite may be a better fit if you spend heavily on dining and prefer Citi's transfer partners. It earns 3 ThankYou points per dollar spent at restaurants, increasing to 6 points on Friday and Saturday evenings (between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. Eastern time). It also offers four Admirals Club passes per calendar year, making it particularly appealing if you occasionally fly American Airlines.

**Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.
***Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Bottom line

The American Express Platinum is most compelling when its benefits fit how you already travel and spend. Lounge access, a well-priced hotel stay and regularly used credits can make its annual fee easier to justify.

For me, airport showers and elevated hotel stays and credits I already use make the Platinum worth keeping.

If you'd get more use from broad spending bonuses or a simpler set of benefits, one of its competitors could be a better fit.

issues.title: Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist
issues.summary: Instead, the travel sector is more concerned about the risk of another major air travel headache like we saw this weekend.
issues.author: Sean Cudahy
issues.content_html:
It appears air travel is back on track after one of the most chaotic weekends we've seen at airports in years.

Flight schedules returned to normal this week after a rare nationwide ground stop created a nightmare weekend for flying. More than 18,000 flights were canceled between Friday and Sunday, affecting millions of travelers. It appears there will be no spillover from that meltdown into the big Thanksgiving travel week that's on the horizon, though.

The bigger concern is long-term.

It's not so much a safety question — industry experts steadfastly agree that air travel is still remarkably safe.

But there are plenty of worries about the possibility of another major air travel headache like we saw this weekend.

And that's a stressful and costly reality whether you're a passenger, a crew member, an airline executive or a front-line aviation worker.

Is there risk of another air travel meltdown?

In recent years, travelers have gotten one reminder after another about how strained our aviation infrastructure is.

For years, the Federal Aviation Administration has been plagued by both severely outdated technology and short staffing in air traffic control.

Those concerns have grown even louder in the wake of several recent incidents.

After 9/11, the U.S. went more than 20 years without a nationwide ground stop like the one we saw on Friday.

We've now seen two happen since 2023. Both instances involved outages to critical FAA systems.

Meanwhile, the vital air traffic control workforce that directs the flow of planes in our airspace has been chronically understaffed. Controllers routinely work six-day weeks and mandatory overtime.

Together, these problems have fueled several of the most high-profile air travel disruptions in recent memory.

Last fall, ATC staffing was a major factor in the mass flight cancellations and delays we saw at the height of the government shutdown.

In 2025, equipment outages plus undermanned air traffic control centers contributed to the weeks of chaos travelers endured at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

In the wake of the latest technology failure on Friday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford was asked bluntly whether he could say for certain that there wouldn't be a repeat of this past weekend's chaos.

"I can say with certainty that the system is really, really old," he told CBS News Tuesday.

"Let's not kid ourselves," Bedford added. "This system has been fragile, and it does go down."

Will the problems finally get fixed?

There has been momentum to fix both problems, which have festered for decades under the leadership of both political parties.

In recent years, the FAA has upped its air traffic control hiring efforts, in a push to reduce long-standing vacancies.

Meanwhile, Congress last year earmarked $12.5 billion for infrastructure upgrades.

The Department of Transportation has started that work, but says it needs a lot more money to make truly sweeping upgrades.

The travel sector has broadly supported that request: "They need to get to 100% staffing and to have the funds to modernize the technology," United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby wrote in a social media post Sunday.

But securing that funding will hinge on political dealmaking in Washington, D.C., which in January will be led by a divided government.

And however that fight ends, these problems won't be solved overnight.

It takes years to fully train air traffic controllers.

And to add to the complexity, overhauling aviation infrastructure while tens of thousands of flights operate each day is painstaking work with significant consequences — even if the money is there in the first place.

Look no further than last week's FAA outage, where crews replacing a router apparently triggered a chain-reaction outage that upended air travel in the U.S. for days — a disruption American Airlines now counts among the most significant in its 100-year history.

"The transition itself needs to be carefully analyzed and tested," said Capt. Shem Malmquist, a longtime Boeing 777 captain and visiting professor at the Florida Institute of Technology's College of Aeronautics. "Otherwise, an upgrade intended to solve one problem can introduce another."

Flying remains safe, even as concerns persist

Despite all the concerning headlines, industry experts largely agree:

  • Passengers should feel safe going to the airport this Thanksgiving and beyond.
  • Changes still need to be made.

"Both things can be true," Malmquist said, pointing to the many safety layers that allow planes to safely operate even when problems arise.

Keep in mind: Every plane that was in the sky during last week's FAA disruption landed safely.

And the move to halt thousands of flights? That was ultimately meant to protect travelers, leaders have emphasized.

"Passengers experience delays and cancellations, but those restrictions help keep the system safe," Malmquist said. "That doesn't mean the underlying vulnerabilities are acceptable."

Whether you're stocking up on household staples or preparing for Black Friday deals to tackle your holiday shopping, there are many ways to save on Amazon orders.

Typically, using Membership Rewards points for Amazon purchases isn't a great option, as the value per point is below that of most travel redemptions. However, right now, you can save as much as 50% on an Amazon purchase by cashing in as few as 429 Membership Rewards points with some current targeted offers.

Other cards also have Amazon offers right now.

Some TPG staffers received offers as high as 50% (up to $50), which is one of the highest we've ever seen.

Others had smaller offers of 15% off (or none at all).

The requirement to spend at least 429 Membership Rewards points is better than many of the times we've seen this offer. Back in November 2025, the requirement was 714 points, but previously it had been as low as 1 point.

To get in on this offer of saving up to 50% on an Amazon purchase when redeeming as few as 429 Membership Rewards points, you'll need a card that earns Membership Rewards points, such as the American Express Platinum Card®, the American Express® Gold Card.

Offers available when using Membership Rewards points to pay for Amazon purchases

Not all Amex cardholders will be targeted with the same Amazon offers, so check your account. For example, at the time of publication, some saw offers to save 15% (up to $10 or $15) — but, as I mentioned, a few of us saw an offer for savings of 50% (up to $50).

Remember that these are targeted offers, so they will vary. Hopefully, you are targeted for the larger offers.

It used to be that only products sold by Amazon were eligible for the discount, but now, the terms indicate that it has expanded beyond items shipped and sold by Amazon to include "a wide selection of eligible products." The trade-off may be that the offer used to trigger a discount on third-party gift cards, but that option no longer seems to be working for us.

Shop TPG's favorites: Holiday gift guide

How to save up to 50% by redeeming Amex points

Here are the steps you should take in order to turn Amex Membership Rewards points into serious Amazon savings:

  • Link your eligible Amex card to your Amazon account. You can do this through the Amex app or the Amazon website.
  • Check whether you have a targeted offer.
  • Activate the offer in your Amazon account.
  • Load your shopping cart with eligible items.
  • We do not recommend paying for the entire purchase with points, as it may not be the best use of your Membership Rewards points. Instead, use as few points at checkout as possible for your specific offer (as shown below). You'll need to use an American Express card that earns Membership Rewards points as your payment method.

Assuming everything works, you should see the offer reflected during checkout. You'll need to cover the rest of your transaction with an Amex card, though you can also apply an Amazon gift card balance if there's one attached to your account.

Other offers may be available, including from Citi

You might find similar offers with other rewards programs from time to time. For example, we've previously seen offers for 40% off (up to $20 back) when using Discover rewards on select Amazon purchases.

We are also seeing a deal for Citi cardholders to get up to 40% off by redeeming just 125 Citi ThankYou Rewards points. There's reportedly another deal to get up to $25 in Amazon gift cards.

As you can see, TPG's Eric Rosen received an offer of 25% off eligible purchases when using at least 125 Citi points. You can check your Citi Amazon offer here. He has the Citi Strata Premier® Card (see rates and fees), but any card that earns Citi ThankYou Rewards points, like the Citi Strata® Card (see rates and fees), should also work.

Additional past offers allowed targeted customers to use 1 Capital One mile for up to $20 off and 100 Chase Ultimate Rewards points for up to 50% off.

Additionally, some TPG staffers have stackable offers to earn bonus Amex Membership Rewards points on Amazon purchases by registering for an Amex Offer on the American Express page, such as 1,200 bonus Membership Rewards points for $150 spent at Amazon on a registered and eligible card.

You can also sometimes find targeted offers on Amazon product pages underneath the item's price, so keep your eyes peeled when browsing.

issues.title: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center in Cincinnati, Ohio
issues.summary: The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States. Referred to as a
issues.content_html:
The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States. Referred to as a "museum of conscience", The Freedom Center is dedicated to exploring the struggle to abolish human enslavement. During the era when the Underground Railroad was active, Cincinnati was a major gateway across the Ohio River where freedom seekers escaped from southern slave states to the northern states or Canada, making the Center's location rather significant.

Having opened its doors in 2004, the Freedom Center uses immersive exhibits across multiple floors to convey an account that is simultaneously rich in the cultural traditions of the enslaved, as well as steeped in the violence and tragedies that were endured. The histories are told through a combination of permanent and traveling exhibits that utilize storytelling, film, artwork, hands-on activities and more.

Perhaps one of the most impressive and prominent displays at the center is an authentic, 19th-century reconstructed slave pen that was obtained from a farm in Kentucky. It stands as America's only remaining, pristinely preserved slave pen and stands as a stark reminder of the atrocious conditions that were endured.

The pen, originally built somewhere around 1830 by a wealthy Kentucky farmer, runaway slave catcher, and slave trader, was used as a holding facility for captured and purchased enslaved men, women and children. It was discovered, quite by accident in 1998 when a farmer, who was preparing to demolish an old barn on his property, discovered that the barn had been built up around this old pen, thus protecting and preserving (and hiding) the slave pen for more than 100 years.

During its unfortunate years of use, enslaved people would be kept in the pen, often for months, until the slave trader accumulated a large enough "stock" to march them further south to be sold. These forced marches would often cover upwards of 750 miles. Conditions in these pens would be brutal, offering no sanitation, lighting or warmth. As many as 65 enslaved people would often be housed in this small pen. Also very moving is the memorial room dedicated to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, as well as the Freedom's Eternal Flame Terrace which overlooks the Ohio River and the city skyline.

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center is a beautiful and meaningful tribute to the human right for freedom, and to the brave men, women and children who stood up to the inhuman treatment of themselves and of others; and to those who continue to fight for the cause of freedom through out the world today.

issues.content_html:
Above the village of Kalnik in northern Croatia, the walls of Veliki Kalnik Castle rise from a jagged rocky ridge. Built across several levels, the medieval stronghold follows the natural contours of the rock, making its surviving towers and walls appear to grow out of the mountain.

First documented in 1243, the castle is best known for a story involving King Béla IV of Hungary and Croatia. According to local legend, the king took refuge here during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century. As the siege dragged on and supplies dwindled, villagers kept the defenders fed with plums.

The grateful king is said to have rewarded his rescuers with noble status. They became known as the kalnički šljivari—the “plum nobles of Kalnik.” This tale remains part of the region’s identity, connecting an imposing fortress with an unexpectedly humble fruit.

The ruins visible today developed over centuries. Their towers, fragments of walls, and elevated viewpoints reveal how the builders used the steep terrain as part of the castle’s defenses. From the heights, the view opens across the villages, fields, and wooded hills below.

issues.title: The Crucified Tongkonan of Tolu Deri in North Toraja Regency, Indonesia
issues.summary: In the highland villages of North Toraja, the skyline is dominated by tongkonan —traditional ancestral houses with sweeping, boat-shaped saddle roofs that loom dramatically over the landscape. For centuries, these wooden structures have served as the spiritual and social anchor for Torajan clans, decorated strictly according to Aluk Todolo ("the way of the ancestors"), the indigenous animist belie
issues.content_html:
In the highland villages of North Toraja, the skyline is dominated by tongkonan—traditional ancestral houses with sweeping, boat-shaped saddle roofs that loom dramatically over the landscape. For centuries, these wooden structures have served as the spiritual and social anchor for Torajan clans, decorated strictly according to Aluk Todolo ("the way of the ancestors"), the indigenous animist belief system. Their facades are traditionally adorned with carved geometric patterns (pa'ssura'), water buffalo horns (kabongo'), and sculpted wooden heads (katik) symbolizing wealth, status, and protection.

However, in the small hamlet of Tolu Deri, just north of Rantepao, one particular tongkonan stands out as a striking, visually arresting symbol of modern Torajan syncretism. Mounted directly onto the front gabled peak of the structure—occupying the exact position traditionally reserved for ancestral motifs—is a massive wooden crucifix bearing a carved figure of Jesus Christ.

While the majority of the Torajan population converted to Christianity (predominantly Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Catholicism) during the 20th century, the integration of Christian motifs into traditional architecture usually remains subtle, such as small carved crosses on support beams or church roofs built in the tongkonan shape. Seeing a full-scale, dramatic crucifix physically fused into the facade of a traditional house—standing directly above the customary buffalo head and skull mountings—is exceptionally rare.

This unique blending of iconographies visually captures the lived reality of Toraja today: a culture where deeply rooted Christian faith does not replace ancestral traditions, but rather sits alongside them in a harmonious, visually striking synthesis.

issues.title: National Geographic reveals its Pictures of the Year 2026, from spawning moray eels to a Greenland shark under the ice
issues.summary: Chosen from more than a million images, this year’s 25 selections range from a six-month solarigraph over an ancient Peruvian observatory to a camera trap on a Kenyan riverbank.
issues.author: Dale Baskin
issues.content_html:
Chosen from more than a million images, this year’s 25 selections range from a six-month solarigraph over an ancient Peruvian observatory to a camera trap on a Kenyan riverbank.

If there’s one name that’s synonymous with great photography, it’s National Geographic, which has just announced its Pictures of the Year for 2026.

National Geographic’s editors sifted through more than a million images captured by its photographers to arrive at the 25 that make up this year’s selection. That ratio alone says a lot about what it takes for a photo to make the cut. But in National Geographic’s tradition, these aren’t just great images; the publication emphasizes that they reflect the patience and dedication its photographers bring to its visual storytelling.

This year’s selections cover a wide spectrum, from the first-ever images of eels spawning in the wild, to a climber suspended from a sea cliff in Spain moments after a total solar eclipse, to Kiliii Yüyan’s encounter with a Greenland shark in the sub-freezing waters near Kulusuk in East Greenland.

Many of the images are as notable for how they were made as for what’s in them. Diego López Calvín used solarigraphy, a single continuous exposure lasting six months, to trace the sun’s path between the solstices over Peru’s ancient Chankillo observatory. Will Burrard-Lucas hid a camera trap on a remote riverbank in Kenya’s Masai Mara, and Prakash Matada mounted a fisheye lens on a telescoping pole to photograph a troop of endangered golden langurs at close range.

National Geographic’s editor-in-chief, Nathan Lump, suggested the selections are also a response to a changing photography landscape, citing the value of documenting reality. “Together, these images remind us how much there is still to discover about our planet, and that the deeply human work of documenting what’s real is more valuable than ever in a time when fakes are everywhere,” he said.

Below are a few of our favorites from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026. All 25 images will appear in the December issue of National Geographic and can be seen now on the National Geographic website. [Editor’s note: National Geographic requires users to register for a free account to view the full set of images.]

A Greenland shark, the oldest vertebrate on Earth, swims underneath the meter-thick sea ice near the village of Kulusuk in East Greenland, as diver Philipp Oppermann watches. This shark came up from the depths into the shallows at night to follow the scent of a Greenlander’s bait, frozen ringed seal. This photograph was made March 17, 2026, in early spring, when the sea ice remains strong and the visibility of the water is spectacular, over 50m (165ft).

A crack of rifle fire marks the finale of a performance of tbourida, a Moroccan equestrian tradition in which a team of riders act out a cavalry charge. Women are gradually gaining a foothold in the centuries-old sport. At the festival pictured here, all-female brigades represented two of the 140 competing troupes.

Climber Chris Sharma dangles from a completely horizontal limestone face in the moments after August’s total solar eclipse in Spain.

Apparent path of the sun as seen from the western observation point at the Chankillo Solar Observatory in Casma (Ancash), Peru. The six-month-long continuous exposure (solarigraphy) taken between June 21 and December 21, 2025, accurately shows the sun’s path, with the winter and summer solstices located at the ends of the structure outlined by the silhouette of the towers.

Deep in Kenya’s Masai Mara, a reserve bordering the northern edge of the Serengeti, photographer Will Burrard-Lucas worked with a team of rangers to hide a camera trap high on a riverbank and waited for action. The images that came back revealed something extraordinary. The secluded crossing turned out to be a high-traffic wildlife thoroughfare. Among the passersby: a pair of slinking lions, unusual visitors here.

A pair of Abbott’s moray eels (Gymnothorax eurostus) reaching the pinnacle of their spawning run, three-tenths of a second after leaving the cover of coral. The male on the left is just releasing the jaw of the female, with both eels sending gametes into the water. Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan.

A curious troop of Gee’s golden langurs – named for a naturalist who documented them in the 1950s peer into a fisheye lens that Prakash Matada affixed to a telescoping pole. The endangered canopy dwellers here have formed a rare bond with humans and proved anything but camera-shy, gazing at their own reflections.

issues.summary: Something for the videographers to look forward to.
issues.author: Mitchell Clark
issues.content_html:
Something for the videographers to look forward to.

Currently, there are no lenses that can make use of the zoom rocker on the SHX1’s grip. But that seems set to change.

Alongside its new cinema-focused SHX1 camera, Panasonic quietly announced that it’s working on something else for videographers: a power zoom lens. While there are pretty much no further details, it’s exciting to hear, as it’ll be the first full-frame power zoom option for L-mount.

The lack of any such options has been a bit of a notable omission for the mount, especially given how many video-focused cameras use it. There are, of course, Panasonic’s hybrid cameras like the S1II, S1RII and S5II series, which many videographers use, but BlackMagic Design sells pro-level studio cameras that use the mount as well.

The only mention of the lens is buried in the press release for the SHX1. In it, Panasonic says that it “is also developing a power zoom lens designed for the LUMIX SHX1 and for remote production.” To us, both the mention of remote production and the lens’s announcement being tied to a pro camera indicate that it’ll be a higher-end option, rather than a more consumer-oriented one like we’ve seen from Fujifilm, Canon and Sony. (Sorry, S9 vloggers hoping for a way to zoom in and out smoothly).

As for details like price, release date and focal range, we’ll just have to wait until Panasonic’s ready to share more. We combed through the SHX1’s announcement video to see if the company included any footage of it, but we couldn’t find any. Interestingly, one lens in the video looks an awful lot like a power zoom, but its design and the red ring near the flange strongly suggest a Canon model.

If you’re a videographer who shoots on L-mount, sound off in the comments below. Are you excited about finally getting a power zoom option, and, if so, what kind of option are you hoping for?

About the Author: Mitchell started taking pictures at 10 and hasn’t stopped since. It’s been a wide-ranging adventure, spanning a wide variety of genres and locales, and occasionally dipping into fascinations with video and filmmaking. They honed their technical knowledge doing documentation, programing and QA, writing for The Verge, and just generally messing around on the computer to see what breaks.

issues.title: VSCO brings its film-inspired presets to the desktop with a new Raw editor
issues.summary: VSCO’s first standalone desktop editor brings film-inspired presets, batch Raw editing and client delivery to macOS, with plans starting at $5 a month.
issues.author: Abby Ferguson
issues.content_html:
VSCO’s first standalone desktop editor brings film-inspired presets, batch Raw editing and client delivery to macOS, with plans starting at $5 a month.

VSCO has announced Studio Pro Desktop, the company’s first standalone desktop photo editor, available for macOS. The launch builds on Studio Pro for iPhone and VSCO One, announced in June as part of the company’s push to bring editing and photography business tools into one ecosystem.

The new desktop app combines VSCO’s film-inspired presets with non-destructive Raw editing, batch adjustments and direct publishing to VSCO Galleries. Ahead of the launch, I spoke with VSCO CEO Eric Wittman and product manager Kyle Hale, who demonstrated the editor and explained where it fits into the company’s plans.

VSCO originally built its reputation on film-emulation presets for desktop software like Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom, but discontinued them in March 2019. Now, Studio Pro Desktop takes things a step further, giving photographers a standalone application built around its looks.

The move also takes VSCO in the opposite direction from companies expanding their desktop editors onto phones and tablets. Wittman said the desktop app is intended to support photographers who started on mobile and are taking on more demanding work.

“At some point, as you become more successful, you need desktop,” Wittman said. “And so, we want to be that place where they can continue to evolve in their creative career, and not just have to go to somewhere else.”

Presets, editing tools and performance

Studio Pro Desktop includes more than 200 presets, including looks inspired by Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia and Kodak Tri-X. That many options can feel overwhelming, but, as in the mobile app, photographers can filter the library by preset category or narrow it to popular looks. Hovering over a preset also brings up information about its origins and what it does, and provides a preview of the look. The ability to favorite presets is planned for a future update.

There’s also a new preset developed with photographer and former VSCO employee Joe Greer. Called IOE1 PRO, it combines warm tones and subtle saturation with a film-inspired rendering, according to VSCO.

Beyond presets, Studio Pro Desktop offers tools you’d expect in editing software: exposure, contrast, white balance and HSL adjustments, along with cropping, straightening and perspective correction.

“We also have our own bespoke grain tool that we modeled off of actual film grain,” Hale explained during the demonstration. He also showed that you can adjust the strength, size and color of the grain.

Wittman emphasized the development work behind that tool. “There’s a lot of R&D that went into producing a brilliant grain tool,” he said, pointing to its use of color rather than purely monochromatic grain as an example of the company’s attention to film rendering.

The company says its new Reflex image engine supports real-time adjustment previews, with Raw support covering more than 800 cameras across 20 brands. Photographers can also batch-edit more than 500 images at once.

“We are optimizing for speed in this app,” Hale said. “We want to be the fastest in the business in terms of how we allow people to edit their Raw images.” That mindset reflects the app’s focus on getting through a set of images quickly.

Hale, who previously worked as a wedding photographer, said that emphasis comes from the demands of running a photography business. “Their time is limited,” he said. “They’re trying to run a business, and so editing is one small sliver of the work that they do.”

File handling and client delivery

Once images are edited, photographers can publish full-resolution versions directly to VSCO Galleries without manually exporting and uploading them to a separate service. During the demonstration, the app processed the edited Raw files into JPEGs for delivery, while allowing other work to continue in the editor.

“It’s just nice, that seamless integration between the editing side, being able to push that to galleries, go back to editing,” Wittman said. “That’s kind of the beauty of just one system.”

Hale specified that edits are non-destructive, with adjustments stored within the application rather than applied to the original Raw file. Removing an image from Studio Pro Desktop also leaves the original on the computer or external drive.

Some workflow features won’t be available at launch. During the briefing, Hale said Projects, culling and star ratings were tentatively planned for January, with saved editing recipes and an AI-powered Remove tool targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Curves are also planned for a post-launch update.

An assistive approach to AI

Asked about AI, Wittman described VSCO’s approach as “human-centered, AI-assisted,” with an emphasis on helping photographers with tasks rather than replacing their work. “We want to preserve the integrity of the photo, but allow you to do things like maybe retouching, or maybe remove that street sign,” he said.

Wittman also said VSCO is not training generative AI models and has partnered with companies it says will not train on its data. He emphasized that the presets and some effects do not use AI, leaving photographers the option to edit without those tools.

Pricing and availability

Studio Pro Desktop is available for macOS as a free download. Access to the full editing experience, including all presets and batch editing, requires a VSCO Pro or VSCO One membership. VSCO Pro memberships start at $5 per month or $60 per year.

For photographers on a tighter budget, that could make VSCO an attractive option. Adobe’s Lightroom plan starts at $11.99 per month with an annual commitment, while its Photography plan, which adds Photoshop, costs $19.99 per month, also with an annual commitment. VSCO’s editing tools are less comprehensive at launch, but photographers who primarily want film-inspired looks, batch editing and client delivery may find its lower price appealing.

About the Author: Abby Ferguson holds an MFA in photography and blends a fine-art background with extensive editorial and commercial experience. She built and led an in-house imaging program for a large vacation rental company and has served as an associate editor at Popular Photography. She also teaches at a local community college and serves on its Photographic Technology Program Advisory Board, sharing her knowledge and enthusiasm for the medium.

Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just ann
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

Yes.

That’s as simple as the answer need be, but that’s not the point of this article.

Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just announced the Smartphone Xenon Flash A2, and their tagline is “Your phone, now a pro camera” which isn’t exactly factual, but also, the definition of “pro camera” is very loose.

The thing to keep in mind with ANY small light source is that its going to be harsh – there’s stuff you can do about it, though. You can diffuse it, bounce it (though a small light like the A2 might not give quite enough output to do much there) but even things like bouncing it off a close wall or even a sheet of paper in a pinch – use what you have, experiment.

I love the idea of small portable lights, this one is certainly an interesting addition to your phone photography – maybe worth giving a try, it’s certainly a good starter to your photography lighting journey.

Here’s the Godox Press Release (With a little bit of my own ramble)

Smartphone Photography, Now With More Zap

Phone cameras keep getting better, but low light, backlighting and mixed lighting can still make them sweat. Enter the Godox A2: proper pro-style lighting for your phone, with more control over your light and a lot more room to play.

Its short, punchy burst of xenon light freezes motion in its tracks, which is great for action shots and stylized looks.

Xenon Flash: Bring Your Subject to Life

Go bold with direct flash, or add a subtle lift to a backlit portrait. With a guide number of roughly 15 (ISO 100, metres), the A2 has plenty of oomph for close-range shots. When flash is your main light, that quick burst also helps freeze movement. *For best results, keep the A2 within 2 m of your subject. Want more power or wider coverage? Pair Godox’s upcoming smartphone wireless flash trigger (sold separately) with Godox speedlights or outdoor flashes.

TTL and Manual Modes: Stay Spontaneous, Get Precise

Fast and flawless when the moment’s fleeting, or hands-on when you want to flex your creative muscles. TTL and Manual modes have you covered both ways.

High-Speed Sync: Find Your Balance

Why banish that bright background when it can star in the story? With high-speed sync up to 1/8000s, the A2 lets you control ambient exposure while lighting your subject. Balance a face against a sunlit scene, or go for a faster shutter speed to keep the action crisp.

Bi-Color LED: True Color for Everyday Stories

Truer colors and flattering skin tones make portrait videos look natural and beautifully textured. Low light or indoors, the results feel authentic and ready to share. Your content doesn’t just look good, it feels right, and it’s always social-media ready.

Godox Camera App: Your Look, at Your Fingertips

Find your look right on your screen. Built on Godox’s TTL know-how, the Godox Camera app keeps exposure simple in Auto (A) mode, with Natural, Even and Contrast flash effects to try out. Feeling fussy? Switch to Manual (M) mode and tweak shutter speed and flash output yourself. Bluetooth with NFC-assisted setup lets you adjust flash and LED settings wirelessly, on or off camera.

Dual-Side Magnetic Mounting: Snap On, Explore New Angles

The A2’s dual magnetic design isn’t just for the back of your phone. Snap it to any metal surface or pop it on a stand and you’re ready to roll. On the front, the magnetic ring lets you attach accessories to shape the light exactly how you like. Simple, flexible and always creative.

Magnetic Accessories: Change the Light, Set the Mood

Go moodier and more dramatic with optional extras like a honeycomb grid, barndoors or a snoot to aim your light and tame the spill. Add a touch of warmth with a full CTO magnetic filter. *For best results, use the A2 off-camera with light-shaping accessories.

Compact. Magnetic. More Ways to Light.

Pro flash power in a palm-sized body. Pocketable, portable and happy to go anywhere you do.

Four Colors, A Style of Your Own

The A2 brings pro lighting to your phone in four distinctive colors. Pick a finish that suits your everyday style, and make your kit as personal as the photos you take.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Do people still print their photographs? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is still printing out their photographs?

We celebrated my dad’s life recently, and at the wake my brother had printed out a couple hundred photographs that showed the life and times of dad and those he cared about. There’s something very real about having a print you can hold in your hand, nothing to log in to, no computers to boot up, just a square of paper and your memories.

Before we share this press release, here’s a challenge: In the next couple of months, aim to have one of your photographs printed, and to take that one step further, I was just listening to a clip from a podcast (You can see it here) Print Swap, what a great idea, print one of your images and send it to someone – to have and to hold.

Right, the Godox P100, it’s not an A3 Epson printing onto some beautiful Canson Rag, but it’s WITH YOU, you can print images and have them. (I’ve been grabbing frames with the beautiful FujiFilm Instax Mini 99 which prints a little 45x62mm photo)

On with our press release, please keep in mind we have not tested the P100 ourselves.

Godox Introduces P100 Portable Color Photo Printer

Godox has announced the P100 Portable Color Photo Printer, a compact dye-sublimation printer designed to turn digital images into physical prints wherever you are.

The P100 uses 300 dpi high-precision dye-sublimation printing, with 1,256 printhead heating elements and support for 16.7 million colours. According to Godox, the combination is designed to produce smooth colour gradations, fine detail and vivid colour reproduction.

Each print also receives an automatic protective overcoat, helping protect the finished photo from dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion.

Print and personalise from your phone

The P100 connects to the Godox Cam APP via Bluetooth, while NFC tap-to-connect provides another quick way to pair the printer.

From within the app, users can capture and print photos directly, or work with images already on their device. Creative options include filters, frames, stickers and templates, along with tools for creating ID photos and collages.

The app also allows users to check remaining paper and battery levels, making it easier to keep track of the printer’s status.

Designed to travel

With its compact design and lightweight construction, the P100 is intended to be easy to take along to parties, family gatherings, housewarmings and other everyday occasions.

Rather than leaving photos sitting on a phone or buried in a cloud library, the P100 gives users a simple way to turn them into physical prints that can be displayed, collected, added to a scrapbook or shared with friends and family.

Automatic protection

The P100’s automatic lamination process adds a protective overcoat to every finished print. Godox says this helps protect prints against dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion, as well as humid conditions.

The process happens automatically after printing, so there is no additional lamination step for the user.

All-in-one cartridge

The P100 uses an all-in-one photo paper cartridge, designed to make replacing the printing supplies quick and straightforward.

Combined with wireless connectivity and the Godox Cam APP, the system is designed to keep the process from capturing a photo to holding the finished print as simple as possible.

A physical home for digital memories

The P100 is ultimately aimed at something increasingly familiar in photography: we take plenty of photos, but relatively few ever make it off our phones.

By combining portable dye-sublimation printing with a range of simple editing and personalisation tools, Godox says the P100 is designed to make printing those images easier, whether you’re sharing them with friends at a gathering or simply putting a favourite photograph somewhere you’ll actually see it.

The Godox P100 Portable Color Photo Printer is now part of Godox’s expanding range of photography accessories.

You can get them online for around $200 Aussie, do a Google and see what you can find!

Don’t forget, PRINT YOUR WORK.

National Indigenous art prize puts Lismore on Australia’s cultural map

Some of Australia’s most exciting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists will compete for $23,000 in prize money in Lismore this year, as finalists are announced for the 2026 Koori Mail Indigenous Art Award.

Run nationally from Lismore Regional Gallery in partnership with the Koori Mail Newspaper, the biennial award has grown into a significant platform for contemporary Indigenous art, attracting artists from across Australia and spanning painting, sculpture, photography, ceramics, moving image and fibre art.

This year’s prize pool has expanded to $23,000, with the Major Award doubling from $10,000 in 2024 to $20,000 and a new $3,000 Youth Award for artists aged 18 to 25.

Lismore Regional Gallery Director Susi Muddiman OAM welcomed the announcement of this year’s finalists.

“This award demonstrates that nationally significant contemporary art does not have to be centred in a capital city. From Lismore, we are providing a national platform for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists and bringing extraordinary work from across Australia to audiences in regional NSW,” Ms Muddiman said.

“Combined with the Youth Award this year, the shortlist highlights incredible fresh talent alongside established artists whose work commands attention on the national stage. It promises to be an inspiring and powerful exhibition that we are honoured to present.”

The 2026 finalists are:

Major Award Finalists

Michelle Anderson, Kieron Anderson, Sonya Breckenridge, Luke Close, Ralph Close, Chris Curtis, Louise Daniels, Joe Dhamanydji, Jodie Dowd, Troy Firebrace, Margaret Rarru Garrawurra, Donna Gayford McLaren, Maddison Gibbs, Jodie Harris, Melinda Ingram, Clare Jaque Vasquez, Kieren Karritpul, Virginia Keft, Jaymi Lawrence, Tara Lloyd, Zali Morgan, Amber Morris, Kent Morris, Jodie Munday, Gail Naden, Ian Nicholas, Tracey Piccoli, Ross Potter, Brandi Salmon, Damien Shen, Kyle Slabb, Valerie Smith, Jasmin Stanford, Douglas Tamwoy, Anthony Walker and Jeremy Worrall.

Youth Award Finalists

Cameron Cooper, Keesia Close, Levi Roberts, Monique Vuong and Mayarr Yanner.
This year’s entries are being judged by Yorta Yorta curator, writer and academic Dr Kimberley Moulton, Senior Curator Exhibitions at Melbourne’s RISING festival and former Adjunct Curator of Indigenous Art at London’s Tate Modern.

Reflecting on the shortlisted works, Dr Moulton praised the remarkable breadth and strength of the entries.

“It’s an honour to judge this year’s Koori Mail Art Award. With a diverse combination of local and national works, city based and regional, it’s an incredibly strong year with artists sharing their stories, connections to country and culture,” Dr Moulton said.

Koori Mail Cultural Lead Trevor Kapeen said the award created opportunities for First Nations artists to share their work with a national audience.

“Every year this award brings a magnificent gathering of First Nations artistic talent into focus,” Mr Kapeen said.

“For the Koori Mail, supporting these artists is about creating tangible opportunities for national visibility and cultural exchange. We congratulate all the 2026 finalists and look forward to celebrating their achievements when the exhibition opens.”

Finalists will come together at Lismore Regional Gallery for a major exhibition opening on 7 November, putting regional NSW at the centre of a national showcase of established and emerging Indigenous artistic talent.

Council and the Lismore Regional Gallery are incredibly thankful to the generosity of the major sponsors, the Koori Mail Newspaper and Hurford Hardwood, and to the Friends of the Gallery for their contributions to the prize pool.

issues.title: How “American Gothic” Took On a Life of Its Own
issues.summary: After decades of collecting pop culture riffs on the iconic 1930 painting, Wanda M. Corn traces the work’s canonization and the life of its maker Grant Wood, whose story remains largely overlooked.
issues.author: Lauren Moya Ford
issues.content_html:
You already know the image by heart: Two stern figures stand before an old wooden house. To the left, a blonde, blue-eyed woman wears an apron and a somber expression. Beside her, an unsmiling man in glasses and overalls grips a pitchfork. Since it was first exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1930, Grant Wood’s painting has joined the ranks of art historical touchstones and shown up in countless ads, books, and memes. But what made this unassuming image so popular, and why does it continue to captivate us today?

In The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon (2026), art historian and curator Wanda M. Corn provides some compelling answers. The author began writing about Wood’s painting in 1981, and she has spent decades amassing an archive of “American Gothic”-related imagery that tracks the farm couple across General Mills cereal ads, Gordon Parks’s 1942 portrait of African-American janitor Ella Watson during his fellowship with the Farm Security Administration, magazine covers, COVID-era cartoons, and other surprising riffs. Her book traces the painting’s history from the controversy behind its creation and the bitter fallout it brought to its hapless maker through to its transformation into a pop culture cornerstone and a symbol of Wood’s home state.

issues.title: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works
issues.summary: The artist filed the complaint six months after terminating her relationship with dealer Richard Saltoun.
issues.author: Phillip Pyle
issues.content_html:
Conceptual artist Eleanor Antin is seeking the return of at least 179 works or $975,000 in compensatory damages in a lawsuit against her dealer, Richard Saltoun. The complaint was filed in New York State Supreme Court on July 29, six months after the artist terminated her relationship with Saltoun’s namesake gallery, which operates locations in New York, London, and Rome.

Filed by the 91-year-old artist’s son and attorney-in-fact, Blaise Antin, and her studio, Paranoid Productions, the suit claims that Saltoun “initially purported to agree to return all of the works it held” upon their business separation at the gallery's London location on January 16. News of the lawsuit was first reported by Artnet.

Saltoun claimed in February that the gallery had returned all of Antin’s works to her family, according to filed documents. However, later that month, the artist’s archivist, citing an inventory produced by Saltoun himself, allegedly discovered that Antin was still missing at least 179 works, the majority of which were still held at the London gallery.

issues.title: Vilcek Foundation Launches Open Call for 2027 Grants Offering $200,000 in Funding to US Nonprofits
issues.summary: The foundation invites applications from mission-aligned arts and science organizations for grants of up to $20,000 through March 31, 2027.
issues.author: The Vilcek Foundation
issues.content_html:
This week, the Vilcek Foundation announced its third annual open call for grant applications. The organization invites nonprofits whose work aligns with the foundation’s mission to elevate immigrant contributions in the United States and foster an appreciation for the arts and sciences to apply for funding now through March 31, 2027.

The foundation will award a total of $200,000 to US-based nonprofits as a part of its 2027 grants cycle. Individual organizations may apply for a grant of up to $20,000.

Applicants should lead innovative initiatives that generate measurable impact within and beyond their immediate communities. Strong applications demonstrate both a unique vision and clear plan of action for uplifting immigrants, the arts, or the sciences. Qualifying organizations must be recognized as tax-exempt under Section 501(c)(3).

The Vilcek Foundation is actively expanding the geographic reach of its grantmaking with the goal of supporting organizations across all US states and select territories. The 2027 grant cycle aims to support nonprofits based around the country, including those in the following locations not previously represented in the foundation’s grantmaking: Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Iowa, Mississippi, Nevada, South Carolina, South Dakota, West Virginia, Wisconsin, American Samoa, Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and the US Virgin Islands.

Since its founding in 2000, the Vilcek Foundation has remained steadfast in its philanthropic mission. To date, the foundation has provided more than $7 million in grants to nonprofits in 40 states, two US territories, and Washington, DC.

Earlier this month, the foundation announced the 12 organizations receiving funding as a part of its 2026 grants cycle. Situated across the country, the 2026 grantees include the Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts; Counterpublic, whose Triennial is currently on view in St. Louis; Delaware Contemporary Arts; and the Japanese American National Museum.

The 2027 Vilcek Foundation grant period will run from September 1, 2027 through August 31, 2028.

Organizations may apply for either project support or operating support.

Interested nonprofits should submit applications via the foundation’s Grants Portal by 11:59 pm (ET) on March 31, 2027.

For full eligibility requirements and application details, visit vilcek.org/grants .

issues.title: Anti-Monuments to Trump
issues.summary: How do we memorialize the Trump era? Plus, an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act, and having a beer with Outarra Watts.
issues.author: Hyperallergic
issues.content_html:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, I was in the last place I wanted to be: Washington, DC. Where would I go? I wanted nothing to do with his administration’s empty grandeur. I spent the day at Maya Lin’s Vietnam War Memorial, a dark wound in the earth. In this much more hopeful moment post-midterms, Ed Simon asks a related question: How should memorials remember the MAGA era? He points to historical anti-fascist examples in Germany — and also suggests the bulldozing of Trump’s ballroom to rubble as its own kind of monument.

Satire’s not a bad strategy to record this era, either. Also today, Greg Werkheiser pens an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act. The act’s next of kin, the National Register of Historic Places, he writes, “is said to be concerned about its own health.”

Finally, don’t miss the newest installation of Jennifer Samet’s “Beer With a Painter” column. She interviews Ivorian painter Ouattara Watts, who works only at night, when the veil between this world and the next is thinnest. Plus, The Met and the Shanghai Museum are teaming up, just weeks after MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Museum joined forces. They say art imitates life; I just didn’t know that meant we were getting museum oligopolies.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy. | Ed Simon
