issues.title: Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast
issues.summary: “The academic community are kind of stuck in their ways,” Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt told Fortune. "They don’t like to change."
issues.author: Nick Lichtenberg
issues.content_html:
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt has a problem with the four-year degree, and he brought it to a room full of the people who hire its graduates.

“The academic community are kind of stuck in their ways. They don’t like to change,” Stitt said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel with U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt. He said when he digs into the degree programs at the University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma State, “there’s a book this thick and then you’ve got like three people graduating from these different things.”

He added: “I’m not saying that degree is not important, but you can’t be all things [to] all people.”

His fix is a 90-credit bachelor’s degree, 30 credits short of the standard 120, or roughly a year less of tuition. In-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges averaged $11,950 in the 2024-25 school year, according to the College Board. Stitt said the idea is to keep the rigor of the requirements, trim some electives, and “get kids ready for the workforce quicker.”

RAND counted 119 reduced-credit bachelor’s programs publicly announced across the U.S. as of May 2026, up from five in 2024, most of them in “applied and workforce-facing fields.” Jason Lee, a senior policy researcher at RAND, has since told the Wall Street Journal the number of shortened bachelor’s programs announced this year are up to roughly 150.

From executive order to diploma

Stitt signed an executive order in February ordering a 90-day study of 90-credit “accelerated” degrees, and the Legislature followed with HB 3315, which required the State Regents to study feasibility. In June, the regents took action to create a framework for the degrees.

“A three-year degree speeds up workforce entry and makes so much sense for students who are ready to work and support a family, right here in Oklahoma,” Stitt said in a statement at the time.

On Sept. 3, the regents approved four reduced-credit degrees ranging from 90 to 103 credit hours, according to the Oklahoma Council of Public Affairs: social work at the University of Oklahoma, two at Oklahoma State, in artificial intelligence and in business, and workforce development at Rogers State University.

“A college degree doesn’t have to take four years just because it always has,” Stitt posted on X.

Other states are moving, too. Tennessee’s higher education commission approved a policy in July allowing bachelor’s degrees of as few as 90 credit hours. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott directed the state’s coordinating board to develop pathways in August. The University of North Carolina system approved a pilot in April, and 11 campuses have submitted proposals, according to the James G. Martin Center.

What a fourth year was buying

The three-year degree tests an old question in economics: how much of a degree’s value comes from what students learn, and how much from what it tells employers. Michael Spence shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in economics, in part, for showing how education can work as a signal, costly proof of ability that employers can’t see directly. A shorter degree is cheaper to get. Nobody knows yet whether it signals as much. Much of Europe has run three-year bachelor’s degrees since the Bologna reforms began in 1999.

RAND found that business, information technology, and cybersecurity look most workable for shorter degrees, while fields with clinical or licensing requirements are less adaptable. How graduate schools, employers, and licensing boards will treat the degrees remains uncertain, RAND found.

“We don’t have employers who said, ‘Gee, we’ve had three-year graduates,’” Madeleine Green, executive director of the College-in-3 Exchange, told Inside Higher Ed this month.

The programs are still small. Johnson & Wales University has 135 students across four three-year programs, and Weber State has 30 across three, according to Inside Higher Ed.

Faculty groups have pushed back. The American Association of University Professors and the American Federation of Teachers objected to Massachusetts’ approvals on grounds of “academic integrity.”

“This is not innovation. This is just cutting corners,” AAUP president Todd Wolfson told the Associated Press in August. A year less of tuition is also a year less of revenue for the schools.

Stitt’s other pitch to the CEOs was apprenticeships. He said he had visited Switzerland and Germany, where compulsory education stops after the first year of high school and students start working inside companies, and that Oklahoma made liability insurance fixes so companies could take on high school students. He told the room about a 19-year-old in Switzerland who wanted to be an architect. After three years at an architecture firm, she could work as a draftsperson, and university was still open to her.

“We’ve got to rethink that in our workforce needs here in the U.S.,” Stitt said.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: Home Depot’s incoming CEO says homeowners are ‘feeling pressure.’ A quarter can’t cover a $5,000 repair
issues.summary: A third of homeowners have put off repairs, and many are now doing the work themselves.
issues.author: Bilin Lin
issues.content_html:
Richard McPhail, a 21-year Home Depot veteran who was named the retailer’s next CEO on Tuesday, has been watching financial pressure build among American homeowners. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call the same day, he acknowledged that “a rising interest rate environment puts pressure on our customer and our business.”

McPhail, Home Depot’s CFO since 2019, takes over as CEO on Nov. 23. Ted Decker, who recently returned from a medical leave, will step down as CEO and remain chair of the board.

That’s a problem for a retailer that booked $164.7 billion in revenue last fiscal year, the bulk of it from people fixing up homes they already own. Homeowners are “one of the most resilient customer cohorts in the economy,” McPhail told Yahoo Finance in a February interview. “But they’re feeling pressure like everyone else.”

“If you look at housing turnover, that’s actually been frozen for three years,” he said, adding that turnover has sat at historical lows three years running. He also pointed to customers’ “concerns around housing affordability, general affordability” and “broader concerns over uncertainty and job loss.”

Wealthy on paper, stretched in practice

Owning a home has long been considered a path to financial security in America. But even homeowners with considerable housing wealth feel squeezed by the rising cost of living, and some struggle to afford the upkeep of their biggest asset.

Nearly two-thirds of homeowners (63%) say owning a home causes them at least moderate financial stress, up from 55% in June 2025, according to an October survey of 1,000 homeowners conducted for Hometap, a home equity financing company.

That stress comes even as Americans sit on a record $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity as of the second quarter of 2026, according to First American Data & Analytics. That’s the amount owners could borrow against while keeping their combined loan-to-value at 80% or below.

But housing wealth isn’t disposable income. Even owners who locked in rock-bottom pandemic-era mortgage rates aren’t immune to rising property taxes and insurance premiums or climbing utility bills. The typical homeowner now spends $16,566 a year on costs beyond the mortgage, about two-thirds of it on upkeep, according to Zillow.

Job worries are adding to the strain. In the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s October Survey of Consumer Expectations, released last week, consumers put the odds of higher unemployment a year from now at 45.3%, the highest reading since April 2020. Their perceived chance of losing their own job also ticked up to 13.9%.

Delayed repairs are getting more expensive

A LendingTree survey conducted in September found that 34% of homeowners had postponed at least one necessary repair or maintenance task over the past two years. Among those with outstanding repairs, 32% said they simply couldn’t afford the work.

A surprise $5,000 repair would be entirely out of reach for a quarter of homeowners surveyed. Another 30% could cover it only by substantially draining their savings.

Among homeowners who needed repairs over the past two years, 37% dipped into emergency savings, and 33% cut spending on essentials such as groceries, healthcare, or childcare to pay for the work.

Waiting tends to cost more. Among respondents whose homes currently need repairs, 34% said delaying the work drove up the price, and a quarter said it caused damage elsewhere in the house.

Home Depot is growing anyway

Decker sounded a similar alarm in February, telling analysts that “our customers are telling us that they’re not investing” in bigger projects, citing affordability, the jobs picture, and weak consumer confidence.

Even so, the business has grown this year. Home Depot reported third-quarter sales of $43.4 billion on Tuesday, up 4.9% from a year earlier, with comparable sales up 2.2%. “Third quarter results exceeded our expectations,” McPhail said.

Homeowners may be shelving kitchen remodels, but smaller repairs and maintenance jobs have kept customers coming in. In August, McPhail, then CFO, credited “broad-based demand across the business as customers continued to engage in smaller projects.”

Tight budgets are also pushing homeowners to pick up the tools themselves. Among LendingTree respondents who completed at least some repairs, 60% did some of the work themselves because they couldn’t afford a professional. Among millennials, that figure reached 72%.

At the other end of the market, Home Depot has been courting professional contractors, builders, and remodelers. SRS, the building-materials distributor it acquired for $18.25 billion in June 2024, delivered “almost $5 billion in sales in the quarter,” McPhail said. Executives said on the call that cross-selling between Home Depot and SRS is on track to generate $400 million in sales this year, a figure the company aims to double in 2027.

The company has also been investing in AI and digital tools that help pros plan projects, manage material lists, and track orders. Its express delivery service now reaches customers within two hours from virtually all of its stores, incoming president and COO Ann-Marie Campbell said on the call.

Home Depot now expects total sales to grow about 4.5% in fiscal 2026, with comparable sales up roughly 1.4%. McPhail is betting that speed will keep winning over a cautious customer: “Our investments in express delivery and in AI customer and associate enablement are making a meaningful difference.”

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: Chipotle, Macy’s, and Ally CEOs on why loyalty perks matter more as shoppers balk at high prices
issues.summary: Top brands are using loyalty programs to satisfy deal-seeking consumers.
issues.author: Phil Wahba
issues.content_html:
When Chipotleoverhauled its rewards program in April, it made perks like free chips and guac easier to snag and added half-off entrées, as diners started to balk at high prices.

For the burrito chain, the program helps it weather inflation and keep customers in the Chipotle habit. It now counts more than 24 million active members, and they drove a third of sales in the third quarter, the highest share Chipotle has reported.

“I think in this modern world, you have to be really up to speed on what’s going on with your loyalty consumer because arguably it’s the most valuable consumer within your ecosystem,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel moderated by this reporter.

Loyalty programs have become a front line in the fight for market share. The freebies get people in the door, but the bigger prize is the data: a detailed record of what customers buy and when, which lets brands tailor offers and makes it harder for shoppers to stray. Boatwright, Macy’s CEO Tony Spring, and Ally Financial CEO Michael Rhodes run very different businesses: Macy’s is No. 192 on the 2026 Fortune 500, Ally is No. 275, and Chipotle is No. 351. All three are leaning on that math.

Chipotle won’t shrink the rewards

Boatwright said the pull to trim perks is real. As a rewards database grows and inflation squeezes margins, he said, “The gravity pulls brands toward, ‘ How do I capture some margin here.” His own team brought him ideas for cutting rewards.

“We are unwilling as a brand to do that,” he said. “I said, come back to me with 10 ideas on how to increase value for the consumer and let’s have a conversation.”

That stance tracks with Chipotle’s refusal to chase traffic with deep discounts. In February, Boatwright said he didn’t want to “devalue our core offering” with McDonald’s-style deals and planned price increases below the rate of inflation. Loyalty perks let the chain hand its most frequent diners more value without cutting menu prices for everyone.

The same logic shaped Chipotle’s answer to GLP-1 weight-loss drugs: a high-protein menu with low-priced add-ons rather than markdowns. “You’ve got to have innovation that doesn’t discount the core offering, but meets a consumer need state,” Boatwright said.

Macy’s wants rewards in your wallet before you pick a store

Spring, who took over as CEO of Macy’s Inc. in February 2024, has been steering the 168-year-old department store operator’s turnaround. He said a loyalty program only works if shoppers believe it does.

“Loyalty is integral, I think, to the relationships people have with brands,” Spring said. “And we are constantly striving at Macy’s, Bloomingdale’s, and Bluemercury to make sure that the loyalty program has value in the eyes of the consumer, not in our eyes.”

The payoff comes when a shopper decides where to look first, at the mall or online. “If the Macy’s app or the Bloomingdale’s app is there and I already have rewards in my wallet, it’s going to encourage me to go there maybe and complete my activity,” he said.

Macy’s program is built to be easy to join, Spring said, with rewards that don’t depend on how a customer pays and bigger ones for Macy’s credit card holders. The most committed shoppers can earn perks like free merchandise, free delivery, and after-hours shopping. “If you are more committed to us, we want to provide that value to you,” he said.

Spring is also thinking about what happens to those perks when an AI agent does the shopping. Macy’s has started working with Google’s Gemini on agentic commerce, he said, and the priority is making sure reward points, gift cards, and delivery promises still work when a bot places the order.

A bank tries to win devotion

Food, clothes, and home goods offer sensory experiences that financial services can’t match, and few people feel much affection for their bank. Ally Financial, which bills itself as the largest all-digital bank in the U.S., is trying anyway. In May, it rolled out Loyally, a fee-free rewards program open to customers regardless of their account balance.

“The question really is how can we add some real value for customers that gives them reasons they want to keep on coming back to our site and engaging with us,” Rhodes said. “We’ve literally had it for like six months now, but the early results are really encouraging.”

Ally is starting from a strong base, by Rhodes’ account. He said customer retention runs well over 90%, about 15% of new account volume comes through referrals, and 70% of customers are Gen Z or millennials.

Rhodes argued that AI search is raising the stakes on every customer interaction, because what customers and employees say about a brand feeds the engines that make recommendations. “There are people who spend 10 times what we spend,” he said of Ally’s marketing budget. “Yet in the AI search engines and unbranded inquiries in consumer banking, we show up number one.”

Rewarding regulars without shutting out newcomers

The harder balance is rewarding regulars while still persuading new customers to try a brand. Spring said that’s where a retailer’s customer data comes in: breaking shoppers into cohorts and targeting each one, both to drive new traffic and to “create extraordinary value for your highest, most loyal consumers.”

“It’s not a one-size-fits-all approach,” Spring said. “It needs to be very bespoke. And you have to leverage tools like, dare I say, AI.”

Boatwright said every change to Chipotle’s program aims to draw more users in at the top of the funnel, then “make it much more sticky within the funnel and get those consumers coming back more often.”

The next test may come when the customer isn’t the one searching. Boatwright said agentic AI ordering is coming whether brands are ready or not, and Chipotle has to make sure it shows up “when you ask your agent, tell me the best burrito in town.”

issues.title: Alex Karp put Palantir’s early sales team in the Mandarin Oriental instead of a Motel 6—at 10x the price
issues.summary: Palantir’s 10th employee recalls why Alex Karp booked the Mandarin Oriental over a Motel 6—a perception play.
issues.author: Steven John
issues.content_html:
The old advice to dress for the job you want can apply to lodging, too—at least in the thinking of some enterprising executives. In its early days, Palantir Technologies put its young staffers up at a luxury Mandarin Oriental for sales trips instead of booking a budget chain like Motel 6.

The call came from Alex Karp, Palantir’s cofounder and CEO, and the logic was simple: In enterprise sales, appearances can matter as much as the bottom line. Even companies that will someday be worth hundreds of billions often start out with a “fake it ’til you make it” mentality.

Garry Tan, who was Palantir’s 10th employee and is now CEO of startup accelerator Y Combinator, shared the story in a May 2025 post on X:

“Funny early Palantir story.

We were doing some of our first sales meetings for Palantir and (team was all under 25 at the time) and were staying at the Mandarin Oriental.

We said hey this is a startup! Why are we wasting money on this?

Alex Karp said the people you’re selling to will ask you where you are staying. And we aren’t selling Motel 6 software. We are selling Mandarin Oriental software.”

From long shot to a $386 billion company

Karp’s bet on looking the part has aged well. Palantir began trading on the New York Stock Exchange through a direct listing in September 2020 and was valued at about $18 billion after its first trades. As of Nov. 16, 2026, it was worth about $386 billion, per CompaniesMarketCap.

That valuation is disproportionate to its sales. As Fortune has reported, Palantir became one of the world’s 25 most valuable companies while still too small to make the Fortune 500.

None of that was obvious when Karp, Peter Thiel, Stephen Cohen, Joe Lonsdale, and Nathan Gettings founded the company in 2003. Top venture firms passed on it, and Thiel put in much of his own money, alongside backing from the CIA’s venture arm, In-Q-Tel. The CIA became its first customer.

Karp, though, clearly believed in what was coming, and he wanted the company to project it. So even in the early days, staffers checked into a Mandarin Oriental when they traveled to pitch customers.

The price of looking the part

Today, the typical nightly rate for an entry-level room at a Mandarin Oriental is $921, according to Fermata data. A night at a Motel 6, the budget chain Tan mentioned, often costs well under $100; one Albany, N.Y., location lists rooms for less than $65 on Kayak.

Those are 2026 prices, not 2000s rates, but the gap is the point: The luxury room costs more than 10 times as much as the budget one.

Plenty of people who responded to Tan’s post agreed with Karp. The post was viewed more than 830,000 times, and replies included: “Carry yourself as the team you will be, not the team you are today,” and “This is such a sharp reminder that in enterprise, perception shapes value. Sometimes it’s not just the product, it’s how confidently you signal the tier you’re playing in.”

The case for the cheap room

Others weren’t sold on the “fake it ’til you make it” approach. Ryan Rzepecki, who founded the e-bike startup JUMP and sold it to Uber in 2018, posted: “All the way through acquisition we shared hotel rooms and piled into Airbnbs. We even had our clients offer to have us stay in their homes.”

And a user named Avery Haskell posted: “And he’s got the exorbitant P/E ratio to show for it!”

There’s no single right answer. As many X users pointed out, plenty of America’s most successful companies trace their roots to garages and basements, not luxury hotels.

Karp, for his part, still makes no apologies for projecting confidence. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit last December, he told Wall Street critics who call him arrogant to “judge me by the accomplishment.”

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: 19th-Century Philosopher’s Head Examined
issues.summary: LONDON, ENGLAND—English philosopher Jeremy Bentham suffered from painful toothaches and arthritis of the lower jaw, […] The post 19th-Century Philosopher’s Head Examined appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
LONDON, ENGLAND—English philosopher Jeremy Bentham suffered from painful toothaches and arthritis of the lower jaw, according to a statement released by University College London. Bentham is thought to have been the first person to have legally registered the preference for his body to be used for scientific study after death, including preservation as an “auto-icon,” or “self-image.” After his death in June 11, 1832, Bentham’s remains were dissected and his body preserved in the collections of University College London. A team of scientists led by Tim Causer of the Bentham Project carried out advanced CT scanning of Bentham’s head, revealing the poor condition of his teeth and lower jaw. “I have never been fond of having my teeth drawn, but I have more than once submitted to the momentary torment to rid myself of the enduring one,” Bentham wrote to Sir Robert Peel in 1830. The CT scans also confirmed that Bentham’s brain had been removed during the dissection, but some of the outer brain remained in the skull. The glass eyes added to the head in the creation of the auto-icon were found to have been equipped with an anatomically correct optic nerve. The scan also provided a detailed view of the hole driller in the top of the skull in order to attach it to the rest of the auto-icon. To read about some of Bentham’s theories, go to “Alone, but Closely Watched.”

issues.title: Mesopotamian Chronology Refined with Tree Rings and Ice Cores
issues.summary: TUCSON, ARIZONA—Phys.org reports that a team of researchers led by Charlotte Pearson of the University […] The post Mesopotamian Chronology Refined with Tree Rings and Ice Cores appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
TUCSON, ARIZONA—Phys.org reports that a team of researchers led by Charlotte Pearson of the University of Arizona has refined the timeline for historical events in ancient Mesopotamia. First, the team members radiocarbon dated individual tree rings and analyzed tree ring data from timbers unearthed at archaeological sites in Turkey, in order to calculate precise dates for when the trees were felled. These dates helped the researchers to determine when the buildings had been constructed. Then those dates were linked to historical records from the sites that were tied to specific years in the Assyrian calendar. The scientists also evaluated Babylonian records of Venus, noting that sometimes the planet was hard to see because of haze in the atmosphere. They compared these observations with evidence of volcanic eruptions preserved in polar ice cores. The strongest match was found to be an eruption of the Aniakchak volcano in Alaska around 1628 or 1628 B.C. Combining the data, the researchers suggest that Babylon fell around 1587 B.C. , while severe drought between 1194 and 1192 B.C. may have contributed to the collapse of the Hittite Empire. “Single-year measurements of radiocarbon from calendar-dated tree rings offer new opportunities to refine and improve chronologies,” the researchers concluded. To read about evidence of spy craft in Mesopotamia, go to “In His Majesty’s Secret Service.”

issues.title: New Analysis of Hunter-Gatherer Remains Recovered on Danish Island
issues.summary: GOTHENBURG, SWEDEN—According to a report in La Brújula Verde, a team led by Anders Fischer […] The post New Analysis of Hunter-Gatherer Remains Recovered on Danish Island appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
GOTHENBURG, SWEDEN—According to a report in La Brújula Verde, a team led by Anders Fischer of the University of Gothenburg and John Meadows of the Leibniz Centre for Archaeology has analyzed Rødhals Man, the 6,000-year-old skeletal remains recovered from a midden on the Danish island of Sejerø in 1956. Previous genetic study of the bones revealed that Rødhals Man belonged to a group of western European hunter-gatherers. Analysis of carbon and nitrogen isotopes in his bones and teeth indicates that he ate a diet heavy in marine fish. Adjusting for the “old” carbon acquired through consumption of marine fish, the bones were radiocarbon dated to between about 3890 and 3770 B.C. , around the time that the first farmers appeared in Denmark. Layers of dentine in Rødhals Man’s teeth yielded additional information about his diet over time. During childhood, he consumed marine shellfish, flatfish, and eels. But in adolescence, the amount of protein from land sources in his diet increased beyond that usually observed in the remains of other Mesolithic hunter-fishers found in Denmark. It cannot be determined if this land food came from hunting and gathering, or from eating cows, sheep, and cereals raised and grown by farmers. The researchers suggest, however, that the land food was provided by farmers, since Rødhals Man was not also consuming freshwater fish, as inland hunter-gatherers were likely to do. Additionally, the team notes that the burial of Rødhals Man resembles that of the first farmers, including a frame made of flat stones. The researchers concluded that Rødhals Man may have adopted some of the farmers’ way of life, though he kept many of his ancestors’ traditions. Read the original scholarly article about this research in Antiquity. To read about population shifts between the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods in Denmark, go to “Ancient DNA Revolution: Danish Turnovers.”

The post New Analysis of Hunter-Gatherer Remains Recovered on Danish Island appeared first on Archaeology Magazine.

issues.title: Souvenir Collection May Have Begun 500,000 Years Ago
issues.summary: TEL AVIV, ISRAEL—Hominins may have begun collecting relics and keepsakes some 500,000 years ago, according […] The post Souvenir Collection May Have Begun 500,000 Years Ago appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
TEL AVIV, ISRAEL—Hominins may have begun collecting relics and keepsakes some 500,000 years ago, according to a statement released by Tel Aviv University. These possible souvenirs include small, colorful pebbles unearthed in Israel’s Qesem Cave, and handaxes made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological formations that were recovered in the Sakhnin Valley. Ran Barkai and Ella Assaf of Tel Aviv University and their colleagues said that tools showing signs of heavy use, whether resharpened or not, have been unearthed at several sites, such as Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave. These objects may have been kept for their aged appearance, the researchers explained. Just like modern keepsakes, the objects may have been retained in order to trigger memories of a place or personal experience. Use of such items over many generations may have increased evolutionary pressures on brain mechanisms involved with memory and sense of self, the researchers argue. Read the original scholarly article about this research in Evolutionary Anthropology. To read about stone balls found in Qesem Cave, go to “Around the World: Israel.”

issues.title: There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages
issues.summary: Yes, AI is causing all these outages, but not in the way you think.
issues.author: Jake Peterson
issues.content_html:
It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

AI is forcing companies to patch security flaws at historic rates

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Expect outages to become the norm

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

issues.title: Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Ukraine
issues.summary: Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our … Continue reading "Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Uk
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our world.

Our mission at RSE is to help Americans better know and understand our neighbors through travel. But when we bring travelers to another country, we also bring their dollars — dollars that would support Putin’s aggression. Therefore, as of today, we have canceled all 2022 tours that include a stop in Russia.

Of course, we will keep a close eye on unfolding events and monitor any travel impacts through the rest of Europe. But it is important to keep geographic realities in mind and remember that a war in Ukraine is as far from our European vacation dreams as a war in Guatemala would be from Texas or Florida. For 40 years now, we have lived, worked, and traveled through many periods of tragic warfare in lands far from where we lead our tours (and some closer). And at this time, we see no reason to change the rest of our travel and touring plans.

The tragic reality unfolding in Ukraine only reminds me how important it is for Americans to keep on traveling and to do so in a way that makes us better and more engaged citizens of our world. I’m flying to Europe next month for a 40-day trip through a dozen great cities from London to Athens — and I’m proud that thousands of my fellow travelers will experience the European trip of their dreams while having rich learning experiences far from home on a 2022 Rick Steves tour.

In the meantime, let’s be thankful for our blessings, support our nation’s leaders as they do their best to navigate this crisis, and keep the troubled corners of our world (Ukraine, Russia, Afghanistan, and more) in our thoughts and prayers.

—Rick

issues.title: The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way
issues.summary: At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me. For total novices like Shelley … Continue reading "The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me.

For total novices like Shelley and me, it’s wise to be proactive about health and safety. Here are some tips I learned along the way:

Good boots, liner socks, slippery powder, and moleskin for tender skin are essential. We kind of became gear geeks — investing in good day bags (Osprey), woolen clothes (socks, underwear, shirts), and great hiking shoes. I was never so thankful for a wool cap in Europe.

I was skeptical about a lot of “good ideas,” but two things I eventually appreciated were a daily baggie of trail mix and my metal water bottle. (I complained about its steep $40 price tag…but soon came to recognize it was a great value).

I must say, if the weather turned bad and it rained hard, I think much of the trail would become no fun at all. In fact, it would be dangerous. Hiking poles are essential, and even in perfect weather, I would have been worried about a stumble without my own trusty set.

Eat a solid breakfast. The one day we had breakfast with no protein, climbing was tougher.

Put on sunscreen, even if the weather’s bad.

After learning my lesson on other long hikes, I decided to be religious about stretching on the Tour du Mont Blanc from the start. I had a routine of six stretches and spent time throughout the day making sure I didn’t tighten up. Very important!

Don’t be a hero. If skin is getting hot, wrap it up. I did the entire TMB hike without a blister — and then just got one on purpose in the last two hours.

Good gear, smart and proactive ways to stay healthy, stretching, and taking it easy… it all worked just great.

I’ll be sharing more photos, stories, and tips from Mont Blanc on the Nov. 29 edition of Monday Night Travel. Want to come along? Register now for this fun — and free! — event.

issues.title: Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc
issues.summary: While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was … Continue reading "Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was the uphill part, and for others (with weak knees), it was going downhill. We just took it easy, with lots of little breaks.

For long climbs, steady, smaller steps are best. The trail could be really rocky, and I can’t imagine doing it without hiking poles. The trail signs were great, and apps made staying on the trail easy: Just follow the blue dot. And I got good use out of a top-quality printed map. (I’d spend time the night before reading up on the hike and familiarizing myself with the trail on the map.)

While the weather forecast looked threatening, we hiked six days (in September, during the last week of the season) and, thankfully, had only one hour of rain. Still, each day we’d pack rain gear, and we’d add on and take off layers as we gained and lost altitude. After four days, we had it sorted out, and it occurred to us rank beginners, “We’re getting good at this.”

As we were hiking in a big circle around a big clump of mountains and sleeping in charming towns each night, every day seemed to be up and over a daunting mountain pass. A nightly treat was a stroll under a milky blanket of stars.

I’ll be sharing more photos, stories, and tips from Mont Blanc on the Nov. 29 edition of Monday Night Travel. Want to come along? Register now for this fun — and free! — event.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends … Continue reading
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Hiking Europe’s Tour du Mont Blanc was a totally different slice of European culture for me: Coming upon a remote farmhouse-turned-thriving-cafe serving wonderful lunches…flowers and cows (with classic bells) scenically sprinkled throughout…and an esprit de corps where everyone is like family.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends with fellow hikers. It seemed like half the people on the trail were from the US, and I met lots of Seattleites.

And in the interest of hiking light, lunches were very simple — just a sandwich from the hotel, maybe a carrot, a piece of fruit, and water. But upon reaching the mid-day summit, lunch was a marmot’s banquet. (Speaking of marmots, we saw no wildlife except a couple of mice that had been squished under hiking boots on the trail.)

issues.title: New Godflesh & Jesu with Phoebe too
issues.summary: Some of the many reasons it’s been a great year for post-metal.
issues.author: Jeff Bergstrom
issues.content_html:
The great Jon Wurster (The Mountain Goats, The Bob Mould Band, Superchunk, The Best Show with Tom Scharpling) is a prolific drummer and one of the funniest people on earth. One of my favorite Wursterisms™ is that he utilizes the hashtag #rocknrollweirdness on Instagram when posting images of incongruous moments in rock n’ roll. Whether it’s a picture of The Who holding their Who Are You release party on the Hollywood set of the TV show Battlestar Galactica, Oasis hanging with Wesley Willis, or Motörhead drummer Philthy Animal Taylor and W.A.S.P. guitarist Chris Holmes having ice cream on a nice day, Wurster is a master curator of singular images of #rocknrollweirdness.

It’s rare for an instance of #rocknrollweirdness to land so profoundly with me that it gives me the energy to take finger-to-keyboard for the first time in years. Yet it recently came to my attention that master of heviosity Justin K. Broadrick was recently tapped by mainstream indie icon Phoebe Bridgers to play guitar on two tracks of her August 14, 2026 release Lost Weekend. Justin performs on track #5, “Bobby,” as well as on the ‘hidden’ track “Best Dressed” (track D17 on the vinyl and Track 00 on CD). Broadrick is involved with many different personal projects, each with their own particular signature sonic qualities, so it is important to note that he performs on these tracks under his Jesu moniker. And although I find his contributions to be buried under too many layers of over-production, the Broadrick aficionado can immediately recognize Jesu’s signature guitar sound in the first 15-seconds of “Bobby.” Lost Weekend was the Number 1 album in the UK and debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200. This is almost definitely the first time Justin has been that high in the charts.

But there was more! Phoebe Bridgers then released “On Video,” her song from the new A24 film Primetime. You can listen to it below. Oh and guess what? Justin Broadrick played bass and guitar on that song. As you probably know by now, Phoebe is also in the movie, and has been playing the song on tour.

These aren’t the first instances that Justin and Phoebe’s careers have intersected. Back in 2021, again under the Jesu moniker, Justin remixed Phoebe’s Boygenius bandmate Julien Baker’s track “Favor.” Justin not only executed the remix, but he also played guitars on the track which also features Phoebe Bridgers (and Lucy Dacus) on backing vocals. Check that track out below.

In other Justin K. Broadrick news, we’ve had a few months to let it sink in that the mighty Godflesh has retired from touring due to ongoing health issues plaguing Justin. The good news is that prior to his tour-ending surgery, Justin and Benny had an entire new Godflesh album pretty much already in the can. The album, entitled Decay, dropped on September 25 via Relapse Records and is available in all the formats, including vinyl in all kinds of colors and patterns.

Fortunately, all of the recordings for Decay were completed long before the surgery, vocals included… although the back end of a couple of songs were recorded with the hernia itself, and that was a struggle. I was already aware that the GODFLESH shout, so to speak, was exacerbating the hernia greatly, as was every GODFLESH performance in the lead-up to the surgery once the hernia appeared, and the hernia was mostly caused by year upon year of shouting in GODFLESH. The album was mixed post-surgery, and while I was still in some pain and considerable discomfort, but fortunately GODFLESH is generally me expressing my pain, albeit [usually] mental, philosophical and existential, whereas this was physical pain.

You can listen to “Living/Ending” below and do some heavy duty ordering of the vinyl.

I interviewed Justin back in 2014 and would love to interview him again someday to discuss all of his projects BUT Godflesh. Until that happens, both Guitar World and The Guardian have published very good interviews with him that do a great job bringing fans up to speed with the current state of Justin’s world.

See also: it’s been a great year for post-metal.

issues.title: 5 Artists We Want to See at Louder Than Life 2026
issues.summary: Louder Than Life’s 2026 edition is coming. Check out who we’re excited to see.
issues.author: BrooklynVegan Staff
issues.content_html:
Louder Than Life‘s 2026 edition is this weekend: September 17-20 at Kentucky Expo Center in Louisville, KY. As always, we’re figuring out who we most don’t want to miss. We’ll of course be sticking around for big headliners Tool, Iron Maiden, and My Chemical Romance, but the variety of acts we’re excited about across punk and metal genres this year is vast. Here are five artists that we’re especially looking forward to:

Circa Survive

As Andrew Sacherwrote when the band first announced their return:

Circa Survive went on “indefinite hiatus” in 2022, which came as bummer news considering they had just released some of the best music of their career, and the prospect of a reunion didn’t look very good after singer Anthony Greensaid on HardLore in December that what happened in 2022 was more of a “breakup” than a “hiatus” and added, “I don’t know if the band is ever going to do anything ever again… And even if it did, it wouldn’t be the same. It just wouldn’t.” So, it comes as a nice surprise that Circa Survive just announced their first show in nearly five years! They’ll be playing Louisville’s Louder Than Life festival in September, and Anthony Green will be pulling double duty at that fest, as L.S. Dunes are playing too. (Everyone in L.S. Dunes will be pulling double duty at that fest, as My Chemical Romance, Coheed & Cambria, and Thursday are playing too.

We can’t wait!

Haywire

Boston punks Haywire are one of the most exciting, most fun, and fastest rising hardcore bands of recent times, with banger after banger, and with more on the way soon, as they recently announced their second full-length album, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, due October 2 via their new label home, Roadrunner Records. Their raucous live shows continue to be unmissable, whether in a basement, a boxing ring, a club, or at a fest. See you in the pit.

Missing Link

Staying on the fest’s Friday hardcore stage for a second: playing before Haywire and the recently-announed, no-longer secret guest Knocked Loose, we want to highlight NY heavy hardcore band Missing Link whose intesity blows us away every time we get the chance to catch them (including sometimes with Haywire). Great live show. Don’t mess up and miss them in Louisville.

Hot Mulligan

Louder than Life also brings the pop punk, and the post-hardcore and emo-leaning Lansing, Michigan band Hot Mulligan are doing it better than most right now. Now four full lengths into their career, the band has become a festival staple, somtimes a rare mosh pit-inducing band on a lineup (like when we saw them at Gov Ball and Lolla), and sometimes right where they belong like in between Alkaline Trio and Jimmy Eat World in Louisville in Thursday. Always a super fun time, we can’t get enough of their energy, their humor, and their infectious hooks.

Danzig

The man, the myth, the legend. Danzig on this year’s fest officially brings it over the top for this Danzig-obsesed writer.

Check out the entire lineup HERE, and have fun this weekend.

issues.title: Haywire sign to Roadrunner, announce new LP & video, threw $$ into the crowd at Sound & Fury, keep touring & stuff (BV-exclusive vinyl)
issues.summary: The album was produced by Mat from Citizen and mixed by Taylor Young whose band God’s Hate meanwhile surprised the world with a surprise Sound & Fury set followed by a surprise new EP.
issues.author: BrooklynVegan Staff
issues.content_html:
Boston punks Haywire are one of the fastest rising hardcore bands of recent times, and now they’ve announced their second full-length album, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, due October 2 via their new label home, Roadrunner Records. Citizen‘s Mat Kerekes produced the album. Taylor Young mixed it at The Pit. The album was recorded over three months in Leeds, UK and Toledo, OH, and features appearances from members of Nothing and The Aggrolites, along with other friends of the band.

We’ve teamed up with the band for a BrooklynVegan-exclusive vinyl variant of I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, limited to just 300 copies. Pre-order now in the BV Shop.

The first single from I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye is “Interstate Love Affair,” which comes with a Luis Hernandez-directed video. Watch it below.

It follows Haywire’s 2024 great releases, the Conditioned for Demolition LP and For Better or for Worse EP, and 2025 splits with No Guard and Dropkick Murphys ( “Citizen I.C.E.” included).

Constantly on the road (and in our feeds), last year Haywire completed a goal of playing all 50 states, and played an amazing tour with Drain, No Pressure and Secret World. They’re taking a short unexpected break though. They announced this morning that their Australia tour this week is postponed till later in the year, but they’ll be touring again in the US in September, including a Milwaukee show supporting Turnstile, a run opening for Circle Jerks, and appearances at Louder Than Life, Riot Fest, Four Chord Music Festival and CBGB Fest. October brings Aftershock, Furnace Fest, a free University of Connecticut show and Sick New World, followed by Pressure Point Fest and Warped Tour in November.

Haywire revealed that they’d signed to Roadrunner just ahead of this past weekend’s Sound & Fury fest, then celebrated their new record deal by throwing $5,000 in cash into the crowd during their set on Sunday. Watch footage below.

Sunday at Sound & Fury also included a surprise split set from Twitching Tongues and God’s Hate, both bands of brothers Colin and Taylor Young (the same Taylor who worked on the new Haywire album) (and the new Terror record and a million other records). A day after the surprise appearance, God’s Hate revealed that they were ending their hiatus with a new three-song Won’t Be Disgraced EP.

Mat Kerekes’ band Citizen, meanwhile, just released the great new album Halcyon Blues, and we’ve also got a BrooklynVegan-exclusive “Ether” vinyl variant limited to 400 copies.

Again, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye is out October 2 via Roadrunner, and the BrooklynVegan-exclusive vinyl is limited to 300 copies. Here’s the cover art:

issues.title: Trump admin orders Kalshi to halt wagers on what words Trump will say
issues.summary: CFTC: Kalshi bets may violate US ban on contracts that can be easily manipulated.
issues.author: Jon Brodkin
issues.content_html:
The Trump administration ordered prediction market Kalshi to stop offering event contracts that pay out based on whether President Trump will say a specific word before a particular date. Kalshi halted trading in the contracts while the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) conducts a review into whether the Trump mention contracts violate federal law.

CNBC reported yesterday that "Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of 'mention' contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC." Kalshi told media outlets that it is complying with the CFTC order.

The markets taken down by Kalshi allowed users to wager on whether Trump would say certain words, including nicknames and the names of countries and companies. A similar expired event contract that can still be viewed on Kalshi's website asked whether Trump would use the nicknames "Marjorie Traitor Greene," "Sleepy Joe," and "Whack Job" or "Wack Job" before April 2026.

issues.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
issues.summary: Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it's only accelerating.
issues.author: Beth Mole
issues.content_html:
International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings.

After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it "shameful" and a "national embarrassment." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases, more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases. There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.

But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic.

issues.title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
issues.summary: With MyMems , Wright says he wants to "turn the simulation inward."
issues.author: Kyle Orland
issues.content_html:
The computer gaming world hasn't heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright's subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players' memories.

MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright's previous projects by "turn[ing] the simulation inward," as Wright's Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

“If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?" Wright says by way of example in the release. "If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?"

issues.title: It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo
issues.summary: This commuter bike will have you blazing through streets without any range anxiety.
issues.author: Jacob May
issues.content_html:
I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?”

These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark.

But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo. I didn't experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized's 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home.

issues.title: DD415 / MBA: school of profit
issues.summary: Issue 415: MBA: school of profit – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
When I finished high school and started exploring my study options back in Germany, I came across the then-new MBA (Master of Business Administration) and found it a bit baffling. I thought you first had to master a craft, then turn it into a business. The MBA seemed to suggest that the craft was not important and you could just learn how to run any business. The course description was thick with English jargon, which didn’t help. I vaguely remember someone describing it as learning how to make more money without producing anything.

That description came back to me while reading a recent opinion piece by Christopher Marquis, who has spent more than 20 years teaching at famous business schools. His verdict on his own industry: business schools can’t be repaired; it’s time to shut them down.

“I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system – they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to ‘fix’ business schools. We need to abolish them.”

Marquis points to research showing that managers with business degrees cut wages, yet didn’t become any more productive. He concludes:

“What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer – value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.”

He also puts into words what I couldn’t as an adolescent:

“A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice – undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they ‘need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.’”

The tension is usually glossed over with the comforting ‘win-win’ story:

“These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of ‘stakeholder capitalism’: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.”

So what should we teach instead? Marquis points to the idea of “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business:

“Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from ‘How do we maximize shareholder value?’ to ‘How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward – and which should we strengthen?’”

“The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.”

To me, this is what rethinking our economic system could look like at its most basic level. An ethics elective won’t do it. The work starts with how we teach people to think about power and capital: how currently both tend to accumulate at the top, while the ecological and social mess gets filed under ‘externalities’ and left for future generations to sort out.

We need people who can read a balance sheet and run a payroll, of course. But we could also teach them to build co-operatives, strengthen communities and organise around shared interests. Extracting value for personal gain is one model of doing business, with a long track record of consequences, but certainly not the only one.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD414 / Organising the discontent
issues.summary: Issue 414: Organising the discontent – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
I can still feel it – the collective exhale. Ann Friedman calls it ‘the great unclenching’, and Rebecca Solnit writes that a win for democracy of this size deserves a proper celebration. Fair enough.

But while the rest of us were glued to swing-state maps, something remarkable was unfolding in a corner of Europe that rarely makes our news feeds.

In Serbia, a movement led by students forced snap elections and then won them outright, ending more than a decade of autocratic rule. It started in 2024, when a train station canopy collapsed and killed 16 people. To many Serbians, it was corruption made visible. Students blockaded their universities and demanded accountability. Within months, farmers, actors, judges and pensioners had joined them, filling city squares in some of the largest protests the country has ever seen.

What’s amazing is that this ideologically mixed movement hasn’t splintered into rival factions. Instead, it has built a shared identity without a single face on the poster. Its electoral list had no leader. The 250 candidates on the ballot papers were nominated, grilled and voted on by student plenums – open assemblies at each university. This produced something that represents a decent slice of the country: a cardiologist, a grammar school teacher, a coal miner, a social worker, a former central bank governor and, for good measure, a retired basketball star.

I’ve been a fan of citizens’ assemblies for years (see DD220). There is lots of evidence that ordinary people, given time, reliable information and a genuine stake in the outcome, can make remarkably good and fair decisions. Serbia’s plenums aren’t a textbook citizens’ assembly – nobody was picked by lottery – but they share the spirit. The power to choose sat with big, messy rooms full of people. And few people have a bigger stake in the outcome than students, who’ll be living with the results long after today’s power brokers have retired to their holiday homes.

It’s hard not to see echoes of Serbia in the Gen Z protests spreading across the world. Of course, some protests turn ugly, and the looting and vandalism deserve condemnation. But the media is often far more interested in pictures of ghouls smashing shop windows than in understanding why so many people took to the streets in the first place, why so many young people can’t see a future worth studying for. Serbia shows what that frustration can build once it gets organised.

The proof is in the pudding, of course. Leaderless movements can be great at opposing and clumsy at governing. Decision-making by committee isn’t pretty. Consensus takes time, patience and a healthy tolerance for disagreement. But there’s something very inspiring about a political movement that started by asking who should represent it, not who should lead it.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD413 / The lost art of having people over
issues.summary: Issue 413: The lost art of having people over – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
As a kid, I loved our big lunch and dinner parties. There are photos of 30-odd people – friends, family, neighbours – squeezed into our apartment on borrowed chairs around tables that didn’t match. It was chaotic, loud and a lot of fun. They didn’t happen nearly often enough, and I sometimes wonder why something we all enjoyed so much was saved for birthdays and other rare occasions.

Over the years, we’ve actually made them rarer still. Derek Thompson has the numbers to prove it:

“In the last 30 years, Americans have seen double-digit declines in practically every measure of socializing. ... The share of Americans who say they host friends or family at their home at least monthly has fallen from 42 percent in 1975 to 12 percent in 2026 – a 70 percent collapse in a half-century.”

These days, the convenience economy has made staying in so easy that inviting people over feels like a self-inflicted chore.

Elizabeth Oldfield went the other way. For more than a decade, she and her husband have hosted shared dinners every other week, first squeezing eight people around a table in a tiny London flat, now feeding up to 16 at a time in their community house. By her count, around 1,500 people have come through the door. The trick, she says, is putting it in the calendar and refusing to renegotiate:

“This bizarre culture of possessive individualism will always give us reasons not to be together, so sometimes it takes a strong container to push back. ... Always keeping our options open and autonomy over our time sounds good but leaves us lonely and disoriented. Make a commitment and your future self will thank you.”

I love how unbothered she is about the state of the house. As her husband puts it, hospitality is ”not the same as entertaining”:

“To be invited into someone else’s imperfect house is, it turns out, a blessing. I do not tend to find very primped, spotless, Instagram-ready homes especially relaxing to be in. If we are going to move towards each other and build real community we have to let go of the desire to impress people.”

I wrote about the radical act of regular open-door dinners a while back (DD331), and Oldfield’s dinners are about the most practical version of that idea I’ve come across. (Do check out her list of tips in the essay.)

So why don’t more of us do it? Thompson has a pretty good theory:

“Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. ... Compared to TikTok, a dinner party is a terrible leisure technology. It requires matching schedules, cleaning the house, buying food, accommodating children and allergies, tolerating awkwardness, and taking the risk that the evening is mediocre. By contrast, what does television ask of us? Nothing. TikTok? Even less.”

When I look at those old photos and my mum’s kitchen, I notice who’s doing the cooking. Those parties ran on a lot of unpaid labour, mostly by women, and Thompson points out that the social calendar frayed when they took on paid work and the men didn’t pick up the slack. Today’s cost-of-living pressures and two exhausted working parents make the couch and screens combo look very appealing.

Oldfield offers us a way back that doesn’t require a kitchen full of women doing all the work and stressing about being a perfect host. Her dinners run on cheap dahl and wine from Lidl. Guests chop, set the table and stay for the clean-up. Nobody performs, nobody keeps score, and somehow everyone leaves a little less alone.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD412 / Breaking up with Gmail
issues.summary: Issue 412: Breaking up with Gmail – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
On a visit to Google’s HQ in Mountain View in 2007, I watched people run almost their entire working lives out of a browser. Gmail was still new-ish, and the Googlers I met were doing clever things with labels, aliases and filters that made my Outlook setup look like an old filing cabinet.

When Google started offering a paid Gmail version with custom domains, I made the move and Gmail slowly became the app I spent most of my days in. Docs, Sheets and Google Maps followed.

By the time I started feeling uneasy about Google, I was thoroughly entangled. The thought of dragging hundreds of thousands of emails somewhere else, and giving up some of Gmail’s then-unique features, sat in the too-hard basket for almost a decade.

But earlier this month, a friend reminded me of the EFF’s Opt Out October, and that finally gave me the nudge. I know plenty of you are in the same boat, so here’s a quick rundown of how it went.

My emails turned out to be the easy part, which is annoying given how long I spent dreading it. My shortlist came down to Proton, Fastmail* and iCloud. I liked Proton a lot when I trialled it, but its (admirable) emphasis on security means calendars and contacts won’t sync with the native apps on my iPhone. iCloud now supports custom domains, and since I’m already deep inside Apple’s walled garden, it would have been the path of least resistance. It would also have meant handing more money to a different Big Tech company.

So I went with Fastmail, a small Melbourne company (represent!) with a solid reputation. Its migration tool pulled everything across via IMAP in a few hours and mirrored my Gmail labels. On my laptop I use the web interface and don’t miss a single feature. On my iPhone, I can still use the native Calendar and Contacts apps, and Fastmail’s own app for email (it’s good). When I made a mistake during my custom domain setup, an actual human replied to my support request within a day with an answer that helped. I’d forgotten that was possible.

Google itself isn’t disappearing from my life any time soon, though. Too many clients and collaborators live in Docs and Sheets. But, I learned that once you remove your custom domain from Google Workspace, it takes Google about 20 days to ‘release’ it, after which you can sign up for a free Google account with that same custom email address.

What you can’t do is bring your other stuff with you. Ugh. Drive files have to be exported and re-uploaded into the new account. Maps and YouTube have no migration path at all, so I’m rebuilding those from scratch, one saved café at a time. Google Maps’ reviews are hard to beat, sorry Apple.

So yeah, Google does remain a fixture for a handful of ‘free’ apps. But the elephant in the room – my big fat inbox – walked out the door far more willingly than I’d expected. All up, it took a few hours over a couple of weekends. Years of dread, overcome by two weekends of mild admin. Shoulda done it ages ago. (And yet, I was just in time.)

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.author: Ambika Natarajan
issues.content_html: Compared to the countries of Western Europe such as the United Kingdom and France, the women's movement in the 19th century started late in the Habsburg Empire. Perhaps because, unlike in other countries, certain landowning and tax-paying women had the right to vote, access education, and participate in public life in the Habsburg Empire. Moreover, the Industrial Revolution also started late in the Habsburg Empire compared to Western Europe. Nevertheless, in the second half of the 19th century, a women's movement developed around Vienna that would go on to inform feminism in the Republic of Austria after the collapse of the Habsburg Empire in 1918.
